News.title: Exact number of days warm 25C weather will last in parts of UK as Met Office confirms ‘final taste of summer’
News.content:
Next

BRITS are set to bask in the “final taste of summer” over the next few days as the Met Office predicts warm and sunny weather.

Cooler temperatures and rainy conditions have marked the beginning of autumn after record-breaking highs this summer.

However, parts of the UK are set to enjoy 25C highs on Monday and Tuesday.



According to the Met Office: “These temperatures would be notably warm for late September and could offer a final taste of summer before autumn becomes more firmly established.”



This follows changeable conditions and lows of 12C and 13C recorded in parts of the country throughout September.

Before the sunny spells at the beginning of the week, Brits are forecast to see slightly gloomier conditions over the weekend.



Clouds and patchy rain will continue to linger across southern England and Wales today, with sunny spells and blustery showers expected elsewhere.

Dry but cloudy conditions can be expected for tomorrow as the temperatures stay between the low teens and early twenties throughout the day.

Sunnier skies will then return on Monday as temperatures reach highs of 25C in London, Reading and surrounding areas by 4pm.

Large parts of the country, including Birmingham, Milton Keynes, Peterborough and Cambirdge are also forecast for warmer temperatures, with highs of 24C expected on Monday.



Tuesday afternoon will see even more locations enjoy the hotter conditions, with Cambridge, London, Peterborough and parts of the southeast anticipating 25C highs.

News.title: Moment woman joins police chase after giving officer a lift in her tiny Nissan Micra as cop then makes arrest
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a cop hitches a ride in a woman’s tiny Nissan Micra while chasing down and arresting a crook.

The officer had been pursuing erratic Jacob Roberts in South Wales when he was forced to jump in a bystander’s car to catch up.



Police footage captured the initial car chase, with Roberts swerving through narrow streets in Abercwmboi, with officers close behind.

Roberts eventually meets a dead end and runs out of foot.



The officer chases after him across roads and through a park, before stumbling upon the helpful driver.

The woman, driving a red Nissan Micra, responded to the copper’s calls by saying “Get in”.

She can then be heard asking “Where to?”

The officer eventually catches up to the criminal and arrests him shortly after.



People have been quick to hail the woman a hero, with many calling her a “legend”.

One person said: “That member of the public is amazing.

“She’s not a police officer she doesn’t have pursuit training yet was happy to put herself at considerable risk to help the police catch this man.”



Another said: “What a star the female driver was to offer help.”

A third said: “Somebody buy that officer and the assistant in the Micra a well earned pint.”

Roberts, from Mountain Ash, was jailed for one year and two months for dangerous driving and disqualified from driving for three years.

Appearing at Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court on September 16, he was sentenced to dangerous driving, driving whilst disqualified, driving without insurance, failure to stop after a road accident, criminal damage to property, and possession of controlled Class B drugs.

South Wales Police said in an online statement: “When the van’s driver, 25-year-old Jacob Roberts, was asked to pull over, he instead drove off.



“During the pursuit, he twice reverse-rammed the pursuing police car, collided with parked cars, and showed a disregard for pedestrians going about their business.

“After running into a dead end just off Lewis Street, Aberaman, Roberts instead tried to flee on foot – but a police officer, in all his kit, followed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“And when the driver of a red Nissan spotted the officer, she offered him a lift to help him catch up with Roberts even sooner.

“Roberts has now been sentenced for offences including dangerous driving, driving while disqualified, driving without insurance, failure to stop after a road accident, criminal damage and possession of a controlled class B drug.”

News.title: Satellite pictures show Iran rebuilding secretive nuclear base at alarming rate as Putin protects ally from monitoring
News.content:
Next

DISTURBING satellite pics reveal that Iran is rapidly rebuilding a nuclear base just months after Israeli forces blitzed the bunker.

The chilling construction surge comes as Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping block a UN motion to monitor whether Iran is violating its pact not to develop the deadly weapons.



Donald Trump launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran in part to stop the development of nukes in the Middle East.

Previous peace deals have fallen to pieces in part because Iranian mullahs refuse to give up their nuclear development programmes as US drones pound facilities across the region.



Now, chilling satellite images taken on Sunday show that the Iranian regime is ploughing ahead with its deadly ambitions.

Bulldozers, cranes, concrete mixers and dump trucks can be seen swarming around the sprawling Taleghan 2 facility.



Israel first bombed the site back in October 2024 before blasting it again in March.

A large black tarpaulin is stretched over the site to conceal the warbase from prying enemy eyes.

New concrete defences are also springing up around the facility in anticipation of another attack, according to analysis by David Albright, a former UN nuclear weapons inspector.

The photos throw fresh scrutiny on Tehran’s operations at Taleghan 2 – which has long been suspected of harbouring nuclear development facilities.



“What is clear is that Iran remains committed to rebuilding this facility,”, said Institute for Science and International Security who analysed the pictures.

The Washington-based institute described the development as “deeply concerning” because of the base’s previous role in nuclear weapons research.

The bunker formed part of Iran’s secret Amad programme – a plot to develop nukes in the early 2000s.



US intelligence believes the scheme shut down in 2003 – but experts say the bunker still houses a special chamber reinforced for explosive nuclear experiments.

Further scrutiny of the site, however, has been vetoed by Russian tyrant Putin and Chinese dictator Jinping at a UN Security Council on Thursday.

The allies blocked a motion brought forward by the US to continue monitoring Iran’s nuclear activity.

The regime thanked the two tyrants for shutting down what it called a “politically motivated” draft from the US.

“Iran deeply appreciates Russia and China for their consistent and principled positions and decisive actions today,” the regime posted on X.



But Jennifer Locetta, deputy US ambassador to the UN, warned that lifting the ban opened a “monitoring gap” which “only benefits the Iranian regime”.

A worrying uptick in activity has also been spotted around Iran’s notorious Pickaxe Mountain.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Washington fears the regime is building an impenetrable nuclear plant under 300ft of solid granite.

Experts believe the doomsday mountain is the number one target in the crosshairs for destruction by Donald Trump.

News.title: Hundreds of rogue drones target UK bases as Putin warns Brit military facilities are targets and ‘is set to expand war’
News.content:
Next

HUNDREDS of rogue drones are targeting British army bases as Vladimir Putin looks set to expand Kremlin’s war across Europe.

It comes as the flailing tyrant warned that UK military facilities in Ukraine are considered “legitimate targets” for Russian missile and drone strikes.



Brit bases have been faced with drone incidents on a nearly daily basis in the last year, as tensions with Russia and Iran ramp up.

Around 340 security breaches involving the unmanned vehicles were reported in the year up to August 2026, according to a Freedom of Information request by the Independent.



The Ministry of Defence declined to say who was behind the threats, but they come amid escalating tensions between Moscow and Nato.

There were 250 incidents in 2025, nearly double the 126 a year earlier.

An MoD spokesperson said: “The public should be reassured that the UK and its allies remain vigilant against potential threats.

“Adversaries should be in no doubt about this Government’s resolve to stand against aggression towards the UK and our allies.”

They added that Russia is “constantly probing us and testing” the UK and that the government does not believe Putin is looking for a “direct confrontation” with Nato.

Poland’s Donald Tusk, however, has warned that Russia is planning missile strikes, which would be described as “accidental” by the Kremlin to test the alliance.



Western intelligence officials believe Putin is preparing a huge “stealth mobilisation” of some 300,000 troops to feed into his brutal campaign.

Leaders across the continent warned attacks are likely to focus on more intensive drone and missile launches into Nato territory to test resolve.

Constant probing of the alliance’s eastern flank will be combined with hybrid strikes on key infrastructure by Russian agents, plus threats to undersea pipelines and communication cables.



French President Emmanuel Macron announced a plan to protect the nation’s critical infrastructure and defence industries from sabotage.

Alliance countries are sworn to strike back if any member state is attacked.

It comes as experts have warned that Britain must prepare for Russian drones to swarm our skies.

The alleged attempted strike on Boris Johnson’s train was just a warning shot as Moscow draws the UK into a direct “militarised confrontation” that could erupt at any moment.

Speaking to Sam Homewood in The Sun’s new studio, military analyst Michael Clarke told The Sun: “Russia is getting very, very close to committing real violence against the rest of us, not just the Ukrainians.



“What they’re trying to say is, ‘you’re playing with fire. We’re on the road to war’.”

Ex-PM Mr Johnson was travelling close to the Polish border in Ukraine when the service behind his was blown up by Russian forces on Sunday.

Kremlin firebrand Dmitry Medvedev had hinted about Moscow targeting such trains in a sinister threat just days earlier.



The former Russian President branded European leaders “terrorist sponsors” for their support of Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky and vowed “retribution”.

Medvedev tied up his warning with the chilling message: “And they often travel to Kyiv by train…”

Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russian strikes were hitting closer to NATO and EU member Poland.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Putin’s terror is literally knocking on the doors of the European Union and NATO,” he said.

Putin is desperately trying to thwart European support of Ukraine as he prepares to strike Ukraine in the deadliest winter blitz yet.

News.title: Trump announces bombshell deal to take ‘permanent control’ over Greenland’s security and ban ‘all adversaries forever’
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump has struck a bombshell deal with Denmark giving the US “permanent” control over Greenland’s security.

The deal is set to bar adversaries like Russia, China and other non-Nato members from having bases or troops on the strategic Atlantic island.



Trump said it will guarantee America will “forever have complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland” for security.

He added that the US would “immediately” start ramping up its military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory.



The president’s comments give the impression the US now has sole responsibility for Greenland’s security – however, an interview by Marco Rubio with Fox News wasn’t as strong.

The Secretary of State told the outlet that the agreement now gives Washington permanent military rights on the island at zero cost to the American taxpayer.

A senior official said it will give the US access, basing and overflight rights on the island, but stops short of transferring sovereignty.

Trump said: “We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction.



“This solution is a great one for the United States of America, Denmark, Greenland, and all of our Allies.

“We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land.

“We will be very protective of it! This is a dream come true for the United States of America, one that is very important, historic, and special.”

Additional details about the agreement were not immediately disclosed.

Greenland PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it is “gratifying” to announce a deal that will strengthen Greenland’s security and the Western alliance.



He added: “The agreement recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in international cooperation. It is for the benefit of us all.”

Danish leader Mette Frederiksen said she was “pleased” with the deal, which will “strengthen common security” interests in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

Trump has been insistent that Greenland is crucial for US security since his return to the White House, at one point refusing to rule out a forceful takeover.

It was a flashpoint for the Nato alliance, with Denmark and Greenland repeatedly condemning US sovereignty efforts.

But Trump’s post suggests an understanding may have finally been reached to bring an end to the saga.



He said: “For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation. This is an ‘Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end!

“We are very honored and proud of what has just taken place, and everything agreed to today will be cherished by the American People.”

News.title: Fury as MPs ‘waste time’ investigating UK’s ‘dismal’ Eurovision record instead of focusing on economy and migration
News.content:
Next

A WESTMINSTER inquiry into Britain’s Eurovision flops has been dubbed a waste of MPs’ time.

The Commons Culture Committee is probing the UK’s “dismal” performance.



But it has been blasted over its proposals to ask BBC figures and music experts to give evidence in Parliament.

Campaigners say MPs should not be focusing on trivial issues when Britain faces challenges on the economy and migration.



William Yarwood, of the TaxPayers’ Alliance, said: “Britain has soaring debt and a record-high tax burden.

“Yet MPs have decided that the urgent national question is why we’re rubbish at Eurovision.

“They should get back to scrutinising things taxpayers pay them to worry about.”

British entrant Sam Battle, aka Look Mum No Computer, finished last with one point in May.

James Newman got nul points in 2021.

Sam Ryder is the only successful British act this decade, finishing second in 2022.



Committee chairman Dame Caroline Dinenage said: “We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant and on what basis.

“And whether our dismal record in recent years is the result of bad song choice, weak performance or something else.”

News.title: Britain faces fresh demands from Caribbean to pay slavery reparations despite No10 insisting it won’t hand over any cash
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN is facing fresh demands from the Caribbean to pay slavery reparations – despite Number Ten insisting it will not hand over any cash.

Barbados PM Mia Mottley has this week been corralling neighbouring countries ahead of an ambush at the Commonwealth summit being hosted in Antigua.



At a meeting on Thursday they agreed to launch a bid to pursue the issue at November’s annual get-together.

The Caribbean Community confirmed they were “preparing to advance reparations on the agenda of the upcoming 28th Commonwealth heads of government meeting.”



Member countries have long demanded TRILLIONS from the United Kingdom as payback for the transatlantic slave trade.

After participating in the vile practice, Britain went on to abolish slavery in the 19th century and fought to end it across the Empire.

But Mr Burnham is set to continue the UK’s long-standing position of rebuffing the reparation demands.

A Downing Street spokesman said last night: “The transatlantic slave trade was abhorrent. We fully recognise its horrific impacts and the ongoing strength of feeling it arouses.

“The UK’s position is clear: we do not and will not pay reparations.

“The UK is committed to continued dialogue with all our partners on legacies of the past.



Yet the issue of slavery could make the summit uncomfortable for the King who is once again expected to attend.

While dodging the issue of reparations, Charles acknowledged how “painful” the problems of the past were still felt by affected countries.

Earlier this month Jamaica piled pressure on the monarch over cash payments as the country’s culture minister delivered a petition to Buckingham Palace.

Mr Burnham could face similar lobbying when he attends the United Nations in New York next week.

Reform’s Robert Jenrick said: “Reform are putting these countries on notice: if they persist we will suspend all visas.



“The UK sacrificed thousands of lives and billions of pounds ending the slave trade.

“We will not allow other countries to rewrite our history.”

News.title: Knifeman drank dangerous mix of poppy seed tea and vodka before slitting toddler’s throat and slashing child’s face
News.content:
BLADE HORROR Knifeman drank dangerous mix of poppy seed tea and vodka before slitting toddler’s throat and slashing child’s face







Next

A MAN who stabbed a woman and slashed two children was found to have been drinking poppy seed tea and vodka before the horror attack.

Kulvinder Ram, 50, cut the woman’s neck, caused a gaping neck wound to a toddler and slashed the face of an eight-year-old girl.



Ram said he was a habitual drinker of tea made from unwashed poppy seeds and a small amount of morphine was found in his blood.

On the horrific afternoon of October 25, 2024, he was hearing voices after drinking vodka and the tea when he unleashed the attack.



The woman victim had run out of the house with a visible cut to her neck and shouted that Ram was killing her, saying “my baby, my baby”, in reference to the boy inside.

Ram was detained at the scene by an off-duty officer who had been walking home from work when he spotted a woman and her daughter covered in blood.



From a distance, Special Police Sergeant Seff Serroukh thought he was witnessing a Halloween prank, but as he got closer he realised the severity of what was in front of him.

Mr Serroukh said: “I quickly ran towards them and was immediately struck by the extent of their injuries and the amount of blood.



“When I became aware children were involved, I knew I had to act quickly.

“I had no safety equipment, no colleagues to assist, but as a father and a police officer, it was just a natural instinct to respond without hesitation, even without knowing the risk.”

The young boy was found inside the house on top of the dining-room table covered in blood and with a gaping wound to the neck.

All three victims suffered injuries that were so serious they required surgery.

Ram had undiagnosed schizophrenia at the time of the attack and started to believe that he was being watched by cameras.



He had grown increasingly paranoid and erratic, threatening to kill one of the victims two weeks before.

The court heard he was suffering from delusions involving black magic and had auditory hallucinations.

The woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, addressed the defendant directly in a victim impact statement read to the court.

In it, she said: “I don’t know how we got here. Your actions have changed everything.”

Describing physical and emotional scars, she said: “I have been left with a scar to the left-hand side of the neck. Every time I look at the scar in the mirror, I feel upset.



“My daughter has now got scarring to the left-hand side of her face, which will be there for life.

“What happened to me I can bear it but this should never have happened to my daughter. My son has been left with scarring around his neck.”

Ram was found guilty of the attempted murders of the woman and two-year-old boy and causing grievous bodily harm to the girl following a four-week trial at the Old Bailey in May.

Detective Constable Lewis Whitlock, of Scotland Yard, said: “This is a particularly distressing case and my thoughts remain with the victims as they continue to process what happened that day.

“Our investigation left us with no doubt that Ram intended to kill those he targeted.



“I must also recognise the role of SPS Serroukh, who ran towards danger without any hesitation for his own personal safety.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Without him, I have no doubt that Ram would have gone on to inflict further and most likely fatal injuries.

“Similarly, a member of the public who ran into the house and attempted to stem the bleeding of one of the victims played a major role in saving their life. Again, his efforts should be applauded and we hope he recognises how grateful we are for his intervention.”

News.title: Desperate search for swimmer killed in horror shark attack at Sorrento Beach enters second day
News.content:
Desperate search for swimmer killed in horror shark attack at Sorrento Beach enters second day

The search for a 63-year-old swimmer continues as Sorrento Beach remains closed after the horror shark attack on Friday - beaches in the area remain closed while emergency services work to locate the man

View 4 Images The search has entered a second day as emergency services contend with adverse weather conditions (Image: 9News)

The search for a swimmer killed in a shark attack in Perth has entered it second day.

‌



Emergency services were called to the scene at Sorrento Beach, just to the north of the city centre, at 10.15am on Friday following frantic calls for help.Within hours, police confirmed a man who had been swimming with a friend about 15m from the shore had died as the result of a shark attack.

‌



Responders, including Water Police and the Police Air Wing, launched a major search operation on Friday, which remains ongoing.

‌



View 4 Images Police at the scene (Image: 9News)

Two women found dead after being thrown from jet ski in Utah READ MORE :

Suffolk Police investigating 'disgusting' post about death of missing toddler Noah Woods READ MORE :

"The 63-year-old male swimmer has not been located. Police conducted a search of the shoreline this morning (Saturday)," a WA Police spokesperson said on Saturday.

"A WA Police Force Water Police vessel will remain in the area today, weather permitting. Beaches in the area remain closed."

‌



A nurse who was off-duty and visiting the beach at the time of the attack told 9News she saw the man being “mauled” in the water. She recalled: “I’m a nurse, so I mean I obviously see a lot of gruesome stuff, but to see somebody being mauled to death in the water in front of me is pretty hard to clock.”

View 4 Images Life guards and police continue their search (Image: 9News)

Sharks sightings are common in Western Australia, but the Sorrento attack left locals stunned. Mike Munro told 9News : “Everyone knows there’s sharks in the water, but you don’t sort of, come along expecting this. I don’t really know how to put it into words, it’s just a shocking thing.”

‌



Dozens of locals were at the beach when the attack took place, with witnesses describing a 'large pool of blood' in the water.

"Basically the shark grabbed him again, pulled him back down, and then it went out a bit further," local man Ryan Rowe told The West Australian.

He said locals who frequent the stretch of coast were shocked by the incident, adding: "I couldn't believe there was that much blood [coming] out of a human body. We're always sort of in and out of the water and stuff like that - it's so close to home."

‌



View 4 Images The search has entered a second day as emergency services contend with adverse weather conditions. (Image: 9News)

No details about the missing person have been released but it is understood the friend he was swimming with safely made it back to shore.

Some reports have suggested it was a great white shark but the species of shark has not been official confirmed yet.

Article continues below

A spokesperson for the local council The City of Joondalup said: "The City of Joondalup is aware of a reported shark incident at Sorrento Beach this morning. As a precautionary measure, Rangers are closing all beaches within the City’s boundaries until further notice and members of the public are asked to avoid the Sorrento Beach area and follow the directions of emergency services personnel.

"The City would like to thank emergency services and first responders attending the scene."

News.title: September scorcher as Met Office says 'middle of summer temperatures' hit UK this week
News.content:
September scorcher as Met Office says 'middle of summer temperatures' hit UK this week

It's going to reach 25C in parts of the country, but Britain is in line for four consecutive days of 20C-plus weather - before an autumnal cold snap 'may bring overnight frost'

View 3 Images It will hit 25C at 4pm on Tuesday, the Met Office says

Brits are set to enjoy a September scorcher next week as ‘middle of summer’ sweep across the nation.

‌



Meteorologists are predicting four consecutive days when the mercury should pass the 20C mark, with the high coming on Tuesday (September 22) at 25C in south-east England. This weekend is also set to be warm for autumn.

‌



On Saturday (September 19), temperatures should hit 23C and the high will be 21C on Sunday (September 20), both in London. Monday (September 21) will be warmer still at 23C.

‌



The Met Office forecast for Saturday is: “Cloud and patchy rain or drizzle linger across southern England and Wales, though brighter in the east. Elsewhere, sunny spells and blustery showers. Windy across northern areas.”

The outlook for Sunday to Tuesday is: “Dry but rather cloudy on Sunday with some overnight rain. Rather cloudy on Monday and Tuesday with some sunny spells and lighter winds and turning a little warmer.”

View 3 Images Temperatures will be above average for autumn on Tuesday evening

‌



Away from the south-east, temperatures should reach 23C in Cardiff on Tuesday, 19C in Belfast, 18C in Glasgow, and 22C in Manchester at the same time.

There will be some showers across the country on Saturday, with Scotland, south-west England, and Wales in particular set for downpours. However, the skies clear on Sunday to make way for ‘middle of summer’ temperatures.

“We’ve still got some showers early on across Scotland, otherwise it’s simply a drier and brighter picture for Sunday,” said Met Office forecaster Aidan McGivern.

‌



View 3 Images It will be warm on Monday evening, too

“As Sunday ends, higher pressure builds from the south. A warm front pushes across the northwest, bringing some cloud and rain for a time early in the week, but with that high pressure in place on Monday and Tuesday, temperatures will rise back up to the average temperatures for the middle of summer.”

However, it looks like an autumnal cool will from Wednesday (September 23) onwards, which could bring ‘overnight fog and frost’ but ‘temperatures are expected to be slightly above average overall’.

News.title: Two police forces declare 'dispersal zone' for Millwall vs West Ham derby match
News.content:
Two police forces declare 'dispersal zone' for Millwall vs West Ham derby match

Cops have implemented a second dispersal zone ahead of the first east London derby match in 14 years as Millwall host West Ham and The Den on Saturday lunchtime

View 3 Images The last meeting of the two teams required a heavy police presence in 2012

A second 'dispersal zone' has been announced by police in connection to the Millwall vs West Ham east London football derby match on Saturday.

‌



The two east London clubs are due to meet at Millwall's home of the Den for the first time since 2012 at 12:30pm on Saturday (September 19). In the days leading up to the notorious game, two police forces have implemented dispersal orders for the match.

‌



Metropolitan Police chiefs declared a section 35 dispersal order is around the Bermondsey stadium and nearby neighbourhoods. This order grants police the authority to instruct people to vacate a public area within a specified zone.

‌



"As with any fixture, the Sporting Events Act 1985 is in place, which means entering or attempting to enter a ground while intoxicated is strictly prohibited," said the Met. "A Section 35 dispersal order will also be in place, allowing officers to remove anyone causing disorder."

View 3 Images

‌



Now, City of London Police have implemented a second section 35 order, covering the Square Mile and several bridges spanning the Thames.

A spokesperson for City of London Police said: "To assist the policing operation around the Millwall v West Ham match, from 8am today, we're putting a S35 order in place.

"If someone is contributing to crime, disorder or anti-social behaviour, they can be told to leave and not return for a specified period. It lasts until 8pm."

Article continues below

View 3 Images The new dispersal order from City of London Police ahead of the Millwall v West Ham match (Image: City of London Police/X)

Saturday's match marks the first time the two clubs have met in 14 years, and it signifies the 100th competitive match between the east London rivals. West Ham enter the derby as favourites.

Following their relegation from the Premier League last term, the Hammers lead the early Championship standings. Millwall, who were defeated in the play-off semi-finals last campaign, presently occupy twelfth place after just seven fixtures.

News.title: Chancellor John Healey urged to end housing benefit freeze hitting low-income families at Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey urged to end housing benefit freeze hitting low-income families at Budget

The Resolution Foundation warns more than 1.1million are facing a 'cost-of-housing crunch' as the gap between local rents and benefit support people can claim is set to reach a record high this autumn

View 2 Images Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Budget on October 28 (Image: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Chancellor John Healey is being urged to end a freeze on housing benefit at next month's Budget to help struggling low-income private renters.

‌



The Resolution Foundation think-tank warns today more than 1.1million are facing a 'cost-of-housing crunch' as the gap between local rents and benefit support people can claim is set to reach a record high this autumn. The research shows the gap in London is the widest, with a low-income family renting a two-bedroom home in inner-east London facing a typical shortfall of £324-per-month.

‌



Across the rest of the capital, the shortfall is at least £200, and exceeds £100 each month in more than half of all areas in England, the Resolution Foundation adds. Local housing allowance (LHA) rates, which control the maximum amount of rental support people on Universal Credit can get, have been frozen for most of the past decade.

‌



View 2 Images Local housing allowance rates, which control the maximum amount of rental support people on Universal Credit can get, have been frozen for most of the past decade (Image: Getty Images/EyeEm)

Unfreezing the rates and linking them to local rents would cost an estimated £2billion by 2029-30. But charities have previously argued the freeze on LHA rates has pushed cash-strapped families - already struggling with the cost of energy and food - into homelessness.

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham also criticised the freeze - first introduced by the Tories - in a major speech before he replaced Keir Starmer in Downing Street. Mr Burnham, who has promised a massive expansion in council homes, said in June the country was in a housing trap where "we are forced to chase rents in the private-rented sector through the benefits system".

‌



He added: "When governments try to control these costs by freezing Local Housing Allowance, it makes families homeless and places unfunded pressures on councils when they have to pay for temporary accommodation."

Economist at the Resolution Foundation Stephen Hunsaker said: "The gap between average rents and Local Housing Allowance levels is set to reach a record high this October, and failing to re-peg LHA to actual rents in next month's Budget could lock in a freeze for another year, and see the gap reach 30 per cent by March 2028.

"Rather than primarily benefitting landlords, our new analysis shows that the last time LHA was re-pegged to local rents in April 2024 it was tenants that benefited, with the fraction of LHA recipients facing a shortfall between their rents and the amount they could claim dropping significantly."

‌



He added: "With many tenants receiving housing support already going without essentials to pay their rent today, the Government should restore the automatic annual linking of LHA to relieve the pressure on low-income families in the private rented sector."

Mairi MacRae, Director of Policy and Campaigns at Shelter, also told The Mirror : “Caught between an escalating cost-of-living crisis and skyrocketing private rents, families should be able to rely on housing benefit as a safety net to help cover costs. Yet with the freeze on housing allowance, thousands are left desperately grappling to plug the gap between their income and rent.

“Families are being forced to make impossible choices daily between feeding their family or paying their rent. Tens of thousands are stuck homeless in grim temporary accommodation for months or even years on end because there's nowhere affordable for them to move to.

Article continues below

“The government must prevent more families from becoming homeless and help those already in temporary accommodation move into a home by unfreezing local housing allowance in the Autumn Budget, so it covers at least bottom third of local rents. The only long-term solution to provide families with a safe and secure home is for the government to deliver the social rent homes we desperately need.”

A Government spokesperson said: “Local Housing Allowance rates are reviewed annually,and future decisions will be taken in the context of the Government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.

“We know there is more to do. That is why we have launched the £1 billion Crisis and Resilience Fund, are raising the National Living Wage by up to £900 a year for a full-time worker, investing more than £1 billion in homelessness services, and are investing a record £39 billion in affordable and social housing.”

News.title: Suffolk Police investigating 'disgusting' post about death of missing toddler Noah Woods
News.content:
Suffolk Police investigating 'disgusting' post about death of missing toddler Noah Woods

Suffolk Police are investigating multiple reports" of a "disgusting" social media post following the tragic death of three-year-old Noah Woods this week in Brantham

View 4 Images Noah Woods was just three-years-old when he tragically died (Image: Bav Media)

Police are investigating "multiple reports" of a "disgusting" social media post released following the death of three-year-old Noah Woods.

‌



Noah, aged three, was reported missing on the afternoon of Tuesday 15 September, when he became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close. He was reported to have run off down the alleyway beside the playground towards the new-build housing estate and Decoy Pond.

‌



A large-scale missing person investigation was launched involving specialist police search teams, assisted by emergency services colleagues from HM Coastguard, Suffolk Fire & Rescue Service, the National Police Air Service and the Metropolitan Police Dive Team, along with volunteers from SULSAR (Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue)

‌



View 4 Images Up to 1,000 volunteers joined the search for Noah Woods who went missing near a playground. (Image: Suffolk Police / SWNS)

Police share new information eight months after man found dead on Wolverhampton school field by young girl READ MORE :

Further support was provided by the East of England Ambulance Service – including Suffolk HART – and the Environment Agency. All of these resources were supplemented by a huge community response of approximately 1,300 members of the public who assisted with the search for Noah.

On Wednesday 16 September, officers from the Metropolitan Police Dive Team recovered the body of a child from Decoy Pond in Brantham and Noah was formally identified. Noah’s death is not being treated as suspicious but police still have a number of enquiries to complete before submitting a file for the Coroner.

‌



View 4 Images Noah was last seen in a playground before he disappeared (Image: Suffolk Police / SWNS)

Since the tragic news social media users have been sharing their condolences to Noah's family and loved ones but one user caused a huge backlash on Facebook after sharing a 'meme' making reference to Madeline McCann.

Comments have now been removed from the post on Facebook, but a spokesman for Suffolk Police said: "We've had multiple reports of this and it is being looked into."

‌



One outraged social media user wrote: "This is disgusting and needs dealing with. Absolutely vile human to post something like that."

The post's creator posted today: "I'm sorry if my meme caused anyone any harm or serious offence. It was not my intention to distress anyone who may have been affected by my content.

View 4 Images Numerous tributes have been left in Noah's memory (Image: Newsquest / SWNS)

Article continues below

"I have removed the post and I can only apologise for sharing something that causes so many people to feel some way about it. I saw it as dark humour and the timing couldn't have been any worse, I sincerely apologise and will accept any more abuse or death threats, as deserved."

The JustGiving page organised by Good Dads Club has surpassed £80,000 in donations with Ipswich Town footballer Leif Davis donating £2,000.

You can donate to the fundraiser by clicking here.

News.title: Royal Family recap: Earl Spencer claims late Queen asked 'what is Diana up to now?' after hearing crash news
News.content:
Princess Diana's brother Earl Spencer has told the BBC he is 'telling the truth' in a bombshell interview about a phone call with King Charles in the days following his sister's death

Princess Diana's brother has claimed the late Queen asked a 'tetchy' question when she first heard the news that Diana was in a crash, before the serious nature of the accident came to light.

In the latest serialisation of his upcoming book, published in the Mail, Earl Spencer wrote: "When the Queen had heard the first news of Diana's being in a traffic accident, she had asked tetchily, 'What is she up to now?' This, before the seriousness of it all became clear."

It comes as he has doubled down on his claims about King Charles after sparking a row with Buckingham Palace over his late sister Princess Diana's death. Speaking exclusively to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate in Northamptonshire, he was adamant as he said "I'm telling the truth."

In extracts from his new book, Earl Spencer has claimed that Charles was ‘giddily elated’ when he heard of Diana’s death, as well as reportedly saying in the days after her passing that the world would ‘forget about her soon enough’.

Buckingham Palace responded saying the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss." But speaking for the first time since the fallout, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said."

Royal sources have hit back at astonishing claims made by Earl Spencer in his new book, calling the accusations ‘utter nonsense’. Princess Diana’s brother has penned a memoir about his late sister’s life and tragic death sparking a furious war of words with Buckingham Palace.

It comes after Prince Harry ignored questions about the row during his first official engagement since moving back to the UK. This afternoon he made another public appearance by visiting a school in Birmingham to launch a new Invictus Games education programme.

News.title: Donald Trump announces 'ban on the free press' in furious White House meltdown as he kicks out CNN and Politico
News.content:
Donald Trump announces 'ban on the free press' in furious White House meltdown as he kicks out CNN and Politico

In a furious meltdown, the President said CNN, Politico and MS Now, the TV channel formerly known as MSNBC, because they don't report the news in a way that he likes

View 2 Images Trump named three outlets who would be banned from the White House (Image: AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

Donald Trump said he was "banning the free press" last night, as he moved to throw several news outlets out of the White House.

‌



In a furious meltdown, the President said CNN, Politico and MS Now, the TV channel formerly known as MSNBC, because they don't report the news in a way that he likes. Claiming the outlets were "unfair" and "dishonest", Trump said it was a "very simple ban. I don't want them in my office, I don't want them here. I would say the ban will go as far as you can. If they could straighten themselves out I'd love it."

‌



Referring to the move as the "ban on the free press", Trump threatened to ban several other outlets including the New York Times and the Washington Post in future.

‌



And he ranted about ABC News and the BBC - falsely claiming the BBC had edited his incendiary January 6 speech to "put words in my mouth" and make it appear he had said words he had not. Trump tried to ban now former CNN reporter Jim Acosta from the White House during his first term, but the move was overturned by courts.

The access of news outlets to cover the president is protected under the first amendment to the US Constitution - something a reporter reminded Trump of during a wild Q&A in the Oval Office. "Oh, thankyou for telling me that," Trump said, sarcastically.

View 2 Images Reporters gathered in the White House Briefing Room after Trump announced the move on Truth Social (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Asked if he was trying to "intimidate" the press, Trump said: "No, no, no. I dislike dishonest press, like you, I think you're terrible. I like to see honest press."

Asked how the move was constitutional, Trump said: "I don't think someone should be allowed to come in and write fake stories....It's sick. There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories. Now, if they want to write them that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my...into the people's house."

Another reporter noted that Xi Jinping, President of China is coming to the White House next week - and that China is one of the most repressive countries for journalists in the world. "I don't know about that," Trump said, apparently defending China's record. "We're repressive also. We get fake news. We don't repress, but we get fake news."

‌



Trump repeatedly claimed his poll numbers were good, despite them being among the worst approval ratings for any president in history. He's facing a huge humiliation in November's midterm elections, with both the House of Representatives and the Senate, along with several key governor's races likely to go to the Democrats.

Trump last week announced a desperate trillion dollar bribe ahead of the election, offering a $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every American adult if Republicans maintain control of both houses. In the Oval Office, he said: "We are giving Republicans - and I say Republicans because I think everybody's going to be a Republican, actually - we are giving the people of our country $5,000 if the Republicans win."

At the time of writing, CNN reporters said they remained in the White House and no action had been taken to remove them.

Article continues below

"CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government," the network said in a statement. "Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right."

News.title: British Museum evacuated over 'smoke' as thousands of visitors told to leave
News.content:
British Museum evacuated over 'smoke' as thousands of visitors told to leave

Nearly 4,000 people were evacuated from the British Museum in central London, including those waiting to see the famous Bayeux Tapestry

View Image A fire engine in front of the British Museum this evening (Image: @reno_TRPG_0/X)

Thousands of people have been evacuated from the British Museum in London following a suspected fire.

‌



The incident took place this evening following reports of smoke in a gallery, while visitors were waiting in line to see the Bayeux Tapestry. Fire alarms were set off and around 4,000 people were evacuated from the building.

‌



London Fire Brigade explained the smoke may have been caused by an overheating light.

‌



A spokesman for the fire brigade said: "Crews carried out a systematic search of the building to identify the source of the smoke, which is believed to have been caused by an overheating light. Around 3,700 people evacuated the building before firefighters arrived.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Bayeux Tapestry unveiled in UK for first time in nearly 1,000 years as lines of Brits queue up to view artefact READ MORE :

France museum heist sees four August Renoir paintings worth £10million stolen but thieves drop two READ MORE :

"The incident was over for firefighters at 19.27, when responsibility for the site was handed back to the building’s management team."

‌



The evacuation sparked disappointment among visitors, some of whom had been queuing for more than an hour to see the Bayeux Tapestry.

One said on X: "Hope everyone's ok after the evacuation for a fire alarm. Disappointing for those of who spent an hour and forty minutes after our ticketed time queuing to see the Bayeux Tapestry to get to reach it, and then were told to leave."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Another visitor explained that a fire alarm first went off inside the museum at around 6.30pm but no one evacuated and "staff just carried on". However, about 20 minutes later, an emergency evacuation was ordered and visitors were met by fire engines outside.

Another person who was at the museum said: "I was at the British Museum when they started shouting 'Emergency!' and 'Fire!' and hustled us all outside...!!"

A spokeswoman for the British Museum told Mirror Online: "We can confirm that the Museum was evacuated earlier this evening and the Fire Brigade attended what we believe was an electrical fault in a gallery (we’re still investigating). The collection is safe and there are no issues with the Bayeux Tapestry.

Article continues below

"Those that had tickets to see the exhibition but were not able to - or their visit had to be curtailed - have received our apologies for the inconvenience and disappointment and have been asked to contact us to reschedule their date or they can receive a refund."

The iconic Bayeux Tapestry went on public display at the British Museum on September 10. This is the first time the woven chronicle of the Norman conquest has returned to British soil in nearly 1,000 years.

The 70-metre-long artefact will be on display until September 2027.

News.title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
News.content:
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

News.title: Watch: Diana's brother says Charles 'went ballistic' in phone call after her death
News.content:
Princess Diana's brother said King Charles "went ballistic" during a phone call with him in the days after his sister's death.

Earl Spencer spoke exclusively with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg about claims he has made in a new book, alleging the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly-worded response to the book claims, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Read more about Laura Kuenssberg's interview with Earl Spencer.

News.title: Flight chaos caused by software defect in space of a millisecond, report says
News.content:
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe told the BBC he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure."

"You can fly to almost anywhere from almost any airport at almost any time. If that stops, even for a moment, then you get huge disruption.

"My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he added.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of Mr Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.

In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.

The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.

The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.

Mr Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption, saying Nats was "devastated".

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

Nats has "tested these systems so much," he added.

"We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said.

Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.

"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.

This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.

In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.

There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.

Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."

He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".

Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK
News.content:
One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide".

The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter.

In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.

A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply."

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK.

"In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment."

He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved.

Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030.

Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil.

"You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down.

"If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening."

Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security.

Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary.

The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses."

News.title: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
News.content:
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."

"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"

Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.

The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive on Sunday. Her battered and partly burned body was later found in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.

Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.

"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.

"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."

Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni â her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.

The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country â which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.

News.title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
News.content:
Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.

Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe".

His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines.

Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion.

He described the proposed changes as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach.

"Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times.

"Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well."

Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective.

When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour."

He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can".

He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely".

Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence.

They can also consider an order for 16 and 17 year olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences.

However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23.

The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed.

News.title: Brother didn't match description of 'Putney pusher', suspect's sisters tell BBC
News.content:
The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC their brother was innocent, and the police showed "no urgency" to clear his name.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Nicholas Brandram's sisters accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless".

Brandram was found dead on Tuesday evening and his family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the investigation.

Brandram's sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker told Today presenter Justin Webb their brother's mental health deteriorated after his arrest and questioned why the police were not able to carry out DNA tests that could have proved his innocence.

News.title: Temperatures could peak at 26C as summerlike warmth returns next week
News.content:
Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK.

Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September.

Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions.

News.title: Man in court charged with murder over Armadale shooting
News.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with murdering another man who was shot dead in West Lothian.

Police were called to a property on Harestanes Road in Armadale at about 11:50 on Saturday.

Billy Watson, 35, was found injured and died at the scene.

Frank McCarthy, 57, appeared at Livingston Sheriff Court on Friday, charged with murder and attempting to defeat the ends of justice. He made no plea and was remanded in custody.

A 29-year-old man and 44-year-old man have also been arrested in connection with the incident.

Police Scotland said inquiries were ongoing.

News.title: Teen who piloted Channel boat with 165 migrants jailed
News.content:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July - the 16th conviction since the new offence was created in January.

Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.

At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August.

At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified".

She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence.

James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus.

The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels.

News.title: Nottingham attacks family condemn police promotion
News.content:
The father of a student who was stabbed to death in the Nottingham attacks has criticised a move by Nottinghamshire Police to promote the senior officer who led the investigation.

Grace O'Malley-Kumar, Barnaby Webber and Ian Coates were stabbed on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, leading to a public inquiry.

Rob Griffin, of Nottinghamshire Police, was temporary deputy chief constable from 29 April 2025 and was appointed substantively into the role following a selection process in August, the force said.

Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's dad, told the BBC on Friday: "I think this is completely wrong."

Police say the process consisted of an application form, a people panel and external advisors.

Griffin has previously been described by Barnaby's mother Emma Webber as having "blood on his hands", following the force's failure to detain Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, after an arrest warrant was issued in September 2022.

News.title: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case
News.content:
He said "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the neo-Nazi informant.

The security service claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from a woman who was abused by him.

But what MI5 said was untrue. The security service had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

A panel of three senior judges - England and Wales' most senior judge, Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, President of the King's Bench Division Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - is considering what action to take over the false evidence.

In particular, it will decide whether to initiate contempt of court proceedings against certain MI5 officers or MI5 itself. Any such move would be unprecedented.

The report, by then-deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.

He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.

Otty said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" in the report, published in July, and they must never happen again.

He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum.

Otty argued against contempt proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given Sir John's detailed investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform.

He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal.

Lawyers for both officers also argued against launching contempt proceedings.

Matthew Butt KC, for Officer 2, said the officer accepted that his conduct had fallen "below the standard expected of him", for which he apologised and expressed regret.

But he said he denied acting dishonestly or having interfered with the administration of justice, and did not accept the report's findings.

Aaron Watkins apologised on behalf of Officer 3 and accepted his conduct "undoubtably" contributed to the courts and parties involved being misled, but denied it had been the result of dishonesty.

He said the evidence presented by Sir John fell short of the threshold for contempt of court, and said such proceedings would not be in the public interest because there had already been a thorough investigation.

Meanwhile, lawyers for the BBC said the corporation considered the threshold had been met and said there was a "very clear public interest" in doing so.

Jude Bunting KC said providing false evidence was "a particularly serious affront to the administration of justice" and noted that while MI5 now offered a sincere apology to the court, its response when the lies were first exposed was "not consistent with transparency or responsibility".

At the conclusion of the hearing, the Lady Chief Justice said it had been a "serious day addressing serious matters".

She said a judgment will be issued at a later date.

News.title: Tenko and Coronation Street actress Stephanie Cole dies aged 84
News.content:
Solihull-born Cole, who trained at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, after making her stage debut at the age of 17 â playing the 90-year-old medium Madame Arcati in Noel Coward's Blithe Spirit.

She went on to enjoy a lengthy career that spanned TV, radio and film and was perhaps best known for playing Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko.

The series chronicled the lives of British women in Singapore after the Japanese invasion and their consequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp.

Cole, in her breakout role, played a doctor who struggled to look after the women's health, opposite Ann Bell and Claire Oberman.

During this same period, Cole also played the moody customer Mrs Delphine Featherstone, aka "The Black Widow" in the Ronnie Barker-starring Open All Hours.

She would go on to win the award for best TV comedy actress for her part as the sharp-tongued photojournalist Diana Trent in Waiting For God.

But she cited her earlier performance as Muriel in Alan Bennett's monologue Soldiering On, as one of her proudest moments. The series also starred Maggie Smith and Julie Walters.

Her stage highlight, by her account, was in a West End production of A Passionate Woman.

News.title: New sighting of missing Lillia, 13
News.content:
Police have received fresh CCTV of a girl who has been missing from home for a week.

Lillia, 13, from Bolton, was last seen by her family last Friday, but was seen later that evening in Manchester's Picadilly bus station, and at the Trafford Centre the following day.

Officers who have been handing out hundreds of leaflets to try to locate Lillia have now released new footage of her at a McDonald's restaurant in Piccadilly from Sunday at about 20:20 BST.

Greater Manchester Police Ch Spt Int Helen Critchley said: "Officers are making every effort to locate Lillia, and our team have been working through hours of CCTV footage and exploring every avenue to try and find her."

At a press conference on Thursday, Critchley issued an appeal on behalf of Lillia's mother Jessica, saying: "Lillia, if you see this appeal, please know your family love you, miss you and just want to know that you are safe.

"You are not in any trouble, they simply want you to come home."

News.title: Driver who killed woman celebrating 60th jailed
News.content:
The court heard Goulty drank two lagers before he drove his silver Vauxhall Astra at 64mph in a residential 30mph limit area before crashing into 69-year-old Sarwar Mohammad's Peugeot Expert Tepee taxi.

Mohammad, of Willow Brook Road in Leicester, who had been driving the taxi and admitted the same offences, was handed a six-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, and told he must do 100 hours of unpaid work.

Prosecutor Steven Bailey told the court Brighton did not know the Sidsaffs, who had come to Leicester for the Radio 2 in the Park music festival, but they shared a taxi because they were going in the same direction.

Brighton, who was from the city, had been out with her friends celebrating her 60th birthday.

Bailey said the collision happened as a result of the "combined bad driving of Thomas Goulty and Sarwar Mohammad", while the taxi was making a right turn towards Westfield Road across the central reservation of the dual carriageway.

Goulty had been out in the city and sent someone a message minutes before the crash saying he was "just out having a couple of beers", and in a roadside test immediately after the crash tested positive for alcohol in his breath, but later assessments could not conclude that he was over the driving limit.

Bailey said Goulty's speed was "excessive", up to 64mph (102km/h) on approach and 55mph at the point of impact.

"He had left himself little or no calculation time and any braking was far too late," he said.

"He drove too quickly for the road and its conditions, about twice the speed limit, having taken alcohol and in the dark."

News.title: Men lose appeal for harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary
News.content:
The men were attempting to overturn their convictions from February, when they were each sentenced to 200 hours of community service and given restraining orders banning them from contacting or approaching Nye or her partner for 10 years.

They were also banned from entering the London borough where the couple live for a decade.

A year after the initial broadcast of the BBC programmes about the organisation, the Lighthouse group began a campaign of peaceful, and legal, protests outside BBC offices in London, against Nye and the BBC.

"While there were elements of peaceful protest and freedom of expression, their conduct, as we have already identified, was not proportionate to the proper exercise of those rights and went beyond what was acceptable and indeed became criminal", the judge said.

After an interaction with Nye in July 2024, Kamra gave evidence that he was "dissatisfied" and that questions he had for Nye were still not answered.

The group decided to visit her home address, which they found using a private investigator and said that they had looked up BBC guidance of doorstepping.

"The appellants therefore appreciated that there was a line which their conduct must not cross", said Pounder.

"What happened descended into bullying and oppressive conduct", he added, deeming that the behaviour of the three men was not reasonable.

During the first visit to Nye's home address on 29 August, the group had distributed leaflets they had printed to Nye's neighbours.

The judge said the contents were "not confined to criticism of journalism".

"They identified her to those living in the immediate neighbourhood and associated her with serious allegations concerning racism, dishonesty and the concealment of child sexual abuse by family members," he explained.

"That is materially different from distributing critical literature outside the headquarters of a public broadcaster."

The court heard Kamra later returned to the property to post a handwritten letter saying "we will be back", which "materially reinforced" Nye's concerns, Pounder said.

Deichler, Kamra and Singh visited her property again a week later, on 5 September, before they were later arrested.

The three men maintained that they were performing citizen journalism and were at her property to obtain a doorstep interview, as part of their own documentary, and that they were acting in the public interest.

Judge Pounder accepted that they saw themselves as citizen journalists, but underlined their behaviour was not reasonable, as he pointed to their "deliberate acquisition of a private address, attendance of home, distribution of inflammatory literature, indication return visit and subsequent return".

Giving evidence for the second time, from behind a curtain, Nye told the court of her fear when the three accused went to her property.

It was "extremely" distressing, Nye said.

Their actions had resulted in Nye installing CCTV, panic alarms, direct lines with the police and carrying rape alarms, the court heard.

The three men had also claimed that their attendance outside Nye's home was an expression of their religious beliefs.

Pounder said there was no doubt that their views were "sincerely held", telling them that it had been concluded that a prayer they said outside her door was "an incidental part of their attendance at the address".

The Bible they wanted to give her, Pounder said could have been posted to her via the BBC.

On top of their original convictions, the judge has ordered the three men to each pay an additional Â£1,000.

News.title: Johannes Radebe on Strictly and survival: ‘It’s a blessing and a curse to know life in both extremes’
News.content:
