I’ve been in the bottom of the pits and I’ve rubbed shoulders with the King and the Queen,” Johannes Radebe tells me. “I’m a boy from Zamdela who never thought life could possibly turn out this way.” He lets out a hearty laugh, shifting back – as he tends to do – into dazzle mode. “It did give me resilience, my darling.”

Tonight, Radebe will make his debut as one of three new presenters guiding viewers through the revamped Strictly Come Dancing, alongside Emma Willis and Josh Widdecombe. And he’s the only one with connecting tissue to the show’s earlier Tess-and-Claudia incarnation, having served as a professional dancer on Strictly since 2018. He admits he’s nervous, but he’s also made of strong stuff. Growing up in South Africa during the final years of apartheid, the 39-year-old withstood homophobia and a period of homelessness while pursuing a dance career in Johannesburg. Reading an autocue seems a cakewalk in comparison. Still…

“I want to lock myself up,” Radebe purrs, like Eartha Kitt. He’ll tune into tonight’s pre-taped launch show on his own. “I want to keep an open heart and mind because I’m my biggest critic. I don’t want to have opinions around me while I’m watching it. Afterwards, I’ll come out and face the world.”

Nerves aside, Radebe is otherwise giddy as we chat over Zoom. He is holed up in his London flat, still coming down from recording the first new Strictly a few days before we speak. The live shows – a whole other challenge in themselves – properly start next Saturday. Today, Radebe lives up to his warm reputation, and is just as elegant with his softly spoken answers as he is on the dance floor. It’s easy to see why mums across the nation have fallen for him. A powerful memoir and a celebrated run on the West End earlier this year, in Kinky Boots, couldn’t have hurt. He is, to put it succinctly, a star.

open image in gallery Radebe with his new 'Strictly' co-hosts Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe ( BBC/Guy Levy )

So it’s no real surprise that he’s been tasked with captaining the Strictly ship into uncharted territory. As well as out of those choppy, scandal-infested waters. The show is entering its 24th series, its first in its history without Tess Daly, and its first without Claudia Winkleman in 12 years. The stakes have never been higher. Contrary to recent reports, though, presenting duties will be “evenly distributed” between Radebe, Willis and Widdecombe, who’ll be joined by a raft of celebrities – everyone from EastEnders’ Lacey Turner and Gavin & Stacey’s Melanie Walters to dog trainer Graeme Hall – also getting used to the new format.

For Radebe himself, his new job came as a surprise. Just months before he was asked to try out for it, he was contemplating his future with the show. “I had gotten to a point where I was like, ‘What’s next in my life?’” he explains. He remembers having long chats about it with his mother. “She said, ‘What are you thinking for 2026? Are you going to come back home? I’ve missed you.’ That’s the thing a lot of people don’t realise – I don’t live with my family because I am where I am. I’m alone. So, I’ve been craving time with them and seeing my niece and nephew grow up.”

Then there was the spectre of turning 40, which had already led him to think about slowing down on his dancing for his body’s sake. “My bones are tired, my bunions are tired,” he laughs. “I made it my life’s mission to find other opportunities outside of this.”

So how did he find himself up for such a huge promotion?

“Lauren, I don’t know myself!” he hoots.

What he does know is that he received a call early in the year from a Strictly producer, who asked whether he’d be interested in auditioning. “I was like, ‘Johannes, the thought of even saying yes to this opportunity – who the hell do you think you are?’” he says. “But they said, ‘We fully understand you’re not a broadcast or presenter. We know you are somebody who understands the fabric of the show. You love the show and we will guide you.’ If I didn’t have that conversation with him, I wouldn’t have even said yes to that chemistry test. But I also thought… nothing ventured, nothing gained. If anybody else had this opportunity, they would grab it with both hands, right? So why not me?”

open image in gallery Radebe performing on ‘Strictly’ last year with celebrity partner Alex Kingston ( BBC )

After various callbacks and chemistry readings, Radebe found out on a Zoom call that he’d be presenting the show with Widdicombe and Willis. “I screamed,” he grins. “I was alone in the apartment. I think my neighbours must have thought, ‘What is going on?’ But that’s how it played out.”

Since then, the trio have been bonding and swapping showbiz notes. Radebe has given them the lowdown on who’s who and what’s what at Strictly, while they’ve provided him with a crash course on comic timing and presenting. “That’s what got me through the launch show, honestly,” he gushes. “I think Emma held my hand throughout the whole process.”

But he knows that his time on Strictly could have ended very differently. With the show’s new format came a complete shake-up of the professional cast; Karen Hauer, Gorka Marquez and three other dancers moved on to make way for five fresh faces. It’s part of the reason Radebe was ready for change. “Our journey on the show as professional dancers is very short-lived,” he says. “I know people have come and gone and I know that it would have been [my] trajectory. But I’ve always said that if they got rid of me or if I ever stopped, I would [love to] come back and work as part of the crew, just to be part of the magic.”

The brutal nature of showbiz doesn’t faze Radebe, though, given everything he’s been through. He’s been open about the challenges he faced growing up in the mining town of Zamdela, raised by a supportive mother but a father who became violent with alcohol. A lover of Barbie dolls and his mother’s make-up, Radebe was a target of homophobia at school, which at times left him contemplating suicide. Later, he scraped together as much money as he could to live in Johannesburg, paying taxi drivers to sleep in the back of their cars or sneaking into the dance studio where he taught to stay overnight. After working on cruise ships for seven years, he was finally cast in the South African version of Strictly in 2014. Four years later, the UK Strictly came calling.

“I’m grateful now, looking back on everything I’ve been through,” he says. “The bad. The ugly … Because I wouldn’t appreciate what I have now if I didn’t go through all of that. It’s a blessing and a curse to know life in both extremes. I pinch myself every morning when I wake up, [knowing] that I’ve created a life I’ve always dreamt of.”

In his early dance days, Radebe was told by a rival that he wouldn’t “amount to anything” in life. He’s grateful to the UK – of which he became a citizen in February – for proving them wrong. “For a long time, I thought they were right. It took me until my thirties to realise they were wrong,” he says. “It took this country and being seen and appreciated and being championed the way I have in the past eight years for me to come to that realisation.”

open image in gallery Radebe played the role of drag artist Lola in 'Kinky Boots' earlier this year ( Getty )

Strictly has been one of TV’s biggest star-making machines for decades – which only really dawned on Radebe during his 2022 solo stage tour Freedom. Suffering from a bout of imposter syndrome, he was tempted to cancel beforehand. “I just thought to myself, who am I to think that I’m going to sell out theatres around this country?’” he recalls. “My agent said, ‘You don’t realise the impact you’ve had doing what you do and doing what you love.’ I thank God for that encouragement because I wouldn’t have done it honestly.” Radebe pauses. “He did also say to me, ‘If you pull out, our producers will sue us because we’ve signed a contract already.’ I was like, ‘Okay!’”

He still experiences those pangs of self-doubt, he says. But he’s better at dealing with them now. After all, just look at the material.

“I never thought I’d be an author, an actor, or a West End performer,” he says. “Now I’m presenting this show. I didn’t have this in my plans for my life. So I’ve got the tools to deal with imposter syndrome, and I’ve got proof to back it up.”

‘Strictly Come Dancing’ returns to BBC One tonight at 7.25pm

After the hottest summer on record in the UK – with five heatwaves between May and August, temperatures have started to drop from highs of 30C or more – the summer bubble has finally burst.

Although warm temperatures are set to return at the weekend and temperatures could reach mid 20C in the south of England, the extreme bout of one sunny day after another feels like a distant dream.

For a sunshine person like myself, a darkening mood is already on the horizon. I’ve always suffered winter blues and as we transition into autumn, it already feels more extreme. I’m craving carbs and overeating, socially withdrawing, feeling depressed and suffering from fatigue.

And with warnings that the super El Niño will likely bring stormy and wet autumn weather and possibly epic flooding and an ongoing “danger zone of extreme weather” according to the UN, I feel gloomier than ever.

So I am interested to know if moving between seasons after an extremely hot summer is creating a sort of maxxed-out downward spiral effect on our brain and body. I especially want to know, if you are someone who experiences seasonal affective disorder (SAD), will it be worse this year?

Dr Caroline Hickman, a climate psychotherapist and researcher in people’s responses to climate change globally, says that nobody yet understands the impact of heatwaves on SAD – or winter blues – because “it’s unprecedented”.

open image in gallery The drought heatwave is over as we transition into wetter and stormier weather driven by a strengthening El Nino ( AFP/Getty )

“We don’t have a blueprint on how it is going to play out – but what we can say is it’s unpredictable because the seasons are out of whack."

SAD is a type of depression that usually happens in the winter, and according to the NHS, it’s thought to be primarily linked to reduced levels of daylight, which may cause changes to brain chemicals like melatonin and serotonin that affect your mood and circadian rhythms, sleep patterns and mood. And it is because of this that Cathy Wyse, a chronobiologist with research interests focused on understanding the effects of disruption of circadian rhythms on physiology and behaviour, says the heatwaves won’t directly impact SAD.

However, according to the experts, the wobbles I am feeling already are not something I am imagining either. Trevor Harley, Emeritus Professor of Psychology at the University of Dundee, Scotland and author of Head in the Clouds: How the Weather Affects Our Minds and Mental Health, says that at this time of year, around the autumn equinox, as the hours of daylight are shortening at their fastest rate, people suffer from something called “anticipatory anxiety”. And our experiences of the hot summer and the talk of mega El Niños will, he says, “feed this anticipatory anxiety even more”.

“We are worrying about how we are going to feel a little later in the year. And some people might be detecting the first signs of seasonal affective disorder (SAD) – which affects about 10 per cent of the population – which really gets going in November.”

On the other hand, the one per cent of the population who suffer from “reverse SAD”, who feel worse in the summer, are starting to feel better at this time of year, he says, “so it’s not bad news for everybody!”

We don’t have a blueprint on how it is going to play out – but what we can say is it’s unpredictable because the seasons are out of whack Dr Caroline Hickman, climate psychotherapist

It is the unpredictability and change that people find most unsettling, so as the weather becomes more extreme, so could the transition between seasons. But this is psychological rather than physiological. Harley says: “This year is particularly striking because we’ve had a particularly long settled spell, really from the middle of May onwards. So yes, it will be worse for many people’s mood and anxiety levels this autumn and winter because we’ve adapted to dry, pleasant, sunny weather. I know that too dry and too hot can be bad. But, in terms of light, we will notice the lack of it more, and that might lower some people’s mood even more than usual.”

Roland Zahn, professor of Mood Disorders and Cognitive Neuroscience at London’s King’s College, says weather changes have long been known to affect our mood states and even people with non-seasonal mood disorders often notice the impact of the shorter daylight hours towards the autumn, increasing their depression vulnerability, he says. And extreme weather is causing new changes to emerge.

“The relevance of weather changes is quite variable for different individuals ... and it is often difficult to disentangle effects of sleep rhythms and sunlight exposure from reduction of outdoor activities people care about,” he says.

“To add further complexity, many people in our affective disorders services have found this year’s heatwaves quite difficult to cope with and have found relief from the cooler weather which is starting to emerge.”

Hickman says that many of us are “hotwired” in the UK to think that any sunny days are fantastic – and there will be some kind of comedown from it. “Some people don’t want to face the awfulness of climate change because it’s terrifying – and it’s easier to act like we’ve had a wonderful summer – the hottest on record,” she says.

open image in gallery Two paths: many are happy for the extra sun, but Dr Caroline Hickman has also fielded enquiries from those who feel helpless amid a climate catastrophe ( AFP/Getty )

However, she says there is an alternative view that we should be paying closer attention to. This year, she has also been inundated with cases of people in distress about the UK heatwaves. “For a lot of people, the heatwaves are unbearable,” she tells me. “People who come to therapy for climate anxiety hated the heatwave. They couldn’t go outside and now they are just happy to see rain.”

But as there is also the potential for a terrible winter coming with El Nino, people may soon transfer their climate anxiety onto storms or flooding instead. “SAD and winter blues will continue to exist for people, but climate anxiety will become a bigger psychological problem,” she says. “We haven’t faced climate change before, and quite honestly, we don’t have a clue how to manage it emotionally,” she says. “There is no quick or easy solution.”

As all seasons are likely to become more extreme, Hester Parr, Professor of Human Geography at the University of Glasgow, says that looking ahead, the UK needs to be better prepared for the mental health impacts of big seasonal contrasts.

open image in gallery Professor Trevor Harley has written about ‘anticipatory anxiety’, which can kick in when the day gets shorter ( Trevor Harley )

“We know that climate-changed winter weather in the future will get wetter, warmer and wilder. We need to be more prepared for the consequences of this change, especially in terms of our mental health,” she says.

“People with SAD in the UK already adapt to low light in winter every year, but in the future more of us may be affected by low winter mood due to increasingly wilder weather, and we will need more innovative ways to manage this.”

Of course exactly how mood is affected depends on how late autumn pans out. At the moment the signs are of a warm, sunny, settled spell, which will cheer many people up, but then people might feel even worse when really bad weather does set in.

Nobody yet understands the impact of heatwaves on SAD – or winter blues – because it’s unprecedented Dr Caroline Hickman

The good news is that recognising those changes early allows people to put supportive strategies in place before symptoms begin to impact daily life. “Healthy habits support resilience throughout the year,” says Ella Kaur Maan, registered nutritionist and Practitioner Lead at supplement brand, Dr.Vegan

While there’s no single solution for SAD, she says, one area that is often overlooked is the connection between gut health and mood. “Around 90 per cent of the body's serotonin, often referred to as the “happy hormone”, is produced in the gut, which is why supporting a healthy gut microbiome can be an important part of overall mental wellbeing,” she tells me.

open image in gallery Professor Hester Parr says the UK needs to be better prepared for the mental health impacts of such seasonal constrasts ( Martin Shields )

To improve gut health she suggests eating fermented foods such as kefir, kombucha and sauerkraut, alongside a varied diet rich in plant foods. Vitamin D is also another important consideration. As sunlight exposure decreases during winter, many people in the UK struggle to maintain optimal vitamin D levels.

“Rather than looking for a quick fix, it’s important to focus on the basics. Eating balanced meals, prioritising sleep, staying hydrated and remaining physically active can help support both body and mind throughout the year.”

But ultimately there are concerns that SAD will pale in comparison next to climate grief and anxiety. Dr Louise Edgington helps people to live well with their climate emotions, which include a whole array including eco-grief, eco-anxiety and climate distress. “Although SAD is real, the multiple impacts on our mental state from knowledge of climate change and ecological loss – including food shortage as and disease outbreaks – are going to be a lot more severe, significant and wide-ranging.

The emerging climate distress will she believes, be “less about mood” and “a whole coming to terms with ecological collapse – and societal collapse – “and that is scary”.

open image in gallery Dr Louise Edgington says that SAD will pale in comparison next to climate grief and anxiety ( Louise Edgington )

Within that this there are confronting issues of personal responsibility too.

“It’s about paying attention to the world as it really is – not being stuck in denial”, she tells me, and these eco feelings are not something we really want to get rid of. Instead, it’s about moving through difficult eco-emotions and not being afraid “to feel your feelings”.

Feeling you are part of a community doing practical things can help with climate grief too. Rebecca Nestor, co-chair of Climate Psychology Alliance, tells me that this summer’s “brutal” weather has caused a sharp rise in the numbers of people wanting to attend climate café listening circles – “we have had to double the number of these supportive gatherings” – and also in the numbers asking about the individual therapeutic support for the psychological impacts of the climate crisis.

There is no cure for climate change anxiety, but getting support from someone who understands that climate distress is real, rather than treating the concern itself as irrational, can help calm anxiety about what is happening to the planet and what may come next.

While we have always known the weather can affect our moods and emotions, whether it is SAD or climate grief, this year’s wild weather means there will be more of us than ever bracing for the storm ahead.

Sir Ed Davey has accused the Conservatives and Reform UK of planning to turn Britain into a “Trump satellite state”, as he vows to block Nigel Farage’s path to No 10.

The Liberal Democrat leader declared his party’s “orange wall” will stop Reform UK’s rise to power and “setting communities against each other”.

Speaking as he arrived at the Liberal Democrats’ annual autumn conference on Saturday, Sir Ed warned a “unholy alliance” between Mr Farage and Kemi Badenoch is “the only way either can get into power”.

“Together, they want to turn Britain into a Trump satellite state which would trash our NHS, turn our communities against each other, cause untold damage to our environment, and trample over traditional British values of fairness, tolerance, and decency,” he said.

Sir Ed said the two parties can “only offer anger, division, and another con to line their own pockets”, and vowed his party “will not let them pass” on the road to No 10.

"A bigger Orange Wall is the only thing that can stand between Britain and this dangerous experiment, and we will not let them pass,” he said.

open image in gallery Ed Davey has accused the Conservatives and Reform UK of planning to turn Britain into a “Trump satellite state”, as he vows to block Nigel Farage’s road to No 10. ( Getty )

“Liberal Democrats are the only party with a plan to take the brakes off the British economy, get money back into people’s pockets, and defend the traditional values that make our country great.

“Britain feels broken because it’s being held back. This conference, we’ll be setting out our vision to fix our broken politics and change our country for the better.”

Lib Dems from across the country will be gathering in Brighton for the party’s annual conference this weekend.

New YouGov polling has found that support for Sir Ed’s party has remained largely consistent over the last year, but found Britons tend to see the Lib Dems as moderate and tolerant, but also weak and unclear what they stand for.

Sir Ed’s personal ratings have also remained consistent, but when asked to describe him in their own words, 42 per cent of Britons answered ““don’t know” or “who?”.

Closing out the first day of the conference on Saturday, Sir Ed will address a party rally, telling members the Lib Dems “believe in the intrinsic worth of every single human being”.

“When we see injustice, when we see human dignity under attack, we do not look away. We stand up. We care. And we fight…

open image in gallery Reform UK leader Nigel Farage speaking during the Reform UK National Conference, at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire )

“[Reform are] not even trying to win most people’s support. What they’re banking on – what Farage is counting on to get him into Number Ten – is that we don’t care enough to see this fight through. That we’ll get tired. Depressed.

“That the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up.”

It comes after it was revealed Reform UK’s tax plans would hand wealthy crypto investors hundreds of millions in tax breaks if Nigel Farage wins the next election.

British politics has been rocked by two gifts totalling £72m given to the party by crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, who last week handed over £36m each.

The donations have prompted major questions over what the donors want in return for their cash, but Reform insists the pledges are entirely legal and the men are patriots who want nothing but to support the party to get ready to govern.

Now, a new analysis of HMRC data by the Labour Party shows that capital gains tax breaks promised by Reform to crypto investors would be worth more than £100m a year, based on investments in 2025 alone.

And that could go much higher if investing in crypto is incentivised – presenting a huge incentive for investors to back the party.

Bolivian lawmakers approved a $1.9 billion loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund on Friday, delivering the conservative government a key victory in its efforts to ease the country's deep economic crisis as unions threatened renewed protests.

Just hours after Congress approved the loan, President Rodrigo Paz announced an immediate end to subsidies for the diesel powering Bolivia’s trucks, buses and tractors — a step toward meeting IMF demands. Gasoline, used mainly in private cars, would remain subsidized for now, though Paz had already scaled back that support in recent months.

The Senate ratified the IMF agreement a day after the lower house approved it, clearing the final legislative hurdle for the three-year financing program aimed at replenishing dwindling foreign reserves and stabilizing the ailing economy marked by high inflation and weak growth. The IMF first announced the staff-level agreement in July after months of negotiations with Paz’s market-friendly government, which took power last year after nearly two decades of socialist rule as part of a wave of new Latin American leaders allied with the Trump administration.

The program still requires approval from the IMF’s executive board before funds can be disbursed. Economy Minister Christian Morales told senators that the deal would give other lenders, including the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, greater confidence in the government and help it secure about $5 billion in additional financing.

But the assistance is conditioned on tough economic measures, including the elimination of fuel subsidies, that threaten to reignite unrest in Bolivia, where weeks of road blockades in June and July paralyzed much of the South American nation as demonstrators demanded Paz’s resignation. Congress on Thursday extended for another 90 days a state of emergency that Paz had declared to clear roads during the protests. It allows for military intervention and the suspension of some civil liberties.

The Bolivian Workers’ Central, the country’s main labor federation, and other unions have voiced fierce opposition to the IMF loan, warning that the government spending cuts required under the deal would drive up living costs and deepen hardship for struggling families.

Although Paz’s Christian Democratic Party lacks a majority in Congress, the centrist and right-wing lawmakers that dominate both chambers rallied behind the deal. The Movement Toward Socialism, the party that dominated Bolivian politics after the former coca growers’ union leader Evo Morales won the presidency in 2005, now holds just two of the 130 seats in the lower house and none in the 36-member Senate.

Declining natural gas exports have deprived Bolivia of dollars needed to import gasoline and diesel, contributing to chronic fuel shortages that began in 2023 and have persisted under Paz. The Iran war has pushed up global fuel costs, making fuel subsidies an even greater burden on public finances.

“No one can buy something expensive and sell it cheap,” Paz said in his late-night declaration that diesel in Bolivia would now be sold at international prices.

To cushion the blow, he announced about $79 million in cash assistance for 2.9 million Bolivians, along with loans on preferential terms for truckers, small businesses and producers facing higher diesel costs. He pledged to redirect subsidy spending toward schools, hospitals and roads.

He promised the change would end the country’s persistent diesel shortages, which have disrupted harvests and delayed deliveries of imported goods. “With this measure, we guarantee supplies 24 hours a day, seven days a week,” he said.

___

DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina.

News.title: Even as trading and markets moved faster, Warren Buffett made patience profitable and cool
News.content:

Even in the age of algorithms, short attention spans and TikTok teases, Warren Buffett continued to profit with his patient bargain-hunting approach while offering folksy advice on investing and life.

As chairman and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, Buffett became famous for his unwavering and methodical investing style: Buy good businesses when their prices are low, stay on the sidelines when prices are too high and be patient with well-chosen picks. He rode that to decades of beating the rest of the U.S. stock market before he retired as Berkshire's chairman on Friday, less than a year after giving up his role as CEO.

The formula of buying good things at low prices sounds simple, and it’s the foundation of a style of investing called “value” hunting. But it periodically comes under criticism when the hot new thing is enthralling Wall Street, whether it's dot-com stocks in the late 1990s or gold when its price was setting records early this year. (Buffett is famously skeptical of gold as an investment, saying it “has two significant shortcomings, being neither of much use nor procreative.”)

The investing world has had other celebrities. J.P. Morgan built his reputation by investing in railroads during the 19th century. Andrew Carnegie helped build the U.S. steel industry and became famous for his philanthropy. Jim Cramer and Kevin O'Leary are on TV shows. But few ever cracked into the national consciousness like Buffett, and none did so from near the geographic center of the country in Omaha, Nebraska.

Buffett offers enduring lessons on life and investing

Many professional investors also adhere to Buffett's style of bargain-hunting. But none have had the kind of folksy humor and candor that can draw hordes of investors each year, like those attending Berkshire Hathaway's annual shareholder meeting.

More than 40,000 people would pack an Omaha arena on the first Saturday in May to hear from Buffett and his longtime investing partner, Charlie Munger, who died in 2023 and espoused a similar take-it-slow and make-it-right approach to investing. Besides talking about how they hunted for well-run businesses and the news of the day, they would also regularly confess to their own mistakes and crack wise.

“Not a day goes by where what I've learned about Warren doesn't affect me positively, both personally and financially,” said Todd Finkle, a retired professor. He grew up in Omaha, knows Buffett's children and wrote the book, “Warren Buffett: Investor and Entrepreneur.”

When Finkle would bring students to visit the “Oracle of Omaha” for extended Q-and-A meetings, Finkle said the first topic Buffett would discuss was never financial.

“He didn’t say anything about money. The first topic that he would always bring up is that the most important thing you’ll do in your life is to pick who to marry.”

He built a reputation for honesty and trust

Following a scandal at Salomon Brothers, in which Berkshire Hathaway had an ownership stake, Buffett became chairman and testified in Congress. He said all employees were told, “After they first obey all rules, I then want employees to ask themselves whether they are willing to have any contemplated act appear the next day on the front page of their local paper to be read by their spouses, children and friends with the reporting done by an informed and critical reporter.”

That reputation for honesty, along with his famed patience for investments, helped Buffett stay famous even in this “post-truth” era where people scroll through feeds at finger-flicking speed. He's such an icon that scammers would use him in AI-generated videos that appeared to show him endorsing questionable investments or political candidates.

On Reddit's WallStreetBets forum, traders share picks for potential get-rich-quick opportunities in day-trading stocks and options. The discussion jumps from idea to idea, but even the denizens there know Buffett and his famous advice to “be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful.”

His reputation is so strong and his advice so well-known that some memes on the forum ironically joke about doing the opposite, with a picture of Buffett suggesting that everyone freak out and sell in a panic.

Buffett's lessons go well beyond business

Bob Miles, who has taught a college course about Buffett for 16 years, said that people might initially get attracted to Buffett because he is rich and has made many Berkshire shareholders wealthy. But their interest deepens after reading Buffett’s annual letters, which became required reading for many investors, and hearing him speak in interviews.

Through reading and listening, people would glean nuggets from Buffett like his core rules for investing: “Rule No. 1: Never lose money. Rule No. 2: Never forget Rule No. 1.” Or that “you only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out,” referencing how tough times will quickly show who has been taking too much risk. He also suggested that “who you associate with is just enormously important. Don’t expect that you’ll make every decision right on that. But you are going to have your life progress in the general direction of the people you work with, that you admire, that become your friends.”

“People associate him with successful investing, but I look at him more and more as kind of a guide toward how to live a successful life, whatever your talents happen to be,” Miles said.

Few investors have broad appeal like Buffett

At the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School of business, trips for students to Berkshire's annual meetings were always a hot ticket. “I don’t know of any time that it wasn’t popular,” said David Musto, a finance professor at the school and faculty director of the Jacobs Master of Science in Quantitative Finance.

With Buffett’s departure from the stage, the obvious question is whether anyone else could replace him as the world’s most famous value investor.

Musto said some other big names still exist in the investing world, such as Will Danoff at Fidelity Investments, who is retiring from day-to-day management at the end of the year. But it's difficult to find someone with as strong and as long a track record as Buffett's. Or the wit and personality.

Musto said it's important for value investing to remain a force in the market, particularly when traders are jumping into meme stocks, obscure cryptocurrencies and other bets built more on hope that their prices will go up than belief that it's a good business trading at a good price.

“It certainly helps to have people in the middle,” Musto said, “thinking about the value of a stock.”

Italian health authorities see evidence that rising temperatures and longer warm seasons are helping mosquitoes spread West Nile virus across a wider area, during more months of the year.

More than 650 infections have been reported in Italy so far this year, accounting for roughly half of all cases recorded in Europe, according to local health authorities.

“Higher temperatures linked to climate change help mosquitoes reproduce and extend the transmission season, increasing the chances that infected mosquitoes will spread the virus to people,” said Antonino Bella, researcher at Italy’s National Institute of Health, or ISS.

West Nile has been considered endemic in Italy since 2020, when cases started to surge, and is now reported every summer and early fall. About 80% of infected people develop no symptoms, while most others experience a mild flu-like illness. Severe neurological complications occur in a small minority of cases, mainly among older adults and people with underlying health conditions.

Experts say this year’s case numbers are broadly in line with recent seasons.

But warmer temperatures favor mosquito reproduction and can mean the transmission season sometimes lasts as late as November, Bella explained. Areas once largely unaffected are increasingly reporting infections, reflecting a gradual expansion of the virus across the country.

Italy’s experience with the virus is drawing attention from European countries located farther north. A Belgian research team visited the ISS last May to study Italy’s research and surveillance system after the country began recording locally acquired West Nile cases.

The Netherlands this year has reported more than two dozen West Nile cases, the first since 2020, as well as several deaths, according to its public health institute.

“There’s no doubt that warming weather will expand the period of replication for the virus and the vector in more countries,” said Marc-Alain Widdowson, who leads the Pandemic Threats, Communicable Diseases, and AMR Division at the World Health Organization’s Europe office.

“You’ve got to be careful not to say that climate change is all of it, but certainly a warming climate means that we have a longer mosquito season, so that the vectors can survive for longer. Warm temperatures also mean that the virus itself will survive better,” he added.

Experts note that Italy’s extensive monitoring network, which tracks mosquitoes, birds, blood donors and human infections, also helps explain why the country detects so many cases.

“There are definitely trends which we think are contributing to increased activity,” Widdowson said, citing a warming climate, loss of biodiversity and changes in land use. A longer mosquito season creates more opportunities for transmission, he added, while declines in bird diversity may favor species that are efficient reservoirs of the virus.

In June, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control, or ECDC, warned that because Europe is experiencing a warming trend — with heat waves and flooding becoming more frequent and severe, and summers getting longer and warmer — the conditions are more favorable for invasive mosquito species such as Aedes albopictus and Aedes aegypti.

Aedes aegypti — known to transmit dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya, zika and West Nile viruses — has been established in Cyprus since 2022 and may spread to other European countries.

A decade ago, the Aedes albopictus mosquito was established in eight European countries, with 114 regions affected. This year, the mosquito is established in 13 countries and 337 regions, the ECDC said.

Ed Sheeran is set to resume his tour Saturday — possibly solo — after all his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.

It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original U.S. opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.

Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.

Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists' support. As of Friday, tickets were still available for Saturday's show, and his website did not list any replacement acts. A coalition of pro-Palestinian organizations plans to protest outside the show Saturday afternoon.

The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey. Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday.

Within hours of Sheeran's statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.

Macklemore said Wednesday he is donating $1 million to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift; a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million but have not specified where the money will be directed. Sheeran's representatives have not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the No. 3 top-earning concert act since 2021.

Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.

The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.

He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.

While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran's magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

News.title: GPs summoned in Frankfurt as third malaria death reported
News.content:
While malaria is treatable if caught early, the patients were likely not considered to have the disease because they lacked travel history to countries where malaria typically circulates, meaning treatment was delayed.

“This is why we alerted the medical people in Frankfurt, if you have odd cases presenting at your clinic, please also consider that there might be malaria around,” Dr Tinnemann said.

“There is this assumption that people who get sick with a nasty fever in places like Frankfurt and elsewhere that have not travelled cannot have malaria, and we don’t bother to investigate. That’s got to stop. That’s why these people die,” Joe Lines, Professor of Malaria Control and Vector Biology at the London School of Tropical Hygiene and Medicine, told The Telegraph.

Before the two cases in Schwanheim – both of which occurred at least 3 miles from the airport where the first malaria cases were reported – investigators were working on the hypothesis that just a single mosquito was responsible for the outbreak, but the new cases have cast doubt on that theory.

“We expect mosquitoes to live between one and three weeks on average,” said Dr Tinnemann.

“We had five cases in the beginning of July, then another in August - at that point, there was a good chance that potentially it could just be one bug. But now it seems at least there must be one other,” he said.

Frankfurt’s public health board have now shipped blood samples from all eight patients to a specialised lab in Antwerp, Belgium, where scientists can carry out DNA analysis to indicate if the infections came from one or multiple mosquitoes, and are awaiting results.

As temperatures warm, experts fear that several tropical mosquito-borne diseases – including malaria, dengue fever, Zika virus, and chikungunya could become established across Europe.

Earlier this month, a colony of Aedes aeypti mosquitoes – the bugs responsible for transmitting dengue and Zika virus – were found breeding in a residential area in East London for the first time.

Airfinity, the disease-monitoring company, said of the malaria outbreak in Frankfurt: “the risk to the wider public remains low but non-zero.”

“Continued vector surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and ready access to antimalarials are critical to prevent further severe outcomes.”

News.title: Global fund utilises AI to tackle malaria, TB, and HIV amid aid cuts
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is helping to soften the blow from aid cuts, according to one of the world’s biggest development funds.

The Global Fund, which raises and invests billions of pounds to reduce the burden of HIV, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria globally says new AI-driven products like portable pregnancy scanners are helping to mitigate the funding gap.

“[We] have adapted pretty quickly to the changes in the funding environment; it has undoubtedly had negative impacts on health outcomes [...], but in some ways, the resilience of life-saving services has been remarkable,” Peter Sands, the executive director of the Global Fund, told The Telegraph.

The Global Fund is managing a $6 billion (£4.4bn) shortfall for the period 2026 to 2028 and has been forced to make difficult decisions to continue their work, it confirmed this week.

The gap comes as Western governments shift money from foreign aid to defence. The UK reduced its contribution to the fund by 15 per cent last year to £850 million, down from £1 billion.

But Mr Sands said investments in tools to tackle infectious diseases – including those driven by AI – are starting to pay off.

“Innovation is absolutely part of the answer when money is short. One of the few ways you can get to make the money go further is to have a better tool, a better way of doing things,” Mr Sands said.

News.title: Thomas Tuchel faces fight to win trust of England players
News.content:
Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and said: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

News.title: Fiji declares national crisis as HIV epidemic escalates
News.content:
“The rollout has been slow and frustrating, and Fiji will pay for it in terms of lives lost,” said Prof Lisa Maher, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute in Sydney who is supporting Fiji’s response. “This is the only thing that will turn the epidemic around and stop people dying, and stop onward transmission of HIV to the general population.”

But the emergency declaration should provide political cover to introduce the needle and syringe programme, with a Cabinet subcommittee now created to remove barriers to action.

“The government is signalling that it is prepared to act in this particularly important and controversial area,” said Prof Maher. “It’s not coincidental that the draft bill [to legalise the distribution of needles and syringes for certain groups] now looks likely to go before parliament, after being blocked for 10 months… So it’s not just symbolic.”

Dr Jason Mitchell, head of Fiji’s HIV taskforce, added: “Since the government announced [the crisis], it has followed with some very rapid actions in progressing the needle and syringe programme. So that is being fast tracked through the necessary channels, and the government is determined to get that out in the next couple of weeks.

“We’ve gotten to the point where we really needed to take some really strong action,” he told The Telegraph. “This is the government realising that there have been challenges, and they need to step it up.”

It is hoped that the declaration will also turbocharge other elements of the response – for instance the scale-up of the post-exposure prophylaxis (Prep) scheme, which was introduced in May – as the virus gains a foothold in the broader population.

Although there has been a major focus on testing, treatment and education, UNAIDS still estimates that only 39 per cent of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in 2025 knew their positive status. Just 22 per cent were accessing antiretroviral treatment, and 117 people died in 2025, compared to 25 in 2021.

News.title: Floyd Samba’s Man City debut double has father Chris dancing
News.content:
There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.

This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.

But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.

Floyd Samba scored two fine goals and had a hand in another on a dream debut that had his beaming dad up off his seat and thrusting his arms in the air as if ready to party.

If the Samba surname feels familiar, that is because Floyd’s father Christopher played more than 200 games for Blackburn Rovers, Queens Park Rangers and Aston Villa.

In fact, it was very much a family affair as Floyd’s brothers Tyrone and Emerson, who are also in City’s academy and hoping one day to tread a similar path, joined in the jubilant celebrations alongside their mother, a visibly emotional Theresa.

News.title: Banton shows his worth as England cruise to series victory against Sri Lanka
News.content:
A patchy Test team and a one-day international side learning on the job should not obscure the fact that under Harry Brook, England have built a formidable T20 outfit.

Missing a slew of first-choice players, they dispatched Sri Lanka with a game to spare and an emphatic show of their depth in the format, with Sonny Baker and Tom Banton – two men still finding their feet in the side – to the fore. England have now won 20 of the 23 completed T20s since Brook took over last year, and six matches in a row this summer. It is easily their best format and, as Liam Dawson said, they have “match-winners throughout” and plenty of “freak” performers.

In this six-wicket win, Baker’s one for 15 limited England’s target to a paltry 146, which Banton, a natural opener who is being recommissioned in the middle order, helped knock off with 47 balls remaining. “Tonight was a special performance, very clinical,” said Brook.

News.title: Interest rate increase ‘likely’, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Andrew Bailey has said that interest rates are likely to rise if the Middle East war rages on, warning inflation is now on course to hit 4pc.

The Bank of England opted to hold borrowing costs at 3.75pc on Thursday, the sixth time in a row it has left them unchanged.

However, the Governor said a “material” increase in energy prices since July would push up inflation to twice the Bank’s 2pc target.

He warned the outlook for inflation “continues to be on the upside” and criticised the “seeming loss of urgency to find solutions” to the war in Iran.

Oil prices are back above $100 a barrel and analysts expect average gas and electricity bills to rise above £2,000 this winter as the conflict continues.

Mr Bailey said: “So far, higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK.

“But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2pc target.”

Investors expect the Bank to raise interest rates as soon as November, which has pushed average mortgage rates to their highest level in three years.

The average five-year fixed mortgage deal has risen to 5.87pc, according to Moneyfacts, which is the highest level since November 2023 and up from 4.95pc before the Iran war.

Thursday’s rate hold leaves the Bank out of step with central banks around the world after the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank voted to raise borrowing costs this month.

However, economists said there had been a change in tone from policymakers over the threat posed by energy prices and whether this would feed into the wider economy.

The Bank of England predicted that inflation would hit 4pc early next year, just as most workers are negotiating pay rises.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said: “It seems as though a majority of the MPC is on the cusp of wanting to tighten policy.”

In a warning on the impending pain facing households, Mr Bailey told the Chancellor that energy bills would rise by 24pc early next year under the Ofgem price cap.

This will push up annual average bills by £413 to £2,136, which the Governor blamed on the war in the Middle East.

The Governor is required to write a formal letter to the Chancellor every time inflation is more than a percentage point above its 2pc target.

Official data showed inflation rose to 3.1pc in August.

Mr Bailey said: “The energy price shock has been the most important factor driving recent short-term movements in inflation.”

Despite expectations of higher rates, the FTSE 100 rose on Thursday at its steepest pace since July, climbing more than 1pc, as the Bank of England eased the pressure on the UK bond market.

Policymakers also confirmed a Telegraph report that the Bank will stop selling the long-dated bonds it amassed during the financial crisis and lockdown.

The Bank will continue actively selling £20bn of government bonds per year until the rest of the stockpile is wound down to zero in 2034.

The announcement triggered a sharp fall in the cost of borrowing for the Treasury, with the yield on 30-year UK gilts falling at the fastest pace since May.

News.title: Next-generation antivenom fights India’s deadliest snakes
News.content:
The process to make antivenom has barely changed in a century: snakes are milked, their venom is injected into horses, and their antibodies are harvested to form the basis of the product. The resulting treatments are difficult to administer, can trigger severe side effects, and the quality varies from batch to batch.

“The big four snakes contribute to 70 per cent of poisonous bites [in India]… so 30 per cent of poisonous snakes are not covered, even to begin with,” said Dr Yogesh Jain, a public health physician in Chhattisgarh state and a member of The Global Snakebite Taskforce.

“But there are huge quality and efficacy issues even against these 70 per cent of bites. We’re relying on a 100-year-old technique of getting antivenoms, and at least 50,000 people are dying every year,” he told The Telegraph.

“There’s a real need for new technology. We don’t have a safe and appropriate antivenom for the largest majority of people in rural India.”

Now, scientists are hopeful that they have developed a potential alternative.

In the latest study, published last week, researchers showed that an experimental antivenom cocktail with five components protected mice against lethal doses of antivenom in Indian cobras, even when delayed by up to 20 minutes – a scenario that mimics the real-world lag between a bite and treatment.

“If you go 10 years back, people didn’t think you could make sufficiently simple products with new, modern biotechnology that could cover all these different snake venoms,” said Prof Andreas Laustsen-Kiel, head of the Section of Biologics Engineering at the Technical University of Denmark and co-author of the paper.

“People simply believed it was too complex, too expensive to manufacture, and so on… But the data we are gathering is convincing enough to say this is something that could make a huge dent in the lost lives and limbs snakebite causes every year.”

The antivenom itself was based on lab-made nanobodies – antibodies derived from a group of animals including camels, llamas and some species of shark. Scientists believe their structure means they could be a more potent, more precise, more temperature-stable alternative to man-made monoclonal antibodies – and cheaper to manufacture.

“The latest study builds on an earlier discovery of nanobodies that can protect across a broad spectrum of African snakes,” said Prof Nicholas Casewell, director of the Centre for Snakebite Research and Interventions at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, who has previously collaborated with Prof Laustsen-Kiel.

“In this paper they have iterated and demonstrated that a narrow number of nanobodies can protect against Indian cobras and king cobras. This demonstration brings the nanobody technology closer to market,” he added.

But that is likely still years away, depending on how much funding the researchers can attract. The next steps – a larger animal study, scaling up manufacture, and launching human trials – are expensive.

“If money was no issue, we could probably be testing in humans in 1.5 to three years from now,” said Prof Laustsen-Kiel. “But since money is a big issue, it is more likely that human trials won’t be able to start until 2.5 to four years from now.

“But I really think that this [study shows] there’s no doubt that biotech can deliver better antivenoms. The question is whether people are willing to fund it,” he said.

Sports.title: 'Bullied' and 'out of control' - Chelsea's defensive issues laid bare
Sports.content:
"You need to feel it. We're not feeling it," said Xabi Alonso after Chelsea's 3-0 loss at Brentford. Yet Chelsea are stuck in a familiar feeling.

Another defeat, their 11th of the calendar year - more than they had in 2025, with three months of this year to go. At least two goals conceded for the fifth straight Premier League game under Alonso. More set-piece woe.

"We dropped our consistency, our competitive mentality needed in the second half," said Alonso. That will concern Chelsea fans the most. It was way too easy for Brentford to take over that second half.

And there's another continuing trend: Chelsea being outbattled in a match. Remember, they were outrun in the vast majority of their Premier League matches last season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Brentford and Chelsea.

The first thing you think about when you come up against Brentford is set pieces. Long throws, smart corners - the lot. And just like against Hull in their previous game, Chelsea lost control of the match by conceding once again from a set-piece.

This was the fourth goal they have conceded from a set-piece in five Premier League games - taking their overall tally since the start of last season to 23, the joint-worst out of any Premier League side.

Once again, the ball was put right on top of Emiliano Martinez towards the back post and neither the goalkeeper nor the outfield players were able to react. And the worst part of it for Chelsea? Brentford saw it coming a mile off.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jaidon Anthony heads Brentford in front against Chelsea.

"We did target [the back post] at half-time," said Vitaly Janelt to Sky Sports. "There was a big gap at the far post. We targeted that and I think it was our first corner of the second half."

And Chelsea are suffering from all these set-piece woes despite now having the best dead-ball coach in the league in Austin MacPhee. Bernardo Cueva, who was their set-piece coach before MacPhee and now has a different role at the club, was even pinched from Brentford by the Blues.

"We have not been good enough, at times we have been bullied and we need to improve at that," said Levi Colwill to Sky.

Image: Chelsea are struggling at the back

"But we trust in our set-piece coach; we are still adjusting to new things, but we do need to improve as a team."

It is not the only area where Chelsea need to improve defensively. The way they allow teams to penetrate their defensive third is among the worst in the division - they have gone 22 straight Premier League games without a clean sheet.

Image: Chelsea have been struggling all season at the back

On average, Chelsea concede 2.2 non-penalty goals per game. And they deserve to, because the xG numbers say they are expected to allow that same number of shots on target on their goal.

What doesn't help is a clear inability to protect the penalty area. Chelsea are also in the top three this season for conceding shots in their own penalty area on average, allowing around 10 per game. Their goalkeepers get used as a battering ram.

With defensive numbers like these, it's no wonder Chelsea have been unable to hold onto a lead in their last three league games.

They explode out of the blocks so quickly - this was the first Premier League game where they failed to take the lead in the opening 10 minutes of the game, but they nearly did when Pedro Neto had a good chance saved.

And then when Chelsea fall behind, they have been pegged back so many times that the bad habits kick in. "It's about everything. It's about the mentality, the football and the tactical things that we need to keep improving," said Alonso.

"We concede the first goal, you're still in the game but then we lose the shape. We were out of control."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch as Kevin Schade pushes Chelsea's Valentin Barco during Brentford's 3-0 win over Chelsea.

That control could be eased in the future when Moises Caicedo returns, but the lack of solidity they have without the Ecuadorian is a concern.

Two summer recruits in Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco started the Brentford game, but it was the Bees who looked stronger in midfield.

Keith Andrews' side arguably have the better squad depth in that area of the pitch as well - they won the match 3-0 with record signing Mamadou Sangare sat on the bench for over an hour.

Right now, Joao Pedro looks like Chelsea's most influential player from a goalscoring perspective. The 'JP Morgan' frontline was broken up for the first time this season - and Chelsea failed to score for the first time this season.

Of course, it was always going to take time for Alonso to implement his ideas at Stamford Bridge. This was a Chelsea team with seven summer signings in its starting line-up, with the Spaniard the fourth manager to take charge of the club in nine months.

"It doesn't happen overnight," former Chelsea captain Gary Cahill told Sky Sports. "I think with what you're saying he will be judged in the next five, six, seven weeks to get this right because you will have that time on the training ground and then we should start to see his methods coming through because we've seen him in an attacking sense."

"It's not just set-pieces," said Alonso on where Chelsea have to improve. "In defensive duels, build-up and controlling games." That being said, there aren't many more parts of the game besides those four.

"We've got a lot to work on over the international break," added Colwill. He can say that again.

Sports.title: How belief of Wakefield's inner sanctum led to history-making semi-final
Sports.content:
When Wakefield Trinity came back into Super League for the 2025 season, there wouldn't have been many who would have foreseen a semi-final appearance within two seasons- except those in their inner sanctum.

That inner sanctum, among others, consists of owner Matt Ellis, head of recruitment Ste Mills, and head coach Daryl Powell.

Working in tandem, they came up with a plan for how they would continually progress: they have signed raw talent, made them stars, provided a stadium that both home and away fans enjoy attending, and now brought the progressive and rapid success that their most faithful have been waiting so long to see.

An example of turning that raw talent into a shining diamond? Caleb Hamlin-Uele. Wakefield saw something in a player who was not breaking through in the NRL. They brought him into the Championship, moulded him, made him one of Super League's best props, and now he is truly in contention to represent England at the World Cup this autumn.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look as Emre Guler gets sent off for Wakefield Trinity against Leigh Leopards .

Of course, the biggest success of all would be a trophy. But for now, they are through to their first ever Super League semi-final after their 26-16 victory over Leigh in the Eliminators.

Wakefield's victory was down to their immense forward pack which took control early in the second half. Even with Emre Guler shown red on the hour mark for what appeared to be a punch, they had done enough to keep Leigh at arm's length and see the game home.

It is further reward for what has been a remarkable rise from Wakefield.

Image: The Wakefield Trinity faithful were delighted

Image: The full-time celebrations were a glimpse into what the moment means for Wakefield

"We are going to go where we are going to go. We are just going to prepare as best we can," Powell said.

"I think we can beat anybody.

"Wakefield have never won a play-off game - that is a box ticked.

"Now it is whether we can win a Grand Final. We have two games to do something special.

"It is difficult but doable.

"You are one game away from getting to a Grand Final that would be huge for the club.

"You have got to be excited by that. We are all excited about how good we can be as a team.

"We will do everything we need to in order to give ourselves the best chance to do that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look as Caius Faatili barges through to score emphatic try for Wakefield Trinity against Leigh Leopards.

Powell has been there and done this before with a team that was not expected to be at the big dance. Castleford, back in 2017, blew everyone away, won the League Leaders' Shield, then beat St Helens with a Luke Gale drop goal to make it to Old Trafford.

They could not complete the final hurdle.

Wakefield have two more hurdles to go. A semi-final against either Wigan Warriors or Leeds Rhinos. A win in that? Then they go to the Theatre of Dreams trying to complete theirs.

If they do that, the inner sanctum's belief that raw potential can become greatness will have been achieved.

Sports.title: Littler overcomes lively crowd to beat Noppert at World Series of Darts Finals
Sports.content:
Luke Littler battled past Danny Noppert and a lively Dutch crowd to reach the second round at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.

Littler, who has won every major tournament this year, reacted to effectively an away crowd twice in a dramatic contest to beat Noppert 6-4 and keep his hopes of an unprecedented clean sweep alive.

It sparked memories of several nights at this year's Premier League Darts when Littler faced whistles and jeers throughout the series on his way to winning the title, revealing afterwards he wanted to quit the invitational event.

Noppert capitalised on a slow start by Littler to break in the third leg and held a 3-1 lead but the key moment came when he made a mess of a 44 checkout in the sixth leg which allowed Littler to break back and make it 3-3.

After winning that leg, Littler let out a huge roar and put his hands to his ears, asking the crowd for more noise as they booed him loudly.

Noppert missed two darts to restore his break advantage in the next leg and Littler punished him, then the teenager took out a superb 95 checkout with tops-tops to move 5-4 ahead and broke his opponent to win the match.

"Coming back from a losing position to win is always a great feeling," said Littler, who won the World Series of Darts Finals in 2024.

"I'm not putting pressure on myself. I am just focusing on round by round."

Image: Luke Littler reacted to the crowd during the match (PDC/Kelly Deckers)

Should Littler win this weekend and win the following two tournaments, the World Grand Prix and European Championship, he would become the first player to hold every major darts title at the same time.

He would then set about trying to complete a remarkable clean sweep in November at the Grand Slam of Darts and Players Championship finals, but he's taking things one match at a time and will next face Nathan Aspinall in the second round of this week's competition.

"Nathan always throws everything at me. He produces his best, I perform at my best, and hopefully it's another great game tomorrow," said Littler.

"It would be one of the best darts achievements if I could pull it off [the clean sweep], but it's still a very long way away."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stephen Bunting says Luke Littler has 'changed' Darts since bursting onto the scene a few years ago, but says he believes 'The Nuke' won't win as many world titles as darts legend Phil Taylor

A night of close matches

Unlike the first night when Michael van Gerwen was stunned by Daryl Gurney, there were no major surprises as the first round came to a conclusion on Friday.

Former world champion Gerwyn Price raced into a 5-0 lead against Brody Klinge but the Australian fought back to 5-4 before Price stumbled over the line.

It was a similar story for his compatriot Jonny Clayton as he was 4-0 up before missing several match darts on his way to a 6-3 win over Maik Kuivenhoven, who was called up as a late replacement for Lourence Ilagan after the Philippines player withdrew due to visa issues.

Image: Gerwyn Price could be the player to stop Luke Littler at the World Series of Darts Finals (PDC/Kelly Deckers)

James Wade edged out Damon Heta 6-5 after the latter missed a match dart in their deciding leg, while Aspinall fought back from 4-2 down to defeat Raymond Smith 6-4.

Having won six Players Championship events this year, Wessel Nijman is looking to turn that great form into something big on the televised stage and he started off his World Series of Darts campaign with a 6-4 win over veteran Simon Whitlock.

And there were 6-5 narrow wins for Canada's Jim Long over Australia's Adam Leek, plus Alexandra Palace cult hero Motomu Sakai against Callan Rydz.

Sports.title: Ballard heads Bristol City past Watford as they climb to fifth
Sports.content:
Bristol City moved into the Championship play-off places with a 1-0 victory over depleted Watford.

Dominic Ballard's first-half header was enough for all three points for the Robins at Ashton Gate, steering a backwards header in from Rio Cardines' ball into the box.

It was a much-needed win for Michael Skubala's side after back-to-back defeats leading into this clash on Friday night.

Bristol City now rise to fifth in the table ahead of the rest of the weekend's action and then the extended upcoming international break.

Watford, meanwhile, who have an injury-ravaged squad under Alessio Dionisi, remain in the bottom half of the table. They have picked up just a point on the road all season.

The key moments from Ashton Gate

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dom Ballard's superb header saw Bristol City go ahead in the first half against Watford.

3: BIG CHANCE! Bristol City should be ahead. Lovely work from Ballard to jink in down the left and cross into the middle. Knight arrives unmarked but he heads wide!

8: CHANCE! Now a good opening for Watford. Nabizada slinks inside and sees his shot blocked into the path of Kjerrumgaard. He then prods over from 12 yards.

11: PENALTY SHOUT! Atkinson then goes down in the box and wants a penalty after a challenge from Doumbia, but the referee is not interested. Hard to track in real time, but on replays it was clear that Doumbia got Atkinson before the ball.

31: GOAL! Bristol City have the lead that their dominance has earned! Cardines with another assist! His sixth of the season as he whips in a lovely inswinging cross and Dominic Ballard rises with his back to goal to steer a header into the corner!

80: CHANCE! Tolaj could seal it! A long ball forward from Tanner finds the run of the striker. He gets in between two Watford defenders, but then lashes over.

87: PENALTY SHOUT! Boadu feels he's having his shirt pulled in the box as he goes down! But the referee is not interested in the Watford man's protests!

The managers

Bristol City's Michael Skubala:

"Dom's got great movement in and around the box and I thought he could get down the sides of the two centre-halves. I thought he could link quite well. [Lorent] Tolaj does it well as well, but Dom's a really good mover without the ball and he creates little moments for himself.

"I think the goal is just a typical Dom Ballard goal that I've seen over the last few years.

"I was really pleased. It's not easy to come back off a couple of results that we lost, but it really showed some resilience to bounce back. A win's a win and a good clean sheet.

"I thought we showed, especially in the first half, some really good intensity with the ball. We moved it really well, shifted the play and looked really threatening. In the second half, naturally, we were a little bit lower, but we had some fast transition moments to go and get the second.

"We challenged the group with a clean sheet and making sure we defended our box solidly, and I thought the lads were great. The other thing was that I made seven changes, which is showing the squad depth. Not many people make seven changes and some of the lads put in great performances."

Watford's Alessio Dionisi:

"For a lot of matches we played with all the same players, the same line-up. Today it was difficult to ask other players.

"It's not easy because, for example, today on the bench there weren't midfielders, there weren't defenders. It was difficult.

"I'm not happy sometimes with the situation in the last 20 metres because we arrived near the box and then played back. It's not good, but we have a lot of young players.

"Today there were six young players in the line-up. Two 19-year-olds and two 20-year-olds. It's not easy, but I believe in our future because it's important.

"I speak every day with my director, with my owner, with the club. The club knows this situation well because at the start I wasn't happy. It's difficult to start when we had a few players.

"I know a lot of players arrived at the end of the [window], but now it's important to recover a lot of players.

"I spoke in the dressing room with my team. Now it's important to believe, to work together, because I believe in this team, I believe in our job."

Sports.title: Chelsea's defensive woes continue as Brentford win derby
Sports.content:
Chelsea's defensive and set-piece woes continued under Xabi Alonso as Brentford claimed an emphatic 3-0 victory in the west London derby.

It was all too easy for Brentford to win it as first Mikkel Damsgaard's corner was nodded across by Jannik Schuster, leaving Jaidon Anthony to nod home unmarked from a few yards out.

Then with Chelsea pushing for a leveller and moving to a back four, Brentford hit the Blues on the counter as Kevin Schade broke through. His one-on-one was saved by Emiliano Martinez but Igor Thiago struck home from close range to end his seven-game goal drought.

And with virtually the last kick of the game, Fabio Carvalho scored his first Premier League goal since his near-year-long injury lay-off after tucking home Schade's cross while unmarked at the far post.

Image: Igor Thiago celebrates his second

Chelsea have now conceded 12 goals - the most in the league - from five Premier League games as the wait for their first top-flight clean sheet of the season goes on.

Unimpressive in defence, but in attack, Chelsea weren't much better - clearly missing the injured Joao Pedro, with replacement Danny Welbeck failing to generate any clear chances in his place.

Moises Caicedo was another big miss, with his replacement being Jordan Henderson, who made an unsuccessful first start for the Blues at the club he joined them from.

Cole Palmer looked bright in sparks, but the Blues never really generated anything apart from Pedro Neto's ninth-minute effort, kept out by Caoimhin Kelleher.

Brentford - who have become the first team to stop Chelsea scoring this season - continue their unbeaten start to the season to go up to third. Speaking of three, that's the number of Premier League games without a win for Alonso's Chelsea.

The key moments from the Gtech...

9: SAVE! Danny Welbeck tees up Pedro Neto in the area but his shot is saved by Caoimhin Kelleher.

41: BLOCK! Morgan Rogers has a good shooting chance in the penalty area but his effort is blocked by Schuster.

50: OFF THE BAR! Anthony strikes the top of the bar with a header from inside the box. The offside flag goes up but replays showed he was level.

61: GOAL! Brentford take the advantage as Schuster heads Mikkel Damsgaard's corner across and Anthony nods in from a few yards out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jaidon Anthony heads Brentford in front against Chelsea.

82: GOAL! Schade breaks through for a one-on-one but sees an effort saved, yet Thiago taps in the rebound to seal the points.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Igor Thiago scores Brentford second against Chelsea.

90+4: GOAL! Carvalho makes it three by tapping home at the far post from Schade's wicked ball across.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fabio Carvalho scores Brentford third to seal win over Chelsea

Alonso: This is not enough from Chelsea

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso speaking to Sky Sports:

"I'm disappointed with the second half and with the result. This is not enough to compete in the Premier League.

"We were not able to maintain our level for the full 90 minutes and that's why we were punished today.

"It's about everything. It's about the mentality, the football and the tactical things that we need to keep improving. We can do much better."

On whether Joao Pedro's absence played a part:

"It's not about looking for excuses.

"We need to look at each other and know that we have to work and improve because there is still a long way to go. We have to check many things.

"We got into situations, but we were not precise enough with the final action. That's why we didn't score."

Andrews: Something was bubbling at Brentford

Brentford boss Keith Andrews speaking to Sky Sports:

"I think it's important that you enjoy these nights. There's no point hiding it. There are some tough days in the game, and you've got to enjoy the different emotions.

"I felt like there was something bubbling towards tonight. I have this unbelievable calm around the team because I trust them, so it's nice to see it come to fruition.

"I see humility and hunger within the group every day. We're very respectful of each other, but we're going to get better. We have to continue improving in this league.

"We try to push boundaries and be really open with each other. Let's continue on our journey because I'm loving it."
