World.title: WATCH: Tensions flare at meeting over Charles’ Barking Lodge aquaculture project
World.content:
ST THOMAS, Jamaica — A sensitisation meeting over a controversial aquaculture project in Barking Lodge, St Thomas erupted in chaos Tuesday as tensions boiled over amid continued opposition to the development near a primary school in the community.

The meeting, held at the Barking Lodge Primary and Infant School, the institution located behind the proposed fish ponds, ended abruptly when Member of Parliament for St Thomas Eastern Rose Shaw and her team walked out.

Dr Michelle Charles, the former St Thomas Eastern Member of Parliament and director of St Thomas Farms Limited, the company behind the project, had organised the sensitisation meeting for the development which was suspended due to a lack of environmental permits.

At the meeting, an overview of the project was presented along with environmental and safety measures that will guide the development.

WATCH: Charles defends Barking Lodge aquaculture project, addresses safety concerns

Clive Williams, director of the National Fisheries Authority, said the organisation determined that the project was conducted according to agricultural standards and was indeed feasible.

“When we looked at the site, the water source that is available, the proximity to the community, we realised that the project is feasible… We don’t see any challenges of it having an adverse effect on the environment and the community,” Williams said.

Despite Williams’ assurances, tensions flared as critics of the project maintained their skepticism, while Shaw accused the chairman of the meeting of having a political agenda.

“I am utterly disgusted with what is taking place… a politician is cheering the meeting,” Shaw said.

The meeting subsequently erupted in a shouting match before ending prematurely, and even the police had to be called in to quell tensions.

Charles has described the initiative as having the potential to become one of the first major commercial aquaculture operations on Jamaica’s eastern side. She said responsible investment of this nature could contribute to job creation, skills training, infrastructure improvements and sustained economic growth in an area that has experienced limited commercial development since the decline of the sugar industry.

According to Charles, consultations were held with the school’s principal before construction of the ponds began, and student safety has remained a priority throughout the planning process.

World.title: ‘Mommy, them want me turn cruff”
World.content:
BICKERSTETH, St James — The lament of a 10-year-old student struck a chord with residents Thursday after thieves ransacked Bickersteth Primary and Infant School, making off with computers and tuck shop supplies in the fifth break-in there in just seven years.

“Mommy, them people yah want me turn cruff,” was how the boy reacted to news of the break-in, his mother told the Jamaica Observer.

The mother, who asked not be named, said her son, a grade five student, cried on the verandah of their house as he was told that school would be closed on Thursday and Friday because of the crime.

“I told him ‘Son, you nah turn cruff, we will stand with you’,” she related to the Observer.

Cruff is a Jamaican colloquial term for individuals who are deemed lazy, lack ambition, or have poor social etiquette.

The mother is among parents and residents who are now expressing anguish over the situation at the school.

“I usually send him out before me, but he has to stay home with his sister today,” the distraught mother said.

On Thursday morning, school administrators turned up to see windows and doors at the school pried open and items missing.

“They ripped the grill out the wall, broke the window and came in,” Principal Robert Gordon said. “Not even [Hurricane] Melissa did a job like that, the place was ransacked.”

Category 5 Melissa left widespread destruction across western and south-western parishes last October.

Principal Gordon said Thursday’s early morning break-in was the fifth in seven years.

“Last year, this time, they broke into the school twice, but that individual was held. We lost some equipment as well — computers and food items,” Gordon said.

He speculated that the robbery may be connected with others committed in western Jamaica in recent times.

“Based on what is happening now and the series of schools — Bogue Hill, Retrieve, Anchovy — it seems like they are just going through and hitting schools in a series,” Gordon said.

A man who gave his name as Anglin, described the break-in as disheartening.

“I have four daughters and all of them went through here. The last one was head girl at Anchovy, one got 11 subjects at Mount Alvernia, but this is the ground where it all started,” he said.

“This is heartbreaking, man,” he added.

On Thursday, following an emergency meeting of the school board, several members of staff were seen engaged in cleaning-up activities while listening to gospel music amid the sound of power tools as work was ongoing to replace a damaged window.

“We are trying to fix back as best as possible, even though it might be temporary, but we want to secure the area from the elements because rain may fall and the entire area is ripped out and we don’t want the office to be compromised any further,” Principal Gordon told the Observer.

“The gentleman that is working now is a community person; he’s from the area, his children came to school here. We called him, he dropped what he was doing, and he’s here and we are very appreciative of that,” Gordon said, adding that the school will be closed for the rest of the week while they work to sort things out. However, online classes will be held.

“One of the things we looked at is the impact it will have on the students seeing the school ripped apart and that could have a long-term impact on their mental psyche,” the principal explained.

“We said, ‘Okay, let’s sort of fix back the school in a way, because these children are very young, they are very impressionable, and we have to be mindful of what they see’,” he added.

“We have spoken to the teachers and we have asked them to send out work for the students to do virtually,” he revealed.

On Wednesday, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon acknowledged that schools, particularly in western Jamaica, are being plagued by break-ins since the start of the academic year.

“The west has gone through a lot of trauma for us to be dealing with theft of computers for these schools and these children, it is really heartbreaking,” she lamented during the weekly post-Cabinet news briefing.

She said the series of robberies has resulted in her reaching out to the national security minister and police commissioner for assistance.

World.title: ‘It’s a fallacy’
World.content:
ROBINSON... we’re far from being in a good position in the economy

Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson has dismissed as a “fallacy” the rosy picture of the Jamaican economy presented by Finance Minister Fayval Williams during Wednesday’s post-Cabinet media briefing.

Among other things, Williams noted that the rate of recovery from the fallout caused by Hurricane Melissa, which destroyed large swathes of south- and north-western parishes last October, was 18 months ahead of earlier projections by the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ).

However, Robinson is pointing to inflation running at nearly eight per cent and a $30-billion tax revenue shortfall as signs of a struggling economy.

In a video released by the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP) on Thursday, Robinson suggested that the finance minister was merely trying to put a positive spin on the situation. He reminded that in the last quarter the Government’s own projection for revenues was $28.7 billion lower than projected.

“It’s important to note that these projections were done in March 2026, which is after Hurricane Melissa, so they would have factored in Melissa and they would have made their projections,” he said.

Robinson pointed out that the revenue shortfall of nearly $30 billion forced the Government to go back to the market to borrow $30 billion but the Administration was unable to raise the full amount.

“To give this impression that the economy is doing great is really a fallacy,” he declared.

The Opposition spokesman also highlighted what he described as the cost of living pressures facing Jamaicans. He cited that at nearly eight per cent, inflation was “way above the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) target range of four to six per cent”.

“I anticipate that when the BOJ’s monetary policy committee meets, they will be looking to raise interest rates to try and tame inflation,” he stated.

Were the central bank to take such a decision, Robinson conceded that this would put more pressure on businesses which will have to pay more on their loans, and on consumers, who will have to pay more on their mortgages and the various loans they are carrying.

“We’re far from being in a good position in the economy, we’re actually seeing the highest rates of car repossessions; we’re seeing bad loans at banks at elevated rates. So it indicates that there’s significant consumer pressure being faced, people are struggling to meet their basic obligations,” said Robinson.

Anticipating talk from some quarters that the cost of living pressure is being driven by factors outside Jamaica’s control, such as the higher cost for fuel and electricity as a result of the Middle East war, Robinson said while that is true, there are things within the control of the Government that would lessen the pressure on Jamaicans.

“The Government has the control to determine how much imported oil we use, it has been an absolute failure on the part of this Government to increase the amount of renewables that have been added to the grid,” Robinson argued.

“In the 10-and-a-half years that they have been in office, they have added no renewables to the grid,” he said, adding that what was in fact added since 2016 started under the previous PNP Administration with Phillip Paulwell as energy minister.

Pointing out that it took the Jamaica Labour Party Government eight years to issue a request for proposal for renewables, the Opposition spokesman said those companies that have been selected cannot sign private purchase agreements with Jamaica Public Service Company because the company’s contract is in limbo (its licence expires in July 2027).

He asserted that while we cannot control the price of oil, we can determine how much oil we import by building out more renewables. In this regard, he said the Government has failed; a failure with a direct impact on cost of living.

“Because, if we’re less dependent on oil, it improves our financial position and it means the impact is less on consumers,” he said.

Robinson also argued that the minister pointing out that the economy is recovering faster than projected masks certain uncomfortable realities.

“We’re underspending the capital budget. Our capital budget is required to build out schools, hospitals, roads, etc, we’re underspending that,” he reiterated. He argued that such spend is important to ensuring that there’s growth in the economy “because there’s a direct link between your capital budget and economic growth and for the last five years we have underspent it”.

Robinson pointed out that when the capital budget is underutilised, the money is shifted to recurrent expenditure such as wages and salaries. “This makes the fiscal situation look a little better but it does not account for the fact that we have been woefully underspending the capital budget,” he insisted.

He lamented that the vast majority of Jamaicans most affected by Hurricane Melissa — either at the individual or small business level — have received no assistance from Government. This, he said, has made it difficult for them to recover, resulting in lower tax revenues. He insisted that Government has taken too long to get help to those who are most in need.

In her take on the economy, Williams highlighted that in the quarter following the hurricane, the economy contracted 7.1 per cent, then 4.1 per cent in the next quarter and just 2.9 per cent in the quarter after that. She said the 2.9 per cent projection should be finalised by the Statistical Institute of Jamaica by the end of September.

The finance minister argued that the shrinking year-on-year numbers are themselves proof that the economy is recovering, adding further that “an economy in decline produces deepening figures, not improving ones”.

Williams urged Jamaicans to remember that immediately after the hurricane, PIOJ projected that the country would not get back to its pre-Melissa level of output until the last quarter of 2028. She noted that the PIOJ now expects that the economy will begin to see growth by the second quarter of 2027 — “six quarters earlier, a year-and-a-half earlier”. According to her, the PIOJ “has been able to revise their forecast because the out-turn keeps getting better”.

World.title: How Germany’s far right learned to put on a smile to win elections
World.content:
Others have taken note, and it might well serve as a new campaigning template for far-right populists across Europe — at least for those able to flash a credible smile.

“I call it feel-good populism,” said Johannes Hillje, a Berlin-based political consultant who managed the European Green Party’s 2014 European Parliament campaign. “What we saw was a new type of AfD campaign.”

“In the past it has been mainly negative rhetoric, scapegoating migrants, attacking the elite, evoking fear and rage,” Hillje added. “If you really want to mobilize people, it’s not enough just to attack others. You also have to offer a positive perspective.”

At its core, the AfD continues to hold a dark vision of Germany’s path — depicting the country as on the brink of catastrophe due to the destructive forces of migration and deindustrialization. The party’s intellectual ideologues espouse an almost apocalyptic view of the decline of Germany and the West.

Yet in recent elections, the party has papered over this ideological core with a cheerful, reassuring facade, seeking to marry hope with fear.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund was labeled by one magazine “Germany’s most dangerous man.” But at campaign stops and in television appearances, he projected another image: He kept an almost permanent smile on his face, was invariably polite and friendly, took selfies with voters and rode his sky-blue vintage East German-era scooter.

World.title: Berlin election campaign centers around radical-left drive to seize properties
World.content:
Eralp’s far-left party maintains a narrow lead in polls heading into the vote Sunday in Berlin, just ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds the mayor’s office. If her Left party is able to eke out a win, it’s likely to lead a coalition of left-wing parties that excludes the conservatives, who have fought such plans.

The Left party, which traces part of its history to East Germany’s communist party, is enjoying a political revival after winning a new wave of support from young voters mobilized by the far right’s rise. For its Berlin campaign, the party has taken inspiration from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, employing his focus on cost-of-living issues as a model.

Once a city known for cheap rents that helped cultivate an international, bohemian culture, affordable housing has become a particularly pressing issue in the German capital in recent years. Fewer than one in six residents of the city own the home they live in, while rents have risen by about 70% over the past decade.

The Left party is running on a plan to expropriate properties from real estate companies that own more than 3,000 apartments. It’s an idea that has widespread support in a city that has historically leaned left.

Nearly 60 percent of voters backed expropriating properties from major real estate companies in a 2021 referendum. The organization that initiated that referendum estimates that the city could forcibly buy as many as 220,000 apartments for up to 60 percent of their market value — amounting to a total of €18 billion. That money, they argue, could be recovered by the city over the course of a century from rental income.

Stefan Evers, the CDU’s lead candidate in Berlin, says fear of a Left party win is already causing harm to the city’s real estate market.

World.title: ‘There are no decent parties left’: Sham elections underscore Putin’s grip on Russia
World.content:
But other opponents of the Kremlin say Navalnaya’s strategy is giving credibility to sham elections that are only held to justify Russian President Vladimir Putin’s maximalist war against Ukraine and tighten his grip on Russian society.

“To whoever comes to us with a sword — do not expect mercy,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in a campaign ad for Putin’s United Russia party, alongside NHL superstar Alex Ovechkin and the propagandist Margarita Simonyan, who runs the state broadcaster RT.

Putin’s veterans

The Kremlin’s response to the opposition suggests it is worried that people are growing tired of the war.

By removing anti-war candidates from the ballot and promoting pro-war voices, Moscow seeks to overstate public support for the invasion of Ukraine, says Ivan Preobrazhensky, a Russian political scientist based in Prague. “By electing them, people are effectively endorsing the policies of the ruling party and the government,” he told POLITICO, even though voters have no real alternative.

Yabloko received between 1% and 2% of votes in previous parliamentary elections and was seen as “politically dead” by the Kremlin, according to Maxim Reznik, a former party leader in St. Petersburg. By allowing it to run, Reznik said, the Kremlin “wanted to show that just 1.5% of Russians oppose war.”

But reports in Russian media suggested that Yabloko’s recent positioning as “the only peace party,” as well as its advocacy for an immediate ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, had boosted its electoral support. The Nezavisimaya Gazeta reported on a July poll from an unnamed agency giving Yabloko a rating of 9.4%. Faridaily, an outlet founded by independent journalist Farida Rustamova, reported that internal government polling put the party around 5.5%.

World.title: European leaders prepare public for ‘intensified threat’ from Putin
World.content:
The warnings underscore a growing sense of anxiety in Europe amid fast-proliferating incidents of airspace violations and sabotage attempts in recent months. NATO allies have repeatedly said they see the attacks as pressure from the Kremlin to reduce their support for Ukraine but have muted their response over fears of escalation.

French President Emmanuel Macron summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting on Friday to talk about Ukraine, Iran and the growing energy crisis.

He called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented” as he announced a new critical infrastructure protection plan, adding: “In recent weeks … the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and France has intensified.”

Guillaume Lacroix, leader of the Radical Party of the Left, left the meeting saying: “At the age of 50, I have rarely felt such vertigo.”

“It is no coincidence that the Polish prime minister is speaking out so strongly,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said Friday. “We need to take that warning very seriously … we must consistently demonstrate that we do not accept this and that we will take action if necessary.”

On Thursday, Finnish President Alexander Stubb told his country it was “worth mentally preparing for something to happen” including sabotage and Russian drones.

World.title: Australia following Canada as EU associate member is ‘pure speculation,’ says Commission
World.content:
Asked whether the meeting could provide an opportunity to discuss the associate membership idea with Australia, Podestà dismissed the suggestion.

“We have a very strong and close relationship with our Australian partners,” she said. “All the rest is pure speculation, and we’re not going to enter into that.”

Von der Leyen pitched Canada as a potential first EU “associate member” during her State of the Union address on Wednesday. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the ambition behind closer EU-Canada ties but has stopped short of endorsing the proposed status.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola subsequently said countries such as Australia and New Zealand could potentially follow Canada.

But Commission spokesperson Olof Gill stressed that Brussels is currently focused solely on developing the idea with Ottawa.

“What we’re focused on here is putting flesh on the bone on this idea,” Gill said, adding that the Commission is working with member states and Canadian partners to establish what the concept could look like in practice. “All other discussions are subsequent to that.”

World.title: Germany gets its first F-35 as Europe’s fighter plans fall apart
World.content:
But without the FCAS, Berlin is left without an obvious European successor.

“We want and need to maintain nuclear sharing,” Pistorius said ahead of the handover. The F-35, he argued, is currently “the only aircraft in the world” capable of fulfilling that mission.

Under the NATO nuclear-sharing program, Germany and other select allies have aircraft that can carry U.S. nuclear bombs, although the decision to use them remains with Washington.

The first F-35s will remain in the United States for training, with German pilots and technicians preparing for operations before more jets are sent to Büchel in late 2027. Full operational capability is expected by 2030.

Berlin currently operates around 80 Tornados, and some missions will migrate to the Eurofighter Typhoon. But the collapse of FCAS has opened a longer-term gap in Germany's plans for its combat-air fleet.

During June's Berlin Air Show, Pistorius said Berlin is weighing whether to acquire additional F-35s as a “bridge” option after the FCAS failure, to join an existing international sixth-generation program or to develop a national effort headed by Airbus.

World.title: Macron to call emergency G7 meeting as energy prices spike and Russian hybrid attacks mount
World.content:
“The situation we face is serious. It is serious due to the international situation and the consequence of wars that we endure,” Macron said. “In this context we need to stay united.”

France’s dire fiscal outlook, which has prompted the government to pursue a €54 billion budget squeeze next year, will make it difficult for the state to massively subsidize increasingly expensive energy bills. Macron told reporters, however, that the government was working on targeted assistance proposals.

Macron also said he was seeking to firm up French access to oil and gas supplies during recent meetings with leaders from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. He added that he’d discuss France’s trade in petroleum products and liquefied natural gas with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney when the two meet on Sunday.

The president said France was stepping up efforts to protect critical infrastructure and defense production sites amid the uptick in cyberattacks and the intensified threat of so-called hybrid attacks from Russia, including recent ones on a Ukrainian passenger train and at Leipzig airport in Germany. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Thursday that Russia was planning to target Ukraine’s European allies using drones or rockets.

Among those in attendance were center-right former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, centrist Gabriel Attal, conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau, center-left Raphaël Glucksmann, Greens leader Marine Tondelier and Socialist Party chief Olivier Faure. Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who has a commanding lead in the polls, was represented by her party’s president, Jordan Bardella, while far-left hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon was represented by a high-ranking lawmaker from his party, Manuel Bompard.

The politicians who spoke to reporters after the meeting acknowledged the gravity of what had been discussed. Guillaume Lacroix, the head of a small left-wing party, wrote online that the stakes of the three-hour briefing had made his head spin.

World.title: Ukraine’s NATO envoy calls for more air defense donations
World.content:
“We need to stop viewing assistance that enables Ukraine to defend itself as purely a matter of supporting Ukraine. It is also in NATO’s own interest … the more drones and missiles Ukraine can destroy in its own airspace, the fewer will cross the borders of neighboring NATO countries,” the envoy added.

Getmanchuk underlined that Western countries still have stocks of interceptor missiles to donate, including missiles close to the end of their service lives.

“There is hardly a better way to decommission them than by using them in the Ukrainian sky,” Getmanchuk said.

Kyiv is proposing a workaround: allies hand over interceptors from their existing stocks now, and Ukraine replaces them later with missiles it has already ordered.

“It’s a swap — not a donation. What we need is to get through this winter,” Getmanchuk said.

Ukraine is placing substantial orders, using both partner funding and the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan. These contracts cover not only hundreds of Patriot interceptors — both PAC-2s and PAC-3s — but also European systems, including SAMP/T and Aster 30 missiles, IRIS-T and others.

World.title: What happens if a solar farm catches fire? Europe’s biggest battery test centre is finding out
World.content:
Eastern Germany is home to some of the world’s most advanced ‘torture chambers’. Here, water, fire, high-voltage current and even dust are used to press and squeeze, twist and strike, shake and hammer the beating hearts of the technology we use every day, like electric vehicles.

 

At Europe’s largest battery testing centre, they put batteries into every imaginable situation to see what happens. Whether they explode, survive or thrive, it’s better to find out here than in a consumer’s garage.

Batteries are subjected to extreme temperatures and full-blown sandstorms

I am standing beside a long row of garage-sized boxes inside the DEKRA facility in the small town of Klettwitz in Lusatia. Each box has its own unique purpose. Head of DEKRA, Thomas Hucke, is showing me around. Thermometers and warning lights surround me – what do they mean?

“We’re testing how battery prototypes behave at very low temperatures, or at very high temperatures. From Siberia to the Sahara,” Hucke explains. Hans von der Brelie

“We’re testing how battery prototypes behave at very low temperatures, or at very high temperatures. From Siberia to the Sahara,” Hucke explains. “In other words, the classic environmental conditions that a battery like this experiences over its lifetime.” He then walks over to a control panel and, with grim determination, turns it all the way to the minus max level: “Right, minus 40 degrees Celsius – let’s take it right down to the limit…”

Full-blown sandstorm? No problem for Hucke and his team. If a specialised battery is to survive use in the desert, its suitability must be certified before it can be marketed and sold. For that, the DEKRA team naturally have some particularly gruelling dust chambers.

We cross an industrial road and enter a hall on the opposite side. A few staff members hurriedly push plastic crates in front of a prototype that has just been delivered to block the view. “Camera off!” they say. This is top secret.

“We also test very large batteries,” says Hucke, explaining the enormous size of the test hall, “such as stationary energy storage systems, for example.

High-pressure nozzles, fine-spray nozzles, wide-spray nozzles. You could hardly find a better place to submerge a battery – whilst monitoring all parameters from inside. Hans von der Brelie

“Over there,” Hucke points to another test chamber, “we carry out vibration tests. In vehicles, batteries are usually subjected to vibrations. What happens when a vehicle drives over a curb, or when it receives a mechanical impact?” All of this is tested, documented and reported to the manufacturer. Certification is only granted once the new battery model has met all stress parameters to Hucke’s complete satisfaction.

Consumer safety is a top priority in the European Union. “The EU has drawn up a Battery Regulation which sets out the tests that must be carried out on batteries. It’s about sustainability, the value chain, and ultimately, always about safety.”

Thomas Hucke: “The EU has drawn up a Battery Regulation. It’s about sustainability, the value chain, and ultimately, always about safety." Hans von der Brelie

Hucke elaborates: “The energy transition isn’t just about electric mobility. At the test centre, we naturally also test vehicle batteries. But beyond that, we are increasingly testing energy storage solutions for stationary applications. These are mostly intermediate storage systems for renewable energies, namely solar and wind. That is the future.”

Batteries are crushed and burnt – to find out what happens

Hucke smiles as he leads us into the next fiery circle of battery hell.

“What happens in the event of a fire? In an accident? Or if batteries are overcharged or discharged improperly? Batteries must remain safe even in these situations,” he says. “The energy transition [and the associated electrification] must function safely and sustainably. This requires testing service providers who ensure that certain rules and standards are adhered to.”

Euronews Earth inside one of the ‘torture chambers’ pushing EV batteries to their limits. Hans von der Brelie

Hucke nods towards the ‘fire hall’. There, they recently tried to set an entire battery container alight. This is not an unrealistic scenario: planet-heating fossil fuel emissions are leading to increasingly extreme temperatures. Europe experienced this first-hand in a scorching summer filled with devastating wildfires and drought.

It cannot be ruled out that one day a major fire might also reach the buffer electricity storage facility at a solar or wind farm. Up to certain temperature levels, a large-scale battery storage facility must be able to withstand this.

Up to certain temperature levels, a large-scale battery storage facility must be able to withstand. Hans von der Brelie

Opening a high-security airlock, Hucke leads me into a room with a cathedral-high ceiling. Massive metal blocks are firmly bolted to the floor. This is the bunker hall of the ‘crush bed’.

“We’ve got an oversized vice here,” says Hucke, where batteries are clamped to be stress tested. “The battery is squeezed – and the regulations stipulate that absolutely nothing must happen.”

Massive metal blocks are firmly bolted to the floor. This is the bunker hall of the ‘crush bed’. Hans von der Brelie

But what if it does? What if the new prototype can’t take any more, after the water, dust, heat and cold tests? What if it really does crash and explode in the crushing bed between the jaws of the steel clamps?

Hucke points to the special fixtures on the thick walls. “We have pressure relief flaps here – and outside the building, a complete flue gas scrubbing system that extracts the gases in an emergency.”

Hucke points to the special fixtures on the thick walls. “We have pressure relief flaps here – and outside the building, a complete flue gas scrubbing system." Hans von der Brelie

Batteries are key to a safe and sustainable energy transition

Wind and solar power are a rapidly growing source of energy in Europe. Grid constraints and the intermittent nature of these renewables means the need for flexible storage is rapidly increasing.

Battery test centres are “a key component” of the energy transition, says Hucke, ensuring that this renewable power can be stored safely.

Outside the building, a complete flue gas scrubbing system can extract gases in an emergency. Hans von der Brelie

“Standards and regulations have been in place in the automotive sector for some time now. And the same is now happening in the field of stationary battery storage solutions for renewable energies,” he tells me. “This requires state-of-the-art testing laboratories. We ensure that batteries entering service meet all safety requirements.”

What about the test centre’s own sustainability? A huge, ultra-modern battery test centre like this requires a lot of energy. “We’re expanding our solar PV systems,” emphasises Hucke, “and using stationary battery storage to ensure we can recover energy”.

Water, fire, vibrations, extreme temperatures and even dust are used to torture the beating hearts of battery prototypes.. Hans von der Brelie

The DEKRA Group also took a stand at the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos, joining the Alliance of CEO Climate Leaders. “In an increasingly disruptive global environment, in which the urgency and even the existence of the climate crisis is, in some quarters, being called into question once again, we emphasise the strategic importance of jointly combating climate change,” states the Group headquarters.

The DEKRA Climate Impact Programme includes internal decarbonisation and support for external climate projects that make a measurable contribution to the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

World.title: Drums, dancing and definitely no tears: Here’s why you need to experience Nepal’s Sa: Paru festival
World.content:
The sound I most associate with death is silence. Not just the obvious one, in that the dearly departed will never speak, never yell, never cry, never laugh again.

 

Smaller silences, like post-funeral, when the last guest is gone and all you’re left with are your thoughts and an inordinate amount of food shared by well-wishers. Or when weeks have passed and you go to call or text them about your day before you stop yourself because you can’t do that any more.

Even years later, it lingers in that awkward pause when you reveal someone close to you has passed away and the other person doesn’t quite know what to say in response.

Drums and bells, it is not. Music, beyond the songs chosen for the service, feels incongruous. The loud, chaotic energy of a festival? Never.

Yet that’s exactly what Sa: Paru, an annual festival honouring those that have died in the past year, is all about, as I discovered on my recent trip to Nepal’s Bhaktapur.

Celebrated across the Kathmandu Valley by the Newar people, the festival turns the western idea of grieving on its head, giving the dead a joyous farewell as they head towards salvation.

“When people pass away in western societies, people wear black. They grieve in silence – it's a very somber moment,” says Ajay Bahadur Pradhanang. “But in Nepal, everybody comes together and it's turned into this carnival, a real joyous moment of farewell.”

Bamboo structures known as taha: sa are created for the procession through the city Dianne Apen-Sadler

A community coming together

While the festival also takes place in other cities like Lalitpur as well as the capital Kathmandu, which is around 13 kilometres away, the celebration in Bhaktapur takes its own unique form.

Prior to the festival’s main day, which takes place after the full moon during the 10th month of the country’s lunisolar calendar in August or September, neighbours – whether they’ve lost someone or not – gather to create taha: sa.

The bamboo structures, which replaced the cows that would traditionally have been used as part of the procession, are wrapped before a painting of the sacred animal is placed at the top.

It takes skill, and manpower, to complete the whole affair. After the cloth (generally red for women, and white for men) and cow portrait are added, various decorations follow, like a photograph of the deceased, depictions of Shiva, and, finally, an umbrella to shield them from sun and rain – a sign of respect.

“For Sa: Paru, we have to have certain rituals, and these would be impossible if it was just me, or just my family, without the wider community to help us,” Ajay notes.

It might take a village to raise a child, but the celebration in Bhaktapur goes to show that it takes a community to mark the other end of somebody’s life, too.

I’m here at the invitation of The Nanee, a boutique hotel near the city’s centre. Ajay, the hotel’s chairman, lost his mother this year, which means I can see the work underway in the neighbouring courtyard, but any visitor to the city will easily be able to find taha: sa being constructed throughout the day.

The city gets busier and busier as the day goes on Dianne Apen-Sadler

The festival starts early the following morning, with a steady stream of taha: sa passing through the streets accompanied by music, drums, bells and the sound of sticks clashing together as pairs take part in the Ghintang Ghisi dance.

The procession follows a set route, and at the beginning, it seems each troupe is moving to its own beat – some rush, causing the structures to sway, giving the effect of a drunken cow passing by; others march slowly, pausing to dance together. It’s only as the streets begin to clog up and movement reaches a snail’s pace that they move as one.

While some attendees don traditional wear, or modern interpretations of it, you’re just as likely to see people wearing football kits and Hawaiian shirts. Come as you are – you’re welcome to get involved in the festivities, provided you don’t mind crowds.

After taking a pause to catch my breath, I get chatting to Mano Dhaubhadel, a Nepali living in the US who recently lost his younger brother and has returned for the festival.

“This is something you don’t see anywhere else in the world,” he told me. “The culture here is just magnificent, and it’s there for everyone to enjoy, not just Newars. The best way to learn is to get involved.”

Of course, you can also attend the festival with a guide. I’m joined by The Nanee’s curator, Peepul Subedi, a priest and PhD student who is more than happy to explain the meaning behind the festival’s various elements, and its importance.

"The whole city comes together for this festival, and every household who has a family member who has passed away in the past year will take out this sort of structure,” he tells me.

“It represents the message that everyone has to die, and all of us are going through the same sort of sorrow – that's life. We're not celebrating death by dancing and singing, we are celebrating the fact that the departed soul is moving towards salvation.”

Celebrations in most of the valley last just a single day – here in Bhaktapur, the festival continues on for eight, with different dance performances throughout the city.

The exact origins of Sa: Paru, which is also known as Gai Jatra, aren’t precisely known, but historians believe that the tradition may have started in the 14th century.

The name most commonly associated with the festival is King Pratap Malla, who is said to have expanded the festival to cheer up his wife following the death of their son Chakravartendra Malla with the inclusion of satirical elements, which today sees people don satirical masks of political figures like US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin.

Many tourists pass through Bhaktapur on a day trip – but there are plenty of reasons you should linger longer Dianne Apen-Sadler

A reason to linger in Bhaktapur

Travel itineraries for tourists visiting Kathmandu often include a detour to Bhaktapur – but they typically only mention a visit to the Durbar Square, with its various temples and the 55 Window Palace.

Similar to the cruise ship tourists who swarm cities in Europe for a few hours in the summer months, climbing back on board having contributed nothing to the local economy beyond the cost of an ice cream and a fridge magnet, these visitors will spend an hour or two in town before heading back to the capital.

It’s a real shame – not just for the locals, who fail to see the financial benefit, but for the tourists themselves, who miss out on the best Bhaktapur has to offer.

Life is slower here, and the city is best experienced in the early mornings, when you’ll see folks milling about, praying at the Hindu and Buddhist temples, or buying produce at the market.

Aside from the Durbar Square, you can see ceramics drying under the sun at Pottery Square, give pottery a go yourself at one of the workshops, or pick out some pieces to add to your homeware collection.

The Nanee aims to be an oasis of calm within the city of Bhaktapur Dianne Apen-Sadler

The Peacock Shop is another must visit, where the chatty owner is more than happy to talk, and walk you through the traditional Lokta paper making process.

The Nanee was founded by Ajay and Shailaja Pradhanang with a view to encourage people to linger longer while enjoying the comforts of a luxury boutique hotel.

“Bhaktapur is a living heritage site, and we wanted that to continue,” Ajay tells me.

“With The Nanee, we offer guests a small oasis in the beautiful city of Bhaktapur while ensuring that the community, which has done so much to preserve and conserve its heritage, benefits from their stay.”

Experiences offered by the hotel are in partnership with locals, like the morning walk with a housewife, or the evening dinner with an artisan.

Aside from Sa: Paru, there are numerous festivals throughout the year, including the famed Bisket Jatra, celebrated for eight nights each April.

A note on the recent floods

Just hours before landing in Kathmandu for the festival, a series of flash floods near the border with Tibet saw the loss of at least 1,369 lives, with some 5,000 people missing.

Naturally, many people have cancelled or are thinking about cancelling their trips to Nepal as a result, which will have a serious impact on a tourism industry that is already dealing with the impact of the Iran war on flight routes to the country.

Popular tourist spots like the Kathmandu Valley, as well as Mount Everest and other trekking trails, were unaffected by the tragedy, and your tourism dollars are more needed than ever.

Dianne Apen-Sadler was hosted by The Nanee during the Sa: Paru festival. You can reach out to the hotel directly to enquire about your potential stay in order to align your trip with one of Bhaktapur’s many festivals. For more information about Bhaktapur, visit the official tourism board website.

World.title: Fear of AI job losses now outweighs hope of new jobs, study finds
World.content:
People’s view of a country and trust for its artificial intelligence (AI) regulation tend to be closely linked, Moira Fagan, senior researcher at the Pew Research Center and one of the authors of a new study on AI, told Euronews Next.

 

According to the report, in Bangladesh, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the West Bank and East Jerusalem, people trust China more than the United States (US) or the European Union (EU) with AI governance.

And, taking into consideration the other seven middle-income countries where this question was asked, a median of 43% trust China to regulate AI, 35% trust the US and 34% trust the EU.

“Favourable views of China tend to be quite high in middle-income countries – and opinion has risen in many places since last year, likely contributing to some of the high marks we see for trust in China on this particular dimension,” Fagan said.

The report, which was built on a survey conducted between February and June 2026, polling over 50,000 people from 37 countries, also examines people’s opinions on AI’s impact on the job market.

Specifically, more people expect AI to lead to fewer jobs than to job creation, according to the study. A good share of respondents, though, also report uncertainty about the impact AI will have on the number of job opportunities.

The survey also shows that worries about job losses due to AI are particularly high in wealthier countries.

For instance, in Australia, South Korea and the US, around seven-in-ten adults or more believe AI will result in job loss over the next 20 years.

Similarly, richer countries are more concerned about AI increasing economic inequalities than middle-income ones, the report highlights.

According to Fagan, these tendencies appear to be linked to other data, including people’s familiarity with the technological tool.

“People in wealthier countries are more likely to say they have heard or read a lot about AI. And we also found that people with higher AI awareness are more likely to believe it will lead to job loss,” she told Euronews Next.

However, some high-income and middle-income nations are brought together by a shared thread: young adults aged 18 to 34 are more concerned about AI-related job loss than older generations. And this is the case for countries like Canada, France, Singapore, Sweden, Indonesia, India and Malaysia, according to the survey.

Opinion divides are less pronounced when it comes to the rise of AI in daily life. Across the 37 countries, a median of 37% are more concerned than excited, while 41% median are equally concerned and excited, the survey found.

Although the survey was conducted in the first half of 2026, its publication arrives at a very crucial moment for AI.

Leaders of major AI companies, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei, are increasingly concerned about the risks their AI creations pose to humanity and are calling for a slowdown in the pace of AI development.

President of the European Commission, Ursula Von der Leyen, also backed the deceleration effort in her landmark State of the Union address to the European Parliament earlier this week. On this occasion, she also pledged closer safety cooperation with Canada, the UK, and other like-minded partners.

World.title: EU fuel prices hit records as ECB experts see diesel margins peak in October
World.content:
Filling up a car has never cost more on average across the European Union, according to European Commission data going back more than two decades. At the latest average prices, it costs about €103 to fill a 50-litre tank with petrol and €108 with diesel.

 

Retail fuel prices have surged since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, adding to inflationary pressures. Eurozone energy inflation rose to 14.3% in August, up from 10.3% in July, according to the European Central Bank.

A litre of petrol cost a weighted EU average of €2.063 as of 14 September, while diesel reached €2.159 per litre. Both were the highest readings in the Commission’s series, which begins in 2005. Petrol’s previous peak was recorded in 2022, while diesel last approached its current level in April this year.

Prices varied considerably across the EU. Petrol was cheapest in Malta, at €1.34 per litre, and most expensive in Denmark, at €2.56. Diesel ranged from €1.21 per litre in Malta to €2.51 in Finland.

The figures come from the European Commission’s latest Weekly Oil Bulletin, published on 17 September using prices reported for 14 September. They include taxes.

Fuel prices have been rising for months since the war with Iran broke out at the end of February and disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz. International benchmark Brent crude prices rose above $126 at the height of the conflict and were trading at more than $104 a barrel for delivery the following month on Friday. Brent cost about $72 per barrel before the war broke out.

European crude supplies face further disruption after Saudi Aramco told at least two European refiners that they would receive no oil under long-term contracts in October following an attack on the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea, Bloomberg reported, citing people informed of the decision who said it applied to all European buyers.

What makes European fuel prices expensive?

But international crude prices are not the only factor driving petrol and diesel prices higher. Refining costs and margins have also risen significantly, putting further pressure on prices at the pump.

Refining margins reflect the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined products such as petrol and diesel. While petrol margins appear to have peaked, ECB experts told Euronews Business that diesel margins are not expected to reach their highest point until October.

“Looking ahead, based on refined diesel futures from LSEG on 16 September, the margin for diesel is expected to peak in October. Based on refined petrol futures from LSEG on 16 September, petrol margins peaked in August,” they said.

Since the beginning of 2026, the weighted EU average petrol price has risen by about 29%, while diesel has surged by almost 40%.

Higher crude prices have also fuelled energy inflation across both the eurozone and the wider EU. According to an ECB blog published in July, increases in crude-oil prices generally feed through fully to pre-tax pump prices within one or two months. Governments can temporarily cushion the impact through measures such as cuts to fuel duties.

Crude oil accounted for less than a quarter of the euro-area pump price in the ECB blog’s July calculations. The remainder included refining and distribution costs and margins, excise duties and value added tax, helping to explain the significant differences between countries.

The blog’s calculations indicated that excise duties and VAT together represented around 44% of the euro-area diesel price and 52% of the petrol price in July.

ECB experts told Euronews Business that refining margins are now making a large contribution to diesel prices.

“At the current juncture, we have estimated that in the third week of September refining margins have contributed €0.41 (19% of the pump price) and €0.17 (8%) per litre to the retail diesel and retail petrol prices in the euro area, respectively.”

Could fuel prices rise further?

The ECB’s monetary policy statement, published on 10 September, warned: “Renewed disruption of energy supplies could cause energy prices to rise further and for longer than currently expected.”

ECB experts said an end to the Middle East conflict and the restoration of energy and refining flows would be central to bringing prices down.

“For petrol and diesel prices to decline, the key factor would be a cessation of the war in the Middle East, a normalisation of flows through the Strait of Hormuz and a restoration of global refining activity to allow oil inventories to rebuild,” they said.

Such a normalisation could quickly lower crude oil and retail fuel prices. However, disruptions to Russian refining capacity could keep margins elevated even if the Middle East conflict were resolved.

World.title: Russians leave before election ends, fearing mobilisation to follow
World.content:
Russians fearing a new military mobilisation are leaving the country in advance of possible restrictions on departure, according to the anti-war project Ark, after requests for emergency assistance and emigration advice from Russia have nearly octupled since the start of the summer.

 

The surge coincides with Russia's State Duma elections, which began on Friday and run through Sunday.

Kremlin critics and several Western governments have accused Moscow of planning to announce a new call-up to beef up its troops in its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine after the vote concludes, allowing an unpopular measure to avoid affecting the election.

Russia's Vladimir Putin has dismissed mobilisation rumours as "utter nonsense," but independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent draft since the summer.

Jan Slovitsky, a human rights activist and coordinator of the Ark project, said the current wave was driven by lessons learned from 2022.

"Since mid-July a wave of panic has been rising in Russia, linked to the risk of mobilisation, fuel shortages and lack of internet access," he told Ark's network from Yerevan, where he is assisting new arrivals.

"People are leaving in advance because they have seen what happened during previous waves. And Armenia is facing a migration crisis, if we are not already in the thick of it."

'How to leave' online search spikes

The number of daily requests for relocation assistance has risen from around 70 to 120 since July, according to organisations helping Russians move abroad.

Yandex and Google searches for "how to leave" and "mobilisation" reached their highest level since early 2023 during the summer and the first ten days of September, according to independent Russian media analysis.

Preparations for a possible call-up are already visible. Tens of thousands of people have received mobilisation notices setting out the steps required if called up, and an electronic register of summonses has been introduced under which an exit ban takes effect automatically when a notice is issued.

In early September, passport control officers in Krasnodar detained a 24-year-old resident of Rostov region who had completed his military service in 2024 and served him with a notice banning him from leaving the country, the first such case reported at that crossing.

Daniil Neonov, a former candidate for municipal deputy in the Moscow City Duma, described leaving at the last moment.

"If I had waited another day or two, they would most likely not have let me leave, because they would have blocked my exit," he said. "I received an electronic summons. But I still managed to get out."

Fear of mobilisation has also spread to members of the elite and draft office staff, according to international media reports claiming officials have begun opening foreign bank accounts and moving assets abroad.

In August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned of the risk of mobilisation in Russia, citing intelligence data.

Kyiv described a Kremlin plan to rapidly call up several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, with at least as many again the following year. Moscow has not commented on those claims.

Neighbouring countries first

Arrivals are heading primarily to visa-free destinations: Armenia, Georgia and Kazakhstan. Yerevan said in recent days it was ready to assist Russians arriving in the country.

The exact scale of the current wave is unknown, but it is likely less intense than the exodus of 2022, when between 600,000 and 700,000 people left Russia within weeks of the partial mobilisation announcement, according to independent estimates.

That mobilisation has never been formally cancelled, and those called up then have not been demobilised.

"It is very sad to leave Russia," said a 28-year-old marketing specialist, whose name was withheld for security reasons.

"My family lives here, my elderly grandparents live here. My girlfriend is here too, she is still in her medical residency, and it is very hard for me to leave her behind."

Russia's Duma elections, running from 18 to 20 September, include only parties that back Moscow's war in Ukraine. Yabloko, whose platform called for an immediate ceasefire and peace talks, was barred from standing by the Supreme Court in August.

World.title: Trump threatens to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House
World.content:
President Donald Trump has said he is banning three major news organisations, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, from the White House with immediate effect, accusing them of publishing “fake news”, “fiction” and “lies”.

 

It is not yet clear what the ban will entail. Trump also warned that restrictions could be extended to other media outlets.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the president said the three outlets “constantly write or report fiction and lies” about his administration, although he provided no specific examples.

President Trump writing on Truth Social via Truth Social

The move is the latest test of First Amendment protections guaranteeing freedom of the press in the United States.

It is also the latest move by Trump’s second administration to restrict press access. He has already tightened controls over which journalists can join the White House press pool, the small group of reporters who accompany the president into restricted spaces such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One.

CNN is part of the traditional five-network television pool that travels with and covers the president. It is not yet clear whether the new ban will affect that arrangement.

In 2025, Trump restricted Associated Press access to some presidential events after the news agency continued to use the name “Gulf of Mexico” rather than Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America”. AP subsequently launched legal action over the restrictions. The case remains ongoing.

During Trump’s first term, CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins was barred from a White House Rose Garden event after officials said questions she asked the president earlier that day were "inappropriate" for the venue.

While it is extremely rare for a US president to bar an entire news organisation from the White House, previous administrations have also imposed restrictions on individual outlets. President Richard Nixon restricted access for The Washington Post during the Watergate scandal in the 1970s.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A city at the crossroads of history: Unearthing Gaza's ancient heritage
World.content:
Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: Cuba faces another nationwide blackout amid US fuel blockade
World.content:
Millions were left without electricity as Cuba's aging power grid collapsed under the weight of fuel shortages, deteriorating infrastructure and US sanctions.

Cuba's power grid suffered a total collapse on Friday, triggering another nationwide blackout and leaving millions without electricity as the island grapples with an ongoing US fuel blockade.

"A total disconnection of the electrical system has occurred," the Energy Ministry posted on X, as only 5% of Havana had electricity.

State-run utility UNE blamed a failure in transmission lines and unstable weather for the nationwide blackout — the 7th this year and the 12th since late 2024 — as fuel shortages and deteriorating infrastructure take their toll.

"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old Lidia Fernandez told the AFP news agency. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."

Cubans say problem growing

Blackouts lasting more than 30 hours have become common in Havana, while some provinces have endured outages exceeding 60 hours.

In recent weeks, blackouts have lasted more than 30 hours in the capital, while in outlying provinces, they have sometimes stretched past 60 hours [FILE: May 14, 2026] Image: Ramon Espinosa/AP Photo/picture alliance

The power cuts have also disrupted water supplies, cooking gas, telecommunications and transportation.

Cuba, home to more than 9 million people, is also facing a deepening economic crisis.

An independent study released this week estimated that 66% of the population now lives in poverty, up from 45% in mid-2025, citing rising food prices as a key factor.

"No one can stand these constant blackouts. There isn't enough food, there's no water, there's no electricity — you have no idea," Mercedes Rodriguez, 60, told AP. "The country is in such a sad state, and there are no words for what we're going through."

How have US sanctions impacted Cuba?

Cuba's aging power plants rely heavily on imported fuel, which has become increasingly scarce amid US restrictions imposed in January.

US President Donald Trump's administration tightened sanctions and enacted an oil embargo, choking the Caribbean country from importing fuel and replacement parts required to maintain infrastructure.

Havana blames US sanctions for worsening shortages, while Washington claims the outages reflect failures of ⁠the country's state-run economic model.

Trump has even made scarcely veiled threats to take over the island.

World.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked 3 companies during testing
World.content:
During a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, Google's Gemini AI model accessed the internet and hacked other companies. This is the first known instance of Google's AI systems engaging in such behavior autonomously.

Google's consumer artificial intelligence (AI) model, Gemini, hacked into multiple systems by guessing login credentials during tests of its cybersecurity capabilities, the company said on Friday.

This is the latest in a series of cybersecurity breaches involving rogue AI, raising safety concerns about the technology.

The internet giant is the fourth AI developer whose programs have been found to exhibit such behavior, following OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta.

Google only made the incidents — which occurred in May and were discovered by Google in July — public after an inquiry from The Wall Street Journal.

Will AI destroy humanity? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What we know about the incident

According to the WSJ report, there were three instances in which Gemini infiltrated the computers of other companies, whose names were not disclosed.

In one case, the AI guessed passwords to access a protected system. In the other two, it found login credentials in a database.

"In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test," Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, told the AFP news agency in a statement.

"In all three of these instances, the model stopped," Adkins said. "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes."

What is AI's biggest risk: Speed or autonomy? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Autonomous AI agents pose risks

Similar incidents have been reported earlier by Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI. These incidents have raised questions about the necessary safeguards as AI agents become more autonomous and gain access to the internet and computer systems.

AI model developed by OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, escaped from a secure environment during a test in July and infiltrated the computers of another AI company, HuggingFace, unexpectedly.

This prompted rival Anthropic to review its own test runs, during which additional incidents came to light.

Meta subsequently admitted that its AI had hacked into another company's computers due to a system misconfiguration at a testing partner.

This month, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, called for a slowdown in AI development.

In a blog post, he expressed concern that a swarm of autonomous software systems, or AI agents, could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, causing billions of dollars in damage.

World.title: Trump signs broad Russia sanctions bill
World.content:
The bill signed by US President Donald Trump targets officials, banks, and a fleet of shadow tankers that transport Russian energy.

US President Donald Trump signed into law a package of new sanctions against Russia named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, the White House said on Friday.

Earlier, the bill passed Congress with large bipartisan majorities: 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House.

The comprehensive sanctions package is intended to punish and pressure Moscow for its ongoing war against Ukraine.

In addition to the sanctions on Russia, the law establishes a framework to maintain sanctions on Iran until 2031.

What sanctions does the bill include?

The bill targets Russian officials and key sectors of the Russian economy, including banks, and a fleet of shadow tankers that transport Russian energy.

It also instructs Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas. However, some countries are exempt.

The US president can also impose sanctions on the five countries that do the most to help Russia circumvent energy sanctions.

These measures could further strain US trade relations with China and India, both of which buy significant amounts of Russian oil.

How India has become Russia's trade lifeline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What are the reactions?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked Trump for signing the bill, as well as all the senators and members of the House of Representatives who supported it.

"When Lindsey Graham was here in Ukraine, he would always talk about how important it was not to ease pressure on Russia, to strengthen sanctions and seek a path to peace," he wrote on X.

Graham, who played a leading role in advancing the bill, was a staunch supporter of Ukraine. The senator had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly passed away in July.

"The best way to honor Lindsey's memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly. And the best reward for everyone helping us put pressure on Russia to end its war will be peace," Zelenskyy added.

Before Trump signed the bill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that additional US sanctions would hinder efforts to achieve a peaceful resolution in Ukraine.

World.title: Deal with Denmark gives US 'permanent control' over Greenland security, Trump says
World.content:
The deal with Denmark, according to President Donald Trump, would give the US "permanent control" over Greenland's security. Denmark said the deal is "great for NATO and Europe."

President Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had entered into an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the US permanent control over Greenland's security.

"At my direction, ‌we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to ‌guarantee ​that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend ​the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," Trump said on Truth Social.

The US State Department said the deal bars US adversaries from establishing bases there.

"The agreement explicitly guarantees the United States the complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent, including permanent access, basing, and overflight rights," a State Department official said. "This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors."

In his post, Trump wrote that the US would "immediately" begin developing a larger military presence on the Danish territory.

Greenland's ice-covered minerals: No easy option To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Denmark and Greenland say?

According to a joint statement by the Danish and Greenlandic governments, the United States, Denmark, and Greenland have announced a breakthrough in their dispute over the Arctic island.

"I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement.

She added that the deal was "great for NATO and Europe" and recognized "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom (of Denmark) and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."

The agreement is expected to be signed next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Jens-Frederik Nielsen, the head of Greenland's government, said, "It is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States, and the Western alliance."

The deal benefits all three governments and "recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation," Nielsen added.

Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has pressed Denmark to sell Greenland to the United States and even threatened to take it by force, insisting that the island is crucial for US security.

Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly stated that the island is not for sale and have condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there.

World.title: Trump bars CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has accused CNN, MS NOW and Politico of spreading fake news. The outlets have vowed to take legal action against the ban.

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is banning major US media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House.

In a post on Truth Social, he accused them of spreading fake news.

Although Trump did not explain what exactly prompted the move, he said the media outlets were reporting "fiction and lies."

"Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."

He also indicated that other media outlets may also be ejected from the White House.

"Other fake news media outlets to follow," the US president posted, without mentioning any names. He also did not clarify what specific reporting he objected to.

A ban would prevent affected reporters from attending press conferences or events at the Oval Office.

Trumps say comedian Jimmy Kimmel should be fired To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How did CNN, Politico and MS NOW react?

After Trump's announcement, journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico remained on the White House grounds.

CNN called Trump's media ban an "illegal assault" on the freedom of the press, adding that its reporting was "fair and accurate" and was protected under the US Constitution.

Politico, which is owned by the German media conglomerate Axel Springer, headquartered in Berlin and New York, vowed to "vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them."

MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), a liberal cable news channel, has not yet responded to the ban.

The White House Correspondents' Association, an independent organization representing journalists who cover the presidency, said it "stands in defense" of journalists "being singled out for doing their jobs."

Meanwhile, Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said that banning the media outlets would be "flatly unconstitutional."

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," Brown said.

"This is textbook viewpoint discrimination and will be quickly struck down by the courts if challenged," he added.

Trump's uneasy relationship with the media

Donald Trump has a long history of disputes with members of the press corps. During his second term, he became increasingly hostile toward the media.

The US president repeatedly urged broadcasters to cancel comedy or news programs that he disliked or that joked about or criticized him or his administration.

He even called on the Federal Communications Commission to revoke the licenses of stations he disliked.

Trump's administration imposed stricter controls on reporters during his second term. For example, they control which journalists can cover events as part of the "pool" admitted to confined spaces, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One.

Last year, the White House barred the Associated Press from some events because the news agency continued to refer to the "Gulf of Mexico" instead of the "Gulf of America," as Trump had ordered.

In another case, last year Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced new rules for reporters covering the Pentagon. The rules required reporters to sign a document acknowledging restrictions on gathering unauthorized information.

Most major news outlets refused to sign the document and left the Pentagon's press room.
