World.title: Dutch housing update: money for new homes, rising interest rates
World.content:
There was some good news for home buyers in this week’s budget with the announcement of a massive financial package to boost new residential development. There are also signs that house price rises are slowing down, although interest rates are shooting up and the issue of foundations continues to be confusing. This and more in the latest housing news round-up.

Budget briefing

There was not much in the way of direct measures impacting on the Dutch housing market in this week’s budget. For example, the government did not announce any new changes to the current mortgage interest deduction set up, although there will be a slight rise in income tax rate in the first and second tax bands, which will have a minimal impact on your rebate.

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan did come up with a string of measures she hopes will boost supply in the rental sector and new construction, and is pressing ahead with plans to cut the property transfer tax for holiday homes and investment properties from 8% to 7%.

Most relevant for would-be home buyers? “Plenty of investment in large scale developments of new homes, so if you are looking for a new-build property, you could be lucky – although the changes will take time to filter through,” says Matthijs van der Heijden, a mortgage advisor with Expat Mortgages, which has been helping internationals buy a home for over 20 years.

The government is also putting a further €100 million into a special fund to help first-time buyers get a foot on the housing ladder.

Interest rate increases

Over the past 18 months interest rates have been pretty stable but have been trending upwards since the second quarter of the year, and are currently rising sharply as geopolitical uncertainties continue.

“We are not yet seeing these higher rates have an impact on house prices,” says Matthijs, “but there does seem to be a little bit of room for negotiation. And some buyers are able to have a second viewing of a property before they decide whether to put in a bid.

“So there is more opportunity for people who don’t want to rush into a purchase. And we have noticed that some estate agents are helping their clients to negotiate on or just under the asking price.”

The higher interest rates are also making it more important to have some savings if you are planning to buy, just to keep your costs as low as you can. “If you have €50,000 that you can put down towards the cost of your house, that means €50,000 you won’t have to borrow at well over 4% interest,” Matthijs points out.

Ask your mortgage-related questions

Expat Mortgages will be at the IamExpat Fair in Eindhoven on October 3, so come along and meet the team in person, or 

Seminars, whether online or in person, are a great way of getting direct answers to your questions and sharing your experiences with others. “We also try to focus on the more specific situations – people who have not even moved here yet, and entrepreneurs who may not have been active in the Netherlands for more than a year, when most banks want three years,” says Matthijs.

“We’ve also seen an increase in the number of PhD students wanting to buy, and banks are becoming a little bit more lenient. They used to say ‘no permanent contract, no mortgage,’ but that is changing as well.”

More homes on the market?

Despite there being room for negotiation in some parts of the market, the shortage of cheaper homes to buy is continuing, and single people or single-income families wanting to buy a home are still facing an uphill struggle. Demand continues to be very high for properties at the lower end of the market.

“Things have been very slow over the summer, but now more people are getting out there and looking,” says Matthijs. “And you can still expect to have to overbid if you are looking at cheaper properties. Much depends on what areas you are looking in as well.”

The fundamentals of foundations

Since April, banks have been taking more account of a property’s foundations when deciding whether or not to back a mortgage application. As yet, says Matthijs, there is no overall consensus about what to do if a property’s foundations are in need of urgent, or not-so-urgent, action. “It is primarily the bigger banks which have been the frontrunners on this,” says Matthijs. “It is very early days.”

“However, you can assume if the report shows there is €100,000 worth of repairs which need to be done before the house is properly stable, the banks are going to wonder how this is going to be paid. This could be done, for example, by increasing your mortgage loan – although many people are nowadays stretched to capacity because of the high house prices – or through having the savings in your bank account. One way or another, your bank will want to know if you can pay for the work.”

Are you thinking about buying a home in the Netherlands? Make an appointment to talk directly to a mortgage advisor and find out how much you can borrow.

World.title: Courts asked to shut 130 farms for breaching nitrogen limits
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Around 130 farmers risk being forced to give up their businesses after environmental group Mobilisation for the Environment (MOB) petitioned regional courts to tear up their nature permits, according to an investigation by RTL.

The organisation has started legal action in 10 provinces since 2023, asking judges to withdraw the permits of farms that exceed the limits for nitrogen depositions near Natura 2000 conservation areas.

Provincial governments have so far rejected applications from MOB, arguing that the cabinet in The Hague is working on a voluntary buyout scheme and other measures to reduce cattle numbers and nitrogen pollution.

Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, compared to 2019 levels, under the latest package announced by agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen in June. The measures still have to be put before parliament.

The failure of successive cabinets to come up with a definitive plan since the Council of State ruled the system for issuing nature permits illegal in 2019 has prompted MOB to take the provinces to court.

Concentration in south

The majority of requests were made in the southern provinces of Noord-Brabant, Limburg, Gelderland and Overijssel, where pig, poultry and cattle farming is concentrated.

Noord-Brabant decided to withdraw its permits in July after a deadline of a year to settle the issue with MOB expired.

Van Essen said earlier this month that court orders to shut down farms were “exactly what we’re trying to prevent” with the government’s package of measures, which include a 5% to 10% across the board cut to livestock numbers as a last resort.

But Chris Backes, professor of environmental law at Utrecht University, questioned whether the plans went far enough.

“Measures by the national government are only part of the solution,” he told RTL. “For some nature areas they are sufficient, according to research by the Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL).

“But in most cases the provinces will have to implement additional measures.”

World.title: Family of man who died during arrest file manslaughter complaint
World.content:
The family of a man who died after being arrested when police wrongly suspected him of stealing a fatbike have formally accused the force of manslaughter.

Alfredo Goeloe, 51, collapsed as officers restrained him after he was stopped on the bike in Rotterdam on Saturday evening. Police tried unsuccessfully to resuscitate him at the scene using a defibrilator.

In a video clip shot by a passer-by, Mr Goeloe could be heard screaming in pain and protesting that he had diabetes. His family said he had gone out on his sister’s fatbike to fetch diabetes medication while he was attending her baby shower party.

Around 1,000 people took part in a silent vigil on Monday evening and a march to the police station on Zuidplein.

A police spokesman later admitted that the bike had not been stolen. Mr Goeloe was pinned to the ground after he allegedly resisted arrest when police tried to detain him for failing to show ID papers.

The lawyer for the family, Gerard Roethof, said a formal complaint of manslaughter had been filed against the police force, which independent investigators will now have to assess.

“Too fast”

“The family say this is about much more than the order to use force,” Roethof told NOS. “We think this is a case of manslaughter, or in any event severe assault with fatal consequences.”

The prosecution department said on Friday that initial investigations showed he had been stopped by police on suspicion of riding too fast on the fatbike rather than because the vehicle was stolen.

At the time police in the area were looking out for a man and woman described as around 40 years old who had allegedly stolen a fatbike.

The internal police investigations division Rijksrecherche is examining the circumstances of Mr Goeloe’s death, including video footage, and the family’s complaint.

Around 45 pro-Palestinian protesters have been arrested after they disrupted a demonstration by supporters of Israel in Amsterdam.

Police led members of the group away after they sprayed slogans in red paint on the ground in Dam Square, near the national war memorial, where a group of several hundred had gathered for an event organised by Christians for Israel.

Speakers at the event included Chris Stoffer, leader of the orthodox Protestant party SGP, and the Dutch chief rabbi Binyamin Jacobs.

Earlier in the day the group Amsterdam Palestina Coalitie lost a court case in which it tried to overturn a ban by the city council on a counter-demonstration in Dam Square.

A spokesman for mayor Femke Halsema said there was a risk of public disorder if the both groups were allowed to demonstrate in the same place.

Pro-Palestinian protesters who went to the square in spite of the ban were arrested. A giant Palestinian flag that was hung from the upper floors of the H&M store overlooking the monument was removed by police.

The counter-demonstration was moved to Oude Turfmarkt, around 500 metres away on Rokin.

The public prosecution service will now decide whether to bring charges against the protesters in the square.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. We are launching a new format – “C8,” the Carpathian Eight – bringing together us and our… pic.twitter.com/tcIupMsBBK — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342. However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty. Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland. Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage. Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. World.title: Polish ruling party MP stripped of immunity and detained at request of EU prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds were designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colors offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024. World.title: Russia planning “accidental” strikes on eastern NATO states, warns Poland

Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Addressing parliament on Thursday, the prime minister said that “citizens absolutely have the right to know what scenario can be expected based on the information available today”. Intelligence from allies, including the United States and Ukraine, indicates that various scenarios are possible, but one is most likely, said Tusk. Over the next few months, Russia’s recent tactic of using jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine near the Polish border will likely continue, said Tusk, as well as attacks on Ukrainian economic and logistics infrastructure, such as railways. “Russia’s plan, according to intelligence, also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” continued Tusk. “These possibilities have been discussed for some time. This information is now very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Istnieje realne ryzyko, że na teren któregoś z państw NATO mogą wlatywać drony, dokonywać zniszczeń. I te „przypadkowe” według Rosji uderzenia mogą się powtarzać. pic.twitter.com/bScJBjQQF1 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 17, 2026 The aim, said Tusk, would be to “weaken NATO member states’ motivation to apply appropriate NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and there’s no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response”. The prime minister said that the incidents could be similar in nature to the night one year ago when around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace across its eastern border. “These ‘random’ attacks could repeat themselves, becoming an increasingly glaring illustration of NATO’s helplessness, as conceived by the Russians,” said Tusk. In response to last year’s drone incursions, Polish and allied NATO jets shot down some of the drones. Poland then invoked article 4 of the NATO treaty and received increased air-defence support from a number of NATO allies. Russia has recently stepped up its attacks on western Ukraine, including a number of strikes close to the Polish border. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has begun reinforcing security at border crossings, including installing 28 new bomb shelters and expanding air-defence systems The prime minister also confirmed that he would be travelling to Kyiv later on Thursday. He planned, among other things, to discuss with President Volodymy Zelensky how they would cooperate on air defence and utilise Ukraine’s experience and capabilities in this area. On the night of Thursday to Friday, the latest round of Russia attacks on Ukraine prompted Poland to scramble aircraft, activate air-defence systems, and close parts of its eastern airspace – actions that have recently become increasingly common. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026 In his remarks to parliament, Tusk also noted that “announcements by some global leaders that Russia is ready for a kind of ceasefire…have not come true”. He then mentioned President Donald Trump directly. “Since the president of the United States announced that Russia had assured him it was ready to honour such a partial ceasefire with Ukraine, numerous attacks have occurred, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine,” said Tusk. “The information we have received regarding the course of consultations and talks at various levels between the US and Russia is quite clear: Russia is not ready for any serious talks on a ceasefire, let alone peace, without Ukraine’s de facto surrender.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Warsaw launches patrols to crack down on improperly parked electric scooters
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms. According to the city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, more than 140 improperly parked scooters have been towed away within just a few days. Under the agreement, their operators now face potential fines. Nie ma miejsca dla hulajnóg tam, gdzie nie ich miejsce. Zdecydowałem o uruchomieniu specjalnych patroli Straży Miejskiej i ZDM. W ciągu ostatnich kliku dni dzięki ich pracy odholowanych zostało ponad 140 nieprawidłowo zaparkowanych hulajnóg elektrycznych. Taką możliwość daje… pic.twitter.com/U5fd7YDN8U — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) September 16, 2026 “There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.” An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited. It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park. Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list. The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking. Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules. The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries. Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June. Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h. The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters. E-scooters, which are currently unregulated in Poland, have been blamed for hundreds of accidents annually, with half of victims being pedestrians hit by riders https://t.co/TcrfPQocfr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 3, 2021 Under the nationwide legislation, electric scooters must be parked parallel to the outer edge of the pavement, and municipal authorities have the power to penalise those responsible for improper parking – a provision that primarily affects rental companies. A year after the legislation was introduced, after the first report on e-scooter-related accidents showed that they had caused hundreds of injuries and three deaths in 2021, Poland’s police launched a campaign publicising the new rules. At national level, infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak has announced further restrictions the government is working on, including a new law requiring scooters to be collected and left only in specially designated zones. The police have launched a campaign on the legal requirements for using e-scooters, including a warning that riding or parking them on pavements can be illegal. In 2022, accidents involving e-scooters in Poland resulted in 421 injuries and three deaths https://t.co/dMOBiNUBNG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish right-wing opposition MPs call for Independence Day march in Ukrainian city of Lviv
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A group of MPs from Poland’s main right-wing and far-right opposition parties have jointly called on the government to organise a march on Polish Independence Day in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, which was historically part of Poland. The idea has been firmly rejected by figures from the ruling coalition, who have called it “gross stupidity” and “madness”. It is also unclear to what extent the leadership of the opposition parties support the proposal. Pomysł zorganizowania "polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa" połączył polityków całej prawicy: PiS, Konfederacji, Rozwoju Plus i Konfederacji Korony Polskiej. Odsłaniamy kulisy. Pisze @patrykmichalski, autor programu #NewsMichalskiego ⤵️ 🔵 https://t.co/9L0M5lN0zY pic.twitter.com/1W3YxHdXHT — TVN24+ (@tvn24plus) September 15, 2026 The suggestion was made in a so-called parliamentary interpellation – through which MPs can ask questions and make suggestions to the government – submitted this month and signed by a group of 21 opposition MPs. They called on the government to do more to support the ethnic Polish community that still lives in Lviv, arguing that neither the Polish nor the Ukrainian state does enough to help them preserve and celebrate their identity. By contrast, argued the signatories, Polish state entities provide funding for Ukrainian organisations and events in Poland, including celebrations of Ukrainian Independence Day on 24 August. As such, they called upon the government to “organise official celebrations of [Polish] Independence Day in Lviv, including a Polish Independence March through the streets of the city” on 11 November. This would be “a concrete sign of remembrance and solidarity with Poles living in Ukraine”. Among the 21 signatories, 14 are from the caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and now the largest opposition group. A further three are from Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right opposition group. One is from Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a group that broke away from PiS earlier this year; another is from Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian party led by Grzegorz Braun. The final two are an independent, Janusz Kowalski, who recently quit PiS; and Jarosław Sachajko, who was elected in 2023 on the PiS party list but is part of the small Direct Democracy (Demokracja Bezpośrednia) group associated with Paweł Kukiz, a right-wing, anti-establishment figure. Interpelacja do Prezesa Rady Ministrów w sprawie zorganizowania 11 listopada polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa 11 listopada Rzeczpospolita Polska obchodzi Narodowe Święto Niepodległości. Jest to święto wszystkich Polaków, również tych, którzy mieszkają poza granicami… pic.twitter.com/7m6yUg1iKZ — Dariusz Matecki (@DariuszMatecki) August 25, 2026 It remains unclear to what extent the MPs have the backing of their parties in calling for the government to organise an Independence Day march in Lviv. Indeed, when Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of Confederation, was asked about the idea on Wednesday, he appeared to know very little about it. Speaking to broadcaster RMF, Bosak said that he had first heard about the proposal on Tuesday and that, after looking into it, he said it appeared to be a “stunt”, and one that he felt was “unnecessary”. “I think the point is to draw attention to the fact that Polish institutions are participating in the celebration of Ukraine’s Independence Day in Warsaw, and that there should be some symmetry,” said Bosak. However, he added that he felt many people would not understand this intention. “The appeal should be directed at Ukrainian institutions, not the Polish foreign ministry,” he said, adding that the MPs who came up with the idea should better explain it. “Frankly, I have more serious matters to attend to.” Czy przemarsz Polaków ulicami Lwowa z okazji Dnia Niepodległości to dobry pomysł? Zdaniem @krzysztofbosak niepotrzebny, a traktować go należy w kategorii happeningu. Ale jeśli się trzymać zasady wzajemności, to już lepiej organizować coś podobnego… w Kijowie. pic.twitter.com/PxdqNKBlCC — Ekonomat (@ekonomat_pl) September 16, 2026 Throughout much of history, Lviv (known in Polish as Lwów) was part of the Polish state, most recently during the period between the First and Second World Wars. However, amid postwar border movements, it became part of Ukraine along with some other former Polish territories. Many in Poland still feel a sense of attachment to the former Polish “borderlands” (kresy) that are now located in Ukraine, Lithuania and Belarus, and which are still home to at least hundreds of thousands of ethnic Poles (though the exact number is a matter of dispute). In Lviv itself, the most recent Ukrainian national census, taken in 2001, showed just under 10,000 people declaring Polish ethnicity in the city (around 1% of the population), though some estimates put the figure higher. Poland's culture minister has condemned Russia's attacks on the historic centre of Lviv in Ukraine, a UNESCO World Heritage site. She noted that Lviv, which was once part of Poland, represents the "shared history of Ukraine, Poland and all of Europe" https://t.co/qPhqXMAZ9r — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 25, 2026 Last year, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, clashed with the mayor of Lviv, Andriy Sadovyi, after visiting the city and criticising a monument commemorating nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, a figure seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland. Followers of Bandera were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Polish civilians. Poland regards the killings as a genocide but Ukraine rejects that label. The issue has caused renewed tension this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army”, which led the massacres. Any Polish attempt at a state-backed Independence Day march in Ukraine would likely stir further controversy. A leading candidate in Poland’s presidential election has clashed with a Ukrainian mayor after visiting his city and criticising the presence of a monument to Stepan Bandera, who is seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland https://t.co/nA9JzMmBcg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2025 Although the Polish government has not yet officially responded to the opposition MPs’ interpellation, a number of figures from the ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – criticised the idea on Wednesday. Deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk called it “gross stupidity” to think of organising such a march in Ukraine, especially at a time of war. He asked how Poles would feel if Germany tried to organise a similar march in Poland (some of whose current territory was part of Germany before World War Two). Both Dariusz Wieczorek, an MP from The Left (Lewica), and Marek Biernacki from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) told broadcaster TVN that the idea was “madness”. Próba zorganizowania we Lwowie prawicowej prowokacji z udziałem PiS-u, Rozwój Plus i Brauna to jednoznaczne działanie na rzecz Rosji i przeciwko polskiej racji stanu. — Witold Zembaczyński🇵🇱 (@WZembaczynski) September 16, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: European Parliament strips Polish far-right leader of immunity to face Holocaust denial charge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of legal immunity to face charges in his homeland of denying Nazi crimes, an offence that carries a potential prison sentence of up to three years. The decision marks the sixth time that the European Parliament has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial. Braun is already on trial in Poland for an attack on a Jewish religious celebration in parliament and is facing a number of other legal cases. Parlament Europejski w głosowaniu w Strasburgu uchylił immunitet europosła Grzegorza Brauna. Sprawa dotyczy negowania przez niego Holokaustu. Więcej: https://t.co/rB3UPUiS8o pic.twitter.com/icRLEqsWmF — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) September 15, 2026 In a vote on Tuesday, a majority of MEPs voted in favour of a request, submitted in February by Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, to lift the immunity enjoyed by Braun as an MEP. He has sat in the European Parliament since being elected in 2024. In his request, Żurek said that Polish prosecutors wish to charge Braun in relation to “denial of genocide crimes committed by functionaries of the Third Reich in the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp and the Lublin concentration camp (Majdanek)”. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has prosecutorial power, also revealed that the accusation relates to the use of gas chambers at those two camps. Neither the IPN nor Żurek confirmed at the time what specific words Braun had said that prompted the planned charges against him. However, the IPN noted that they had come at a live event broadcast online on 27 September 2025. On that date, Braun took part in a discussion with Jan Żaryn, a right-wing historian and former senator for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, titled “The Polish Underground State and the Jewish Issue”. A recording of the event is still available online. During his remarks, Braun referred to the “fake gas chambers of Majdanek and Auschwitz”, calling them “a dark, monstrous fantasy that has no satisfactory historical or academic support”. He suggested that the idea of the gas chambers had been invented as part of “propaganda and black PR operations conducted by the Soviet and Anglo-Saxon security services during World War Two”, and that the false claim continues to be exploited by Jews today. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 In actual fact, historians estimate that around 900,000 people were killed in the gas chambers at Auschwitz. The vast majority were Jews, but victims also included Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, and ethnic Poles. Meanwhile, gas chambers at Majdanek were used to kill tens of thousands, again mainly Jews. Today, the ashes of the camp’s cremated victims are preserved in a memorial at the site of the former camp. Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, has repeatedly sought to cast doubt on the veracity of Nazi crimes against Jews. Last month, he was charged with denying Nazi crimes in a separate case over earlier comments in which he called Auschwitz’s gas chambers “fake”. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years, for statements he made suggesting that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are "fake" https://t.co/PCssZt5eXD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 25, 2026 In December, Braun went on trial over a separate set of charges relating to four other incidents, including his attack on a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament in December 2023 and his disruption of a lecture by a Holocaust scholar. “I am standing before this court because I dared to defend myself against oppression and the ritual manifestation of Jewish supremacy,” declared Braun at the start of the trial, which remains ongoing. Braun is also facing various legal cases relating to his anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT actions. Last week, he posted a video of himself using a hammer to vandalise a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Police are investigating that incident. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a WWII group that fought against the Soviets but was also responsible for massacring Poles https://t.co/oCYRtNRO9N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2026 Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 8-9%. If it manages to secure that level of support at next year’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition. An MEP from the ruling coalition, Michał Kobosko, welcomed Tuesday’s decision to lift Braun’s immunity, saying that the far-right leader “deliberately and consciously…stokes hatred”. Kobosko said that such actions are particularly dangerous at a time when Russia is “actively waging hybrid and cognitive war against Poland”. He noted that Braun and his party have taken a sympathetic position towards Russia, including calling for Poland to “normalise” relations with Moscow. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: China overtakes Germany as Poland’s biggest source of imports for first time
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, according to new data from the central bank. It ends a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot. The shift came as imports of Chinese goods surged, driven in part by a sharp increase in Chinese cars, while imports from Germany declined. “In July 2026, China was the largest supplier of goods to Poland for the first time, overtaking Germany in that month,” wrote the National Bank of Poland (NBP) in an announcement on Monday. “A significant increase in imports of computer hardware, passenger cars and durable consumer goods influenced the shift in the geographical structure of imports,” added the bank. Znamy już pełne dane handlowe za lipiec 2026 – za miesiąc kiedy Chiny po raz pierwszy w historii stały się największym dostawcą towarów do Polski, przed Niemcami. W lipcu import ogółem z Chin wzrósł o 28,8% r/r, podczas gdy z Niemiec spadł o 1,8% r/r. Import pojazdów… pic.twitter.com/LfJ50nXzNM — PKO Research (@PKO_Research) September 15, 2026 In a comment on the new data, analysts at PKO, a Polish bank, said that the July shift was partly due to “one-time factors” and noted that Germany remains Poland’s largest supplier on a 12-month basis, although its lead has been steadily shrinking. In July, Polish imports from China rose 28.8% year-on-year, while imports from Germany fell 1.8%, according to PKO. Imports of motor vehicles from Germany fell 9.3% year-on-year, while imports from China rose 54.4%. Imports from China of computers, electronics and optical equipment rose 31.5% year-on-year in July, the strongest increase since 2022. More detailed data on trade with the two countries, published also on Tuesday by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, provided further insight into the shift. According to GUS, Poland imported goods worth €36.7 billion from China in the first seven months of the year, giving China a 15.9% share of total Polish imports, up from 14.9% in the same period of 2025. Imports from Germany stood at €43.1 billion in that period, 18.6% of the total, down from 19.4% in 2025. Poland’s third-largest source of imports was the United States, with €12.7 worth of goods, a share of 5.5%, up from 4.9% in 2025. Poland has been NATO's biggest importer of arms over the last five years, according to new data from @SIPRIorg. Over 90% of Polish imports have come from South Korea and the United States https://t.co/jij0nfbhFc — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 Germany has been Poland’s largest trading partner since the collapse of communism, leading both in imports and exports. It overtook the Soviet Union, which had dominated Poland’s foreign trade during the communist era. But China has steadily gained ground as a source of Polish imports since the 2010s, rising to second place behind Germany by the 2020s. In terms of exports in the first seven months of this year, Germany dominates, receiving goods worth €69.8 billion, or 26.3% of all Poland’s exports. It is followed by the Czech Republic (€14.3 billion), France (€14.0 billion), the United Kingdom (€11.6 billion) and the Netherlands (€10.9 billion). World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Two New Squares and a Tower Planned Around Holešovice Station
World.content:
The area around Prague’s Nádraží Holešovice station is set for a major redevelopment after the international architectural competition for the site was won by Czech studio Chybík + Krištof.

The winning proposal envisions turning the current transport hub and surrounding brownfield into a new urban district, with two public squares, improved connections between public transport services and a new high-rise building designed to become a landmark.



The redevelopment covers roughly eight hectares around the station. Its aim is not only to add new buildings, but also to reorganise one of Prague’s important transport nodes and connect it more closely with the surrounding neighbourhood.

The competition jury selected the proposal by Chybík + Krištof as the winning design.

From transport hub to urban district

Nádraží Holešovice is currently one of Prague’s major transport interchanges, but much of the surrounding area has traditionally been used primarily for transport and other infrastructure.

The redevelopment is intended to change that. Alongside new construction, the project places emphasis on making transfers between different modes of public transport easier and fully accessible.

The project forms part of the wider Nové Holešovice development, which brings together the Prague Public Transit Company and private investors.

CPI Property, EP Real Estate, Penta Real Estate and AKIPIA are among the companies involved. The City of Prague and Prague 7 municipal district are also participating in the project.

World.title: ČokoFest to Bring Three Days of Chocolate to Galerie Harfa
World.content:
Chocolate lovers will have plenty to discover in Prague this October as ČokoFest 2026 returns to Galerie Harfa for three days of tastings, workshops, competitions and sweet treats.

The festival will take place from October 16 to 18, 2026, at the shopping center in Prague 9. Admission is free.



Now in its 14th year, ČokoFest brings together Czech and international producers, including established chocolatiers and smaller makers.

Visitors will be able to sample and buy a wide selection of chocolates and confectionery, including handmade and bean-to-bar products, pralines, cakes, cookies and macarons.

The festival will also feature a range of less conventional chocolate and sweet specialties. Among the offerings will be a chocolate fountain, chocolate kebabs, chocolate-covered fruit, as well as chocolate-infused wine and beer. Other products on sale will include jams, liqueurs, syrups, dried fruits, honey products, coffee and tea.

Exhibitors from several European countries will join Czech producers, giving visitors the opportunity to discover different chocolate styles and specialties while shopping at international sales stalls.

ČokoFest will also feature a program of activities for both adults and children. Visitors can take part in tastings, competitions and creative workshops, while children can enjoy a dedicated zone and entertainment from performers dressed as popular children’s characters.

Cooking demonstrations will be another part of the program, with chefs from local restaurants sharing their experience and showing visitors how to prepare various sweet treats. Some workshops will also focus on chocolate-making techniques that can be tried at home.

The festival is designed as a family-friendly event, with activities taking place throughout the three days. In addition to tasting and shopping, visitors can watch pastry chefs at work, take part in competitions and learn more about the production and preparation of chocolate and other confectionery.

Opening hours:

Friday, October 16: 2:00–6:00 p.m.

Saturday, October 17: 10:00 a.m.–6:30 p.m.

Sunday, October 18: 10:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m.

World.title: Poznej Vltavu Festival Returns to Prague on September 28
World.content:
The second edition of the Poznej Vltavu (Get to Know the Vltava) festival will take place across Prague on September 28, 2026.

For one day, the banks of the Vltava will host a programme exploring the river from a variety of perspectives.

The festival will feature workshops, exhibitions, sports activities, boat trips, and tours of places that are not normally open to the public.



Prague’s riverfront embankments and other locations along the Vltava will offer activities for children, adults, and seniors.

The festival aims to highlight the Vltava as a natural part of Prague’s urban environment and an important ecological feature, while giving visitors the opportunity to spend a day exploring the river and its surroundings.

Experts from a range of fields will discuss the Vltava in its broader context and offer insights into lesser-known aspects of the river.

This year’s programme will involve organisations including the Prague Institute of Planning and Development, Prague City Tourism, the Prague City Gallery, the Vltava River Authority, Prague Waterworks and Sewerage Company, the Prague Water Management Company, ROPID, Prague City Forests, the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic, and many others.

The festival area will extend farther along the Vltava this year, reaching Žluté lázně and the new Dvorecký Bridge, which has quickly become a popular destination for Prague residents since opening.

Most events will be free to attend, although some activities will require advance registration due to limited capacity.

More information is available on the festival’s Facebook event.

World.title: Red Arrows to Fly Over Charles Bridge This Friday
World.content:
Prague will hear the roar of Royal Air Force jets on Friday, September 18, when the Red Arrows aerobatic team stages a flypast over the city.

Ten BAE Hawk T1 aircraft from the British RAF team are scheduled to pass over the Charles Bridge at around 2:00 PM. The jets will leave smoke trails in the colours of the Czech flag during the display.



The formation is expected to approach Prague from the north before reaching the area around Václav Havel Airport. The aircraft will then form an arrow-shaped formation and fly around the western and southern parts of the capital before turning north along the Vltava.

The jets are expected to fly at an altitude of roughly 300 metres above the ground. The engines will be clearly audible across parts of the city, although the flypast itself will last only a short time.

After passing through central Prague, the formation will turn northeast and continue toward Ostrava. The city is hosting NATO Days, one of the Czech Republic’s largest military and security events, this weekend.

The timetable and route could still change because of weather or other air traffic in the Prague area. A similar Red Arrows flypast was held in Prague last September, but poor weather delayed the aircraft by more than an hour.

The flypast is being held in connection with Czech Air Force Day, which is observed on September 15.

The Red Arrows are the official aerobatic display team of the Royal Air Force and regularly perform at air shows and military events in Britain and abroad.

World.title: Groovy Market Fest Returns to Riegrovy Sady on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Groovy Market Fest will return to Riegrovy Sady on Saturday, October 3, bringing together food, independent brands, design and live music for its third edition.

The one-day event will take place at Energy Pub from noon until 10 p.m.

Following two editions held during the summer, the organizers are extending the concept into the autumn, with visitors able to browse local products, eat street food and listen to live music and DJs throughout the day.



The market is organised around three main areas. The Food Garden will focus on gastronomy and street food from local businesses, while Palm Street will feature bakeries, artisanal products and other local goods. The Design Zone will bring together fashion, design and products from independent Czech brands.

Live performances and DJ sets will run from the afternoon into the evening, providing the musical programme alongside the market stalls.

Marek Novák, founder of Groovy Market Fest, said the first two editions helped the team establish the format and identify what visitors respond to.

“After two editions, we know exactly what works at Groovy Market Fest: high-quality local brands, good food, and an atmosphere that keeps people coming back,” Novák said. “This third edition is an opportunity for us to show that Groovy isn’t just a summer event, but a festival that holds a firm place in Prague all year round.”

Visitors can buy tickets for either of the two five-hour sessions. The first runs from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., followed by a second session from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m.

A ticket for one session costs 100 CZK, while an all-day ticket covering both sessions is available for 190 CZK. Tickets are sold through GoOut.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Groovy Market Fest (@groovymarketfest)

From Barcelona street food to a Prague market

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food sector.

One of their main inspirations was Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market, an urban market known for combining food, design, music and independent creative businesses.

World.title: Prague Run Day to Bring Six Races to Riegrovy Sady on September 19
World.content:
On September 19, runners of all levels can take part in a new running event combining track and park races in one of Prague’s best-known green spaces.

There are six different races to choose from, so whether you’re looking for a serious challenge or just want to get out and run, there’s an option for you.



Six races to choose from

The programme includes six races, ranging from a short family run to a one-hour challenge.

The day will begin with the 800m Family Run, designed for young runners and their accompanying adults. There will also be an 800m race on the athletic track, offering participants the opportunity to compete over a short distance in a traditional track setting.

For those looking for a longer challenge, the 1 Mile race will take place on the athletic oval. The organisers describe it as a special opportunity to race over the classic distance, with participation limited to a maximum of 30 runners.

The 5km Solo Run will offer a more familiar challenge for runners of different experience levels. It is followed by the 4x3km Relay, a team race in which four runners each complete two 1.5km laps.

The final event of the day will be the Golden Hour Race, a one-hour running challenge taking place during the golden hour.

The event will be based at the Sokol Vinohrady athletic oval, which will serve as the main hub for the day.

Find all race distances, times and registration details at praguerunday.cz

📍 Riegrovy Sady Athletic Oval

📅 Saturday, September 19

🏃 6 races for different levels

🏅 Medal for every participant

World.title: Prague Is Turning a Historic Factory Chimney Into an Observation Deck
World.content:
A glass elevator will carry visitors through the preserved chimney of a former distillery before emerging above its rim to reveal views of the city.

Inside the developing Lihovar district in Smíchov, a historic factory chimney is being transformed into a viewing platform, with visitors set to travel through the structure in a panoramic glass elevator.



The chimney, which stands approximately 50 meters tall, is part of the former Zlíchov distillery. Rather than demolishing the industrial landmark, developers have incorporated it into the redevelopment of the site.

The project is being developed by Trigema, which is building the new Lihovar district on the former distillery grounds.

The elevator itself is one of the project’s most unusual features. Once it reaches the top of the chimney, the cabin will lift a special cap weighing approximately 500 kilograms, allowing it to rise above the chimney’s opening.

The glass cabin will then serve as an observation deck, offering a 360-degree view of Prague.

From industrial site to new Prague district

The Lihovar development is being built on the site of the former Zlíchov distillery in Prague 5. The redevelopment includes new buildings alongside the preservation of selected elements of the original industrial complex.

The factory chimney is among the structures being retained. Another is the historic former brewhouse, which is planned for cultural use.

The opening date for the observation deck has not been announced.

World.title: Moving to Hungary costs less than Spain – and newcomers bring twice as much stuff, new data shows
World.content:
New data based on nearly 200 Hungary-related moving quotes suggests people moving to Hungary tend to relocate much larger households than those leaving the country, while Hungarian routes are generally cheaper than the European average.

Moving to Hungary can be significantly cheaper than relocating to Spain from the same European countries, while people moving into Hungary also tend to bring substantially larger household loads, according to new international moving data covering January to September 2026.

The figures come from Finnish international moving company Flyto Relocation, which analysed 7,754 quoted moves across 1,211 international routes. The company says its dataset includes 197 Hungary-related quotes, covering 48 routes and 29 partner countries. All prices cited are median quoted prices excluding VAT.

The data shows that 108 of the Hungary-related quotes were for moves into Hungary, compared with 90 for moves out of the country.

People moving to Hungary bring much larger households

One of the clearest differences is the amount of belongings being moved. The median inbound load to Hungary was 16.75 cubic metres, more than twice the 7.5 cubic metres recorded for outbound moves.

According to Flyto Relocation, a 17 m³ load would typically correspond to a furnished one- to two-bedroom home, while 7.5 m³ is closer to a studio-sized move or a car full of boxes.

The company says the figures suggest that moves into Hungary more often involve people settling into the country with an entire household, while those leaving Hungary tend to move smaller quantities of belongings, potentially reflecting individuals relocating for work.

The largest number of inbound quotes came from the Netherlands and Belgium, with 18 quotes each, followed by Germany with nine, and Greece and Spain with eight each.

For outbound moves, Spain was the most common destination, with 13 quotes, followed by the Netherlands with 10 and Germany with seven. France and Italy each accounted for six quotes.

If you missed it: Reader’s letter: The things I learned to appreciate about Hungary after leaving

Moving to Hungary can be cheaper than Spain

The data also shows a notable difference when comparing Hungary and Spain as destinations.

For a 20–30 m³ household move, the median quoted price from the Netherlands to Hungary was €4,831, compared with €5,690 for a move from the Netherlands to Spain.

For Belgium, the corresponding figures were €3,998 to Hungary and €5,632 to Spain. From Germany, a 20–30 m³ move to Hungary had a median quoted price of €3,406, compared with €5,797 for Spain.

That means the median quoted price for these Hungarian routes was roughly 15% lower from the Netherlands, 29% lower from Belgium and 41% lower from Germany than the comparable Spanish routes.

Hungarian routes also come in below the European average

The company’s broader European data indicates that Hungarian routes can also be cheaper than the European average for comparable move sizes and distances.

For moves of 20–30 m³ travelling 800–1,500 km, the median quoted price on Hungarian routes was €3,754, compared with €4,566 across Europe – around 18% lower.

For smaller moves of 10–20 m³ over the same distance, the median was €2,888 in the Hungary data, compared with €3,297 across Europe, or about 12% less.

However, Flyto Relocation notes that these comparisons are based on relatively small samples of 14 and 17 quotes respectively, meaning they should be treated as indicative rather than representative of the entire moving market.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

A typical European move costs thousands of euros

Across the company’s full European dataset, a typical mid-range move of 20–30 m³ over 1,500–2,500 km had a median quoted price of €6,279, excluding VAT. For a smaller 10–20 m³ move travelling less than 800 km, the median was €2,394.

The company also warns that simply dividing the total price by the volume of belongings can give a misleading impression of moving costs.

A 3 m³ move costs around 12 times more per cubic metre than a 50 m³ household move, according to the index. This reflects the fact that fixed costs such as collection, transport arrangements and handling do not increase proportionally with the amount being moved.

Hungarians book moves about two months in advance

The Hungary data suggests that people planning international moves generally give themselves around two months to prepare. The median booking lead time for Hungary-related moves was 58 days, almost identical to the European-wide figure of 57 days.

July to October were the busiest months in the Hungary dataset, together accounting for around 70% of quotes. Budapest featured in roughly one in three Hungary-related quotes, followed by Debrecen and Szeged.

The most common Hungary-related routes in the dataset included the Netherlands to Hungary, with a median quoted price of €4,831 for a 21 m³ move, based on 18 quotes. The median for Belgium to Hungary was €3,998 for 20.5 m³, also based on 18 quotes.

For moves in the opposite direction, Hungary to Spain had a median quoted price of €4,398 for 12 m³, based on 13 quotes, while Hungary to the Netherlands stood at €3,021 for 5 m³, based on 10 quotes.

The figures are based on quoted prices rather than final paid prices, and the Hungary sample represents one company’s customer enquiries rather than official migration data.

World.title: Beautiful European destination could become Budapest Airport’s next novelty
World.content:
Zaragoza could soon be added to Budapest Airport’s European route map, after the Aragón regional government and Zaragoza City Council announced a tender covering 31 potential air routes.

New air connection could link Budapest Airport with Aragón

The scheme could connect the airport serving the capital of Aragón with 15 countries, creating new international links while strengthening existing connections. The tender includes 29 cities in total, seven of them domestic destinations. Among the international routes included in the programme are Budapest, Prague, Bratislava, Warsaw and Kraków.

If the Budapest route goes ahead, Zaragoza would become a new Spanish destination available to travellers from the Hungarian capital. According to the information published about the tender, Zaragoza is currently a significant but unserved potential Spanish destination on Budapest Airport’s European network, reports Budflyer.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

A historic Spanish city between Madrid and Barcelona

Zaragoza is the capital of Aragón and Spain’s fifth-largest city. Situated on the banks of the Ebro River, it has a history spanning more than 2,000 years, with Roman, Muslim, Jewish and Christian influences all leaving their mark on the city.

One of Zaragoza’s best-known landmarks is the enormous Baroque Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar. Other major attractions include La Seo Cathedral, associated with the UNESCO-listed Mudéjar architecture of Aragón, and the Aljafería Palace, a former Moorish palace.

A beautiful city that is somehow still overlooked by some

The city’s location between Madrid and Barcelona has also made it an important transport and economic centre. At the same time, Zaragoza remains less familiar to international tourists than Spain’s best-known major cities. For Hungarian travellers, the city could offer a different side of Spain, with its historic centre, riverside setting, Roman remains and El Tubo district, known for its many tapas bars, writes 24.hu.

The proposed route is part of a wider tender process, meaning a Budapest–Zaragoza flight has not yet been confirmed. However, the inclusion of the Hungarian capital in the plans could open the way for a new direct connection between Budapest and one of Spain’s major inland cities.

World.title: Social workers protest for pay rise in Budapest, Péter Magyar meets the demonstrators
World.content:
Social sector workers demonstrated outside the Prime Minister’s Office in Budapest on Friday, demanding an immediate 25 per cent pay rise and improved working conditions. Péter Magyar then went out and met them to hear their demands.

Demonstrators call for higher wages and better working conditions

The protest was organised under the slogan, “We pay our utility bills in one go, so we want our pay rise in one go, too.” Workers said the previously promised 20–25 per cent wage increase, which is expected to be introduced in two stages and may also take into account the minimum wage increase and tax relief, falls well short of their expectations.

Ferenc Köves, president of the Trade Union of Workers in the Social Sector, said employees understood that the government had inherited the problems facing the sector from the previous administration. However, he stressed that the current government was the one responsible for finding a solution.

Péter Magyar meets protesters outside Prime Minister’s Office

Prime Minister Péter Magyar went out to the demonstrators and said the government was fully aware of the difficulties facing the social sector. He argued that even another 25 per cent pay rise would not, on its own, provide a meaningful and genuine solution to the sector’s problems.

Köves handed the prime minister the union’s proposed wage table, along with a list of issues it wants to discuss beyond the question of pay. Magyar invited union representatives to talks, but although they thanked him for the invitation, they suggested holding the meeting at a later date.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

PM Magyar wants a long-term solution

Addressing the demonstrators, Péter Magyar said the government faced a wide range of responsibilities. He said it had taken over a severely depleted budget and would have to decide whether workers should receive a one-off payment or a pay rise this year.

The government must also determine whether next year’s wage increase should be implemented in one or two stages, he added, asking workers in the social sector for patience.
