World.title: This ‘hard to swallow’ Filipino film hopes to make Oscars history
World.content:
‘Filipiñana,’ the country’s official film entry to the Oscars, hopes the international audience sees something different — a ‘different side of the Philippines’ and a ‘different kind of Philippine cinema’

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines attempts to make history after selecting Filipiñana as the country’s official entry to the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards.

A 100-minute film showing the Philippines’ class divide, Filipiñana tells the story of 17-year-old Isabela, who works as a “tee girl” in an exclusive golf club.

“It’s hard to accept a formalist film that isn’t a narrative,” said film producer Bianca Balbuena in Filipino.

Initially a short film, the full-length feature directed by Rafael Manuel and co-produced by Bradley Liew has been praised for its visual storytelling, but has also drawn critique for its slow pace.

“As director Rafael said, how he thought of this is not script-based, it’s more on verses, like music: verses, chorus. So it’s hard to accept. Even us (producers), when we first saw the cut, we said, ‘This is hard to swallow.”

But it’s this unique approach that Filipiñana hopes to bank on when it tries to earn a nomination at the Oscars. Since the inception of the Best International Feature Film category in 1956, no entry submitted by the Philippines has even made the official shortlist of 15 films.

Filipiñana’s strong reception at the international festivals, including the Sundance Film Festival where it bagged the Special Jury Award for Creative Vision, has kept everyone behind the film hopeful.

“I think the international audience saw a different side of the Philippines, and saw a different kind of what Philippine cinema can be and is. They were excited to see something different,” Balbuena said.

Locally, Filipiñana premiered as the closing film of the Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival 2026

“Actually, Cinemalaya was our 22nd film festival,” Balbuena said. “Then now, we are in our 26th. It is going to Bangkok, going to Busan, Tokyo, Vienna, Hamburg, Singapore, and many more. It’s competing in Pingyao, China also.”

‘Filipiñana’ cast members Jorrybell Agoto (third from left) and Nour Hooshmand (left) with producers Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew receive from Film Academy of the Philippines director general Paolo Villaluna (right) their certificates as the Philippines’ official entry to the 2027 Oscars.

Jorrybell Agoto stars as Isabel, whose job as a tee girl includes setting up golf balls for elite patrons, including the country club’s president Dr. Palanca, played by Teroy Guzman.

Paolo Villaluna, the director general of the Film Academy of the Philippines (FAP), which announced Filipiñana’s Oscars selection last September 13, said the body will again support the country’s Oscars campaign.

“The film offers a visually distinct and controversial portrait of the Filipino experience,” said Villaluna. “The Film Academy will work closely with the Filipiñana team throughout the Oscars campaign, providing the support they need and make the most of this opportunity for Philippine cinema.”

Last year, the Philippines’ Oscars entry, Lav Diaz’s Magellan, made a strong push but still fell short of the Academy’s final cut.

But Filipiñana’s producers said they’ve been campaigning for the film internationally, even before it was selected as the country’s Oscars entry.

“Whether or not we get chosen, we already had a plan,” Balbuena shared. “It was [good timing] that we were at the North American release announcing [its selection]. So we can do an email blast to all the members to watch the North American theatrical run. We’ve also covered the biggest cities of the voters: US and UK. So we are ready since then.”

Aside from Filipiñana, FAP threw its support for the Oscars consideration of 58th (Best Documentary Feature Film) and Agapito (Best Live Action Short Film) in their respective categories.

A still from the animated film ’58th, which rotoscopes and dramatizes the 2009 Maguindanao maasacre. Film still courtesy of FFR

58th, directed by Carl Joseph Papa, is an animated docudrama film about the 2009 Maguindanao massacre, which claimed 58 innocent lives, but only 57 were officially recognized as the body of photojournalist Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay has yet to be found.

“We want the film to be a reminder and an eye-opener: this happened in 2009, and it’s still happening all around the world,” Papa said. “I hope it’s an eye-opener and people will remember, so the tragic events won’t happen again.”

“This is officially the deadliest single day for journalists in the whole history that has ever been counted: 32 journalists killed in one go,” added film producer Nessa Valdellon. “We’re hoping that people who cover…who write stories will be able to appreciate it and realize, ‘God, this is the importance of [our] jobs.’”

Agapito, co-directed by Arvin Belarmino and Kyla Danelle Romero, tells the story of manual pinsetters in a vintage duckpin alley and explores the themes of love, family, and patience in a working-class setting.

“Agapito is about a real person, actually. He’s my brother who’s in the autism spectrum, special child,” said Belarmino. “It’s my first time to produce because mostly the films I make before are subcultured, sociopolitical. It’s my first time to show vulnerability to tell about the story of a loved one.”

A movie poster of ‘Agapito,’ a short film featuring pinsetters in a duckpin alley.

“Filipinos are still constantly telling their stories for the Filipinos. It’s just a matter of exposure to everybody,” said Jon Galvez, one of Agapito’s producers.

“My wish is: instead of trailers are shown outside cinemas, I hope it will be short films — to provide space for short filmmakers to show their films outside of festivals. Philippine cinema is worth it. Worth fighting for, worth watching.”

“Let’s just give it a chance,” Galvez added. “There are a lot of factors involved, that’s why it’s not supported all the time, but just give it a shot. The talent of Filipinos, the storytelling, it’s so different.”

The deadline for submission of films to the Academy Awards is on September 30, 2026, with the official shortlist of 15 films to be revealed on December 15, 2026.

In 2027, the five final nominees will be announced on January 21. The 99th Oscars ceremony is set on March 14, 2027 at the Dolby Theater in Los Angeles.

“I hope all eyes are on the Philippines now, all Hollywood eyes. I think we have a good chance with the three titles here,” Villaluna said.

“I hope the Filipinos support all our films. We are the masters of cinema, we are good storytellers.” – Rappler.com

Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

World.title: Anthropic considers releasing new AI model ahead of IPO, sources say
World.content:
ANTHROPIC. The Anthropic logo is seen in this illustration taken March 31, 2023.

Anthropic weighs new AI model launch amid OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra success, as CEO calls for industry slowdown and investors reassess competitive landscape ahead of IPO

Anthropic is considering rolling out a new AI model to counter OpenAI’s momentum since its launch of GPT-6 Astra, according to three sources, ahead of an expected IPO and after its CEO called for an industrywide slowdown.

The timing of a potential launch aimed at addressing competitive pressure from a direct rival follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call on the global AI community to slow down the pace of releasing new capabilities to address safety concerns, the sources said.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a 3,800-word essay on September 12.

The essay, which painted a bleak picture of swarms of AI agents taking over the internet and outpacing human control, drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, released this month, has gained traction among businesses, prompting concerns among some investors who told Reuters they are re-evaluating Anthropic’s position as the leading provider of enterprise AI tools.

Anthropic is evaluating the safety of its next model as part of its deliberations over a release, one of the people familiar with the matter said.

Some of the discussions involve how to balance investment in releasing new models with efforts to strengthen the company’s profitability as rising interest rates make investors more focused on the timing of expected profits, said people familiar with the company’s thinking.

The debate over spending highlights the increasing pressure on the firms at the center of the AI boom to produce sustainable cash flows sooner, thanks both to rising rates and tough competition from open-source AI providers, especially in China.

Anthropic declined to comment for this story.

The potential launch would test how Anthropic can defend its enterprise market position against OpenAI while maintaining the safety-first identity that has distinguished it from competitors.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra gains enterprise traction

OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3, touting gains in computer use, software engineering, cybersecurity and professional work. The model has received a strong response from enterprise users and developers, prompting potential Anthropic IPO investors to scrutinize whether OpenAI could begin taking share from Anthropic, which has been viewed for months as the leader in enterprise AI.

Astra accounted for about 13% of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable, according to the latest data.

Astra has also pulled ahead on OpenRouter, a widely used platform that routes developer traffic across AI models. OpenRouter said its users spent more on OpenAI models than on Anthropic models last week, the first time OpenAI has led on that measure in more than two and a half years.

Anthropic maintains revenue advantage

Some existing investors and those who expect to invest in both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs said they do not believe Astra poses a significant threat to Anthropic, given the size of its lead in the market for enterprise AI tools and the amount of time it takes to unseat incumbent vendors to large companies.

Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate topped $65 billion by the end of July, up from about $9 ​billion at the end of 2025. It is also projecting a 2028 revenue of ‌roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters previously reported. OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate passed $40 billion in July.

Investors also expect leadership among Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and other major AI developers to shift repeatedly as companies release new generations of models, making any advantage potentially short-lived.

Bigger challenges ahead

A potentially bigger challenge for Anthropic and other leading AI providers is the rise of open-source and open-weight models, which can lower token costs and allow companies to build more of their own AI infrastructure rather than rely on providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI, investors said.

The shift could put pressure on the economics of the AI industry as companies have more options to develop and run models outside the leading commercial providers, broadening the competitive threat beyond the race between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Meta Platforms has been among Anthropic’s largest customers, but is looking to reduce its use of Anthropic’s models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, people familiar with the matter said. Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

OpenAI, meanwhile, has taken some pressure off the race to public markets. Its CEO, Altman, confirmed on Saturday that the company would not go public in 2026, saying concerns around AI safety made this an ill-advised time for a listing.

Anthropic could push its IPO to after the November US midterm elections, with the elections not expected to have a major impact on the offering, according to two people familiar with the matter. The IPO has already been pushed back from earlier plans, with Reuters previously reporting that marketing was expected to begin in mid-October at the earliest. – Rappler.com

World.title: The week in photos: September 12-18, 2026
World.content:
CO-EXISTENCE. A dog looks at a stuffed baboon toy during a protest outside the Urban Wildlife Centre near Simon's Town, as wild baboon troops face relocation to the facility, in Cape Town, South Africa, on September 13, 2026.

A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

MANILA, Philippines — On September 14, the Bangsamoro people troop to polling precincts to elect their parliament after decades of armed struggle and historical injustices, years of painstaking negotiations with the Philippine government, and repeated electoral delays.

Election watchdogs report significant irregularities during the polls including reports of pre-shaded ballots, vote-buying, and armed individuals in voting centers. Commission on Elections Chairman George Garcia says election-related deaths rose to at least five before voting ended.

On September 16, four retired Supreme Court justices advised the impeachment court on the conviction threshold debate. Three of them took the position that the number of votes needed to remove the impeached official is not fixed at 16. Retired justice Adolfo Azcuna maintains that all 24 senators should be counted, arguing that a fixed supermajority is necessary to prevent impeachment from being misused for political purposes.

Meanwhile, former president Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the International Criminal Court (ICC) for the third status conference regarding his charges of crimes against humanity related to his drug war, on September 16. Duterte has been detained in The Hague since 2025, and his trial is set to begin on November 30, following the confirmation of three charges against him.

The ICC Trial Chamber III ordered the continued detention of Duterte: “The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions. For these reasons, the chamber hereby decides that the accused shall continue to be detained,” said the chamber’s decision.

World.title: The ‘difficult’ Etta Rosales — and why she stands out in her one-of-a-kind generation of activists
World.content:
Ateneo professor Melay Abao writes about the life and times of Etta Rosales, the former communist who became a lawmaker and eventually headed the Commission on Human Rights

MANILA, Philippines – She’s sharp and passionate as ever, taking time to write more than a few words on each of the book that she signed on Thursday, September 17, at the launch of Difficult: The Life and Times of Etta Rosales at the Executive House in UP Diliman, Quezon City.

She is, after all, the feisty Etta Rosales.

Former chairperson of the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) who had also served as representative of Akbayan for nine years, 87-year-old Loretta Ann “Etta” Rosales was the star of the show at the book launch organized by her family, peers, and comrades-in-arms.

Difficult tells her complex but inspiring journey from an activist to a communist cadre to political prisoner under the Marcos dictatorship — to being a key leader of a leftist political party to getting elected to Congress and to serving as head of a government body that probed human rights abuses.

Written by Akbayan’s first secretary-general and Ateneo professor Carmel “Melay” Abao, Difficult carries six chapters that chronicle Etta’s growing up years as a daughter of a military officer (a West Pointer at that); her political awakening and organizing in the communist underground after the declaration of Martial Law in 1972; marriage and motherhood; her leadership in the human rights movement and shift to mainstream politics; and her various battles with cancer, two strokes, COVID-19, pneumonia.

She would, in fact, ask her doctors: why am I still alive? “‘Malakas kasi ang puso mo (Your heart is strong),’ the doctors would tell her,” wrote Abao.

Etta herself wrote one portion of the book — the one pertaining to her second arrest and detention in 1976, when she was molested and heavily beaten.

COURAGE. Etta Rosales at the launch of a book on her life, written by Carmel Abao.

Such a harrowing experience, and the grace and courage that enabled her to continue organizing, mobilizing, and working on the streets and within the bureaucracy, melted the heart of the late president Noynoy Aquino.

It was Aquino who appointed Etta as CHR chair shortly after he was elected president in 2010.

Quoting Butch Abad, Aquino’s former budget secretary, Abao wrote: “Etta’s greatest contribution back then was her positive influence on President PNoy… PNoy was anti-communist, Butch reveals, but this anti-communism was tempered by his interaction with Etta. Because of PNoy’s knowledge and appreciation of Etta’s life story, he gained a better understanding of why those who had similar experiences during Martial Law took on very hardline positions.”

In her remarks at the launch, Abao shared her biggest takeaway as the author: that Etta’s generation of activists is one of a kind.

“That generation needs to be recognized by my generation and those after me as the generation that risked it all — lives, personal relationships, family, careers, personal development,” Abao said. “Risked it all for the sake of our nation’s democracy. I know that every generation takes risks, but Etta’s generation of activists took risks without keeping score of what they could lose because of their activism, without dwelling on the ‘what ifs.’ What if I took that PhD instead of organizing the teachers’ union? What if I stayed above ground and never left my kids and my husband? What if I just kept silent during those Marcos years?“

AUTHOR. Ateneo professor Carmel Abao after receiving the first copies of the book.

In the many conversations that she had with Etta for the book, Abao said that not once did the “what if” question crop up.

“Having no regrets doesn’t mean, however, that there are no costs,” Abao said. “That generation lost so many great lives that were cut short by the dictatorship. And the children of that generation suffered so much — they lost parents, endured abandonment and basically skipped their childhoods.”

But Etta “clearly stood out” from the rest — “one of a kind,” Abao added. “Because she is so many roles woven into one person – marami ang naging torture victim pero si Etta ang torture victim na naging kongresista, na naging chair pa ng Commission on Human Rights (there were many torture victims, but Etta was the torture victim who became a lawmaker and even served as chair of the Commission on Human Rights).”

Etta felt at home at the launch, which was an opportunity for old comrades to get together again.

“Each one has influenced me in my various struggles in life — above ground, underground, middle ground, and again above ground,” Etta said in her remarks. “They all had one thing in common; they kept me grounded and this helped me remain steadfast in the pursuit of my faith in humanity, its integrity and the inherent right to human dignity.”

Difficult will have a second launch on Monday, September 21 — the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law — at The Loft, Arété, Ateneo de Manila University, from 4 to 6 pm. – Rappler.com

World.title: After SALEX tree-cutting, critics see worse traffic, health, heritage loss
World.content:
PHILIPPINE EXPRESSWAY MAP. The Stop SALEX Movement has released an open map on existing and proposed expressways in the country.

MANILA, Philippines – Groups criticized proposals for new, elevated expressways, showing new research and a map of the expansive existing and proposed projects with a total valuation of at least P2.7 trillion.

“Why are we building and approving more elevated expressways in the Philippines when other progressive cities are tearing them down?” asked Ken Abante of the Move As One Coalition in Filipino during their online press conference, also joined by the Stop SALEX Movement and other advocates, on Wednesday, September 16.

While the minimum valuation of the projects is at P2.7 trillion, the number rises to P3.4 trillion if bridge projects are included. The number is based on declarations made by project proponents, so the final values may still vary upon confirmation of “appropriate government institutions and third parties.”

The groups also discovered that P1.6 trillion of the P2.7 trillion covers unsolicited projects and involves “little to no” competitive bidding processes. Unsolicited projects are project proposals “made by a private proponent.”

These groups likewise called attention to the proposed Southern Access Link Expressway (SALEX) project and its potential risks to affected communities and the environment, calling for an end to its construction.

They warned that the 40.62-kilometer expressway not only worsens traffic and affects its nearby surroundings, but also endangers and damages historical heritage sites, as it passes through major cultural and national structures.

The project forms part of a broader network of expressways planned to provide access to several major roads and transport routes. It includes access to the proposed New Manila International Airport in Bulacan.

Prior to the conference, the group, along with experts in architecture and urban mobility, also convened at the Stop SALEX Movement forum at the Ramon Magsaysay Center on September 12, raising similar concerns about traffic, health and the environment, and heritage.

STOP SALEX FORUM. Experts and concerned citizens gather at the Ramon Magsaysay Center to discuss the potential impacts of the proposed SALEX. Photo by Lance Bustos

Risks to traffic, health, and environment

Sustainable mobility advocates said that adding more expressways fails to solve traffic due to the phenomenon of “induced demand.”

“When you have more and wider roads, you get more driving,” explained sustainable mobility advocate Robert Siy Jr. during the Stop SALEX Movement forum. “People take more trips and before long, you have worse traffic.”

Beyond traffic, Siy also pointed to potential health risks, especially to those living near such expressways. Potential risks include “constant noise and vibrations” due to SALEX construction and operations.

Multiple studies have linked prolonged exposure to noise-induced stress to various health risks, including higher blood pressure, greater risk for diabetes, and neuroinflammation.

ROBERT SIY JR. The sustainable mobility advocate urges the audience to write to local and national officials regarding projects such as SALEX. Photo by Lance Bustos

In addition, paved roads could bring about extreme heat days due to the “urban heat island effect,” according to the group’s research.

The urban heat island effect is a phenomenon where the removal of vegetation and trees, and their replacement with impervious surfaces such as concrete and asphalt results in “significantly hotter” conditions in urban areas.

Such impervious surfaces also contribute to urban flooding, as the loss of vegetation and trees can result in partially submerged or completely impassable roads, leading to reduced accessibility.

In May 2026, 617 trees were marked for removal in Manila to make way for the SALEX project, prompting public backlash and uproar among environmental groups and experts.

Heritage sites affected, at risk

Heritage also became a point of discussion. Their research said that proposed and developing road projects should “account for their cultural costs so that heritage is not sacrificed for car-centric infrastructure.”



A heritage group, Members of Manileños for Heritage, has mapped out 50 cultural and historical sites that could be affected by the SALEX project. This includes Paco Park, Malate Church, the Elpidio Quirino Monument, and the Jose P. Laurel Foundation Building, among many other landmarks.

COVERED. A visualization of Padre Faura St. if SALEX is built.Image by CARe-Centric Ph/Facebook

Architect and heritage advocate Dominic Galicia pointed out that the SALEX project could become obstructions to heritage sites and affect their surroundings by decreasing visibility.

“As we walk on Padre Faura with this giant expressway overheads cast a permanent shadow over what used to be trees, what used to be sun touching the surfaces of these heritage structures… You deprive the people of the natural experience of living and walking in a city,” Galicia said.

He also pointed out that it’s “a matter of livability” as to why these heritage structures should remain visible.

“We understand who we are by the place we occupy… If you wipe out the experience of being in these places, there is nothing to experience and there is less to remember until we will no longer know who we are,” Galicia said.

The movement has also coordinated with members of the academe, particularly with Adamson University.

On June 30, the Adamson University community called for the protection of green spaces and heritage sites, with students and administrators protesting against SALEX as it will pass through the campus on San Marcelino St. in Manila. The university is considered a historical site by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines. – Lance Ariel Bustos/Rappler

Lance Ariel Bustos is a campus journalist from Santa Rosa City, Laguna, studying Political Science and Philippine Media Studies at De La Salle University Manila. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, he is an editor-at-large of The LaSallian.

World.title: Gemini hacked 3 companies in first known breakout by Google’s AI
World.content:
GOOGLE IN EUROPE. A specially designed Google logo, during the opening of Google's new Artificial Intelligence center in Berlin, Germany, March 5, 2026.

The hacks, which occurred in May during a cybersecurity test, were conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations

Google’s Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, the first known example of the company’s AI systems autonomously committing such an act.

The hacks occurred in May during a cybersecurity test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations.

During a standard testing evaluation, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google’s vice president of security engineering, said in a statement.

“We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes,” Adkins said. “These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”

An Irregular spokesperson said the incident involved the same issue that affected other AI labs and that all relevant labs were notified in late July. “All known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago,” the spokesperson said.

Similar incidents linked to Irregular were disclosed by Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI. Meta said in August the incident did not involve a sandbox escape or sophisticated cyberattack, while Irregular said it was working on best practices for securely conducting AI cybersecurity evaluations.

The incidents have raised questions about the safeguards needed as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to the internet and computer systems.

In one of the cases, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to then access protected systems, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the news on Friday.

Adkins said that in all three instances, the model ceased its hacking. – Rappler.com

World.title: Wanderlust wins: Singapore Airlines says travel demand still taking off
World.content:
'We are very positive about the market, and we do see people are still very interested to travel,' Singapore Airlines general manager Liewei Tai tells Rappler

MANILA, Philippines – Even as higher fuel costs put pressure on airfares, Filipinos don’t seem ready to put their travel plans on hold.

Singapore Airlines (SIA) continues to see strong appetite for travel from the Philippines, although passengers are becoming more conscious of how much they are getting for what they spend, according to Liwei Tai, the airline’s general manager for the Philippines.

“I think we see that people are still interested to travel. Perhaps there is a greater awareness now about the value that they get when they travel,” Tai told Rappler on Thursday, September 17.

Tai’s focus on value is unsurprising, as airlines are also grappling with higher fuel costs that can eventually translate into more expensive tickets.

Play Video

SIA Group’s net fuel cost surged more than 78% year-on-year to S$2.25 billion in the April-to-June quarter, following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East. But, it turns out, that hasn’t kept travelers from coming in droves: Singapore Airlines and its low-cost subsidiary Scoot carried a record 10.9 million passengers during the quarter, 6.3% more than a year earlier.

The trend continued into August. The two airlines carried 3.7 million passengers worldwide, up 3.6% year-on-year. And while those figures cover the global network and can’t be attributed specifically to Philippine routes, Singapore Airlines still has a bullish view of the local market.

“For the Philippines, we already added an additional flight out of Manila last year. We are very positive about the market, and we do see people are still very interested to travel,” Tai told Rappler. “We will continue to be here together with Scoot, also our subsidiary airline. We will want to continue to grow in the Philippines over time.”

The airline increased its Manila-Singapore service from four to five flights a day in May 2025, while Scoot launched flights between Singapore and Iloilo in April that year.

Philippine aviation data tell a similar broader story about Filipinos’ willingness to fly. Scheduled international airlines carried 15.27 million passengers to and from the Philippines in the first half of 2026, according to Civil Aeronautics Board data. That was already equivalent to about 52% of the 29.12 million international passengers recorded for the whole of 2025.

For travelers, then, pricier fuel may be changing the calculation more than cancelling the trip altogether.

Tai said SIA is seeing demand across a wide mix of travelers, from solo and business passengers to groups of friends and families, including several generations traveling together.

“We see now different kinds of traveler profiles. Of course, we have families, family with young children, especially in the Philippines, where family is so important, even multi generational travel. But even then, we have friends who are traveling together, even solo travelers, business travelers,” she said.

Beyond fares and flight options, Tai said SIA is also seeing improvements in the travel experience at Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), now under private management by New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC). NAIA may still have a long runway before it can rival Singapore’s Changi Airport, but Tai said the changes are already becoming noticeable to passengers. (READ: Two years and billions later, has NAIA finally leveled up?)

“We do see the improvements as well,” she said, pointing to shorter queues and quicker baggage retrieval. “I think there is very close coordination between different parties to make that possible.”

SIA is also currently holding its latest Time to Fly Virtual Travel Fair with Mastercard, offering discounts of as much as 37% on flights to destinations including Singapore, Sydney, London, Paris, Los Angeles, Manchester, and Madrid. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Cross-Border QR Payments as India’s UPI Offers Blueprint
World.content:
MUMBAI – Kazakhstan is moving toward expanding its domestic QR-payment infrastructure across borders, with India among 11 countries identified for potential cross-border QR-payment cooperation. The initiative comes as cashless payments continue to account for the overwhelming majority of transactions in Kazakhstan.

According to the National Bank of Kazakhstan, 84 million payment cards were in circulation as of Aug. 1, with debit cards accounting for 81.6% and credit cards for 15.5%. In July, transactions using cards issued by Kazakh banks reached 19.9 trillion tenge (US$44.4 billion), covering 1.3 billion transactions.

Non-cash transactions accounted for 17.6 trillion tenge (US$39.3 billion) and 1.3 billion transactions, increasing 8.4% in value and 7.5% in number compared with July 2025. Internet and mobile banking comprise 77.6% of the number and 89.6% of the value of non-cash payments and money transfers, while POS terminals accounted for 21.9% and 10%, respectively.

The figures provide a growing domestic base for Kazakhstan’s efforts to make QR payments interoperable across borders.

Kazakhstan launched its national Interbank Mobile-Payment System on July 19, allowing customers of participating banks to make real-time interbank transfers and payments using phone numbers and a single QR code. The system enables merchants to accept payments from customers of various participating banks without installing new equipment.

The next step is to make such payments work across borders.

India’s UPI model

India offers one example of how a nationally interoperable payment infrastructure can evolve into a cross-border service.

Speaking to foreign journalists in Mumbai on Sept. 16, Sonal Asnani, head of Asia Pacific at NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), outlined how India developed the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) from a domestic payment infrastructure into a system with international applications.

UPI, operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), is a payment infrastructure rather than a standalone application or card. It connects banks, fintech companies and customers through a common framework, allowing users to make payments through different applications while maintaining interoperability.

“It’s not an application, it’s not a card. It’s a payment layer,” Asnani said, explaining the basic architecture of UPI.

According to Asnani, one of the key factors behind UPI’s expansion has been the division of roles across the ecosystem. The Reserve Bank of India acts as the regulator, NPCI operates the national payment infrastructure and establishes standards, banks hold customers’ accounts and funds, while fintech companies develop customer-facing services.

This model has allowed users to make payments through various applications while relying on the same underlying infrastructure.

From domestic payments to international use

NPCI created NIPL in 2020 to take Indian payment technologies and expertise to international markets.

One of its main areas of activity is cross-border merchant payments. Under UPI Global Acceptance, Indian users can make QR-based payments at participating international merchants directly from UPI-enabled applications.

Asnani noted that users can scan a participating local QR code and review the transaction amount, exchange rate, and applicable fees before completing the payment.

She said NPCI International currently works with 11 countries on international merchant-payment acceptance.

The model allows an Indian traveler to use a familiar UPI-enabled application abroad rather than relying exclusively on cash or international payment cards.

“For example, when I travel to other countries, I can scan the local QR with my UPI app and still make a payment,” Asnani said.

For Kazakhstan, which is developing cross-border QR arrangements with India and other countries, interoperability could provide a similar mechanism for travelers and merchants.

The practical question, however, is how two national payment systems can be connected while preserving their respective regulatory and technical frameworks.

Asnani highlighted that such partnerships require due diligence and compliance procedures, while the presence of an established QR-payment ecosystem in the partner country can make integration more straightforward.

“Wherever there is a high level of QR adoption, and there is a QR system, it becomes natural for us to collaborate,” she said, describing the factors considered when establishing international partnerships.

Beyond QR payments

NPCI International’s activities extend beyond merchant payments. The organization also works on cross-border person-to-person remittances and provides technology to countries seeking to develop their own domestic payment infrastructure.

Asnani said some countries have adopted elements of India’s technology to develop sovereign instant-payment or card systems rather than building such infrastructure entirely from scratch.

That approach differs from simply connecting two existing payment systems. It involves sharing technological infrastructure and experience with countries that are developing or upgrading their own national payment systems.

Kazakhstan has a well-developed digital payments ecosystem. The next step is to connect its existing infrastructure with international payment networks while ensuring seamless interoperability and maintaining regulatory oversight.

The potential use cases extend beyond tourism. Cross-border QR payments could facilitate transactions for travelers, small businesses and merchants. At the same time, interoperability between payment systems could also support broader economic and financial links between Kazakhstan and its partner countries.

The country’s growing domestic use of digital payments provides a substantial base for such expansion. In January-July, QR-code payments within Kazakhstan accounted for 2.34 billion transactions worth 11.8 trillion tenge (US$26.3 billion), according to National Bank data.

As Kazakhstan moves from domestic QR interoperability toward international connectivity, India’s experience offers one possible path. This involves building common infrastructure, allowing banks and fintech companies to compete at the customer level, and using interoperable standards to make the payment experience seamless for users.

World.title: News Digest: Rybakina’s US Open Triumph, Kazakhstan-South Korea Ties and Oil Export Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights Elena Rybakina’s U.S. Open victory, strengthened Kazakhstan-South Korea cooperation, Astana Arena’s selection to host the 2028 UEFA Super Cup, and Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its oil export routes.

S. Korea, Kazakhstan sign MOU on preservation of historic sites linked to Korea’s independence movement

South Korea and Kazakhstan have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to help better preserve historical sites in the Central Asian country that are linked to Korea’s independence movement against Japan’s 1910-45 colonial rule, Seoul’s veterans ministry said Wednesday, Yonhap reported on Sept. 16.

“Under the MOU, the two countries agreed to systematically preserve the historical records and cultural value of historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement while also strengthening academic exchanges. There are 25 historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement in the central Asian country, according to the ministry,” reads the article.

Seoul Cyber University chairman receives Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk

Lee Sang-kyun, chairman of Seoul Cyber University (SCU), received Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk, recognizing his contributions to expanding online education and promoting friendly cooperation between Korea and Kazakhstan, reported The Korea Times on Sept. 16.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who visited Korea this week for the first Korea-Central Asia Summit, personally presented the order to Lee on Monday. The Order of Dostyk is one of Kazakhstan’s highest state honors, awarded to figures at home and abroad for contributions to peace, friendship, international cooperation and social harmony.

U.S. Open final: Elena Rybakina smothers Aryna Sabalenka to dethrone reigning champion

For the second time this year, Elena Rybakina is a Grand Slam champion after defeating Aryna Sabalenka. The 27-year-old from Kazakhstan toppled Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday in the U.S. Open final, denying Sabalenka’s bid to win the tournament for a third straight year, The New York Times reported on Sept. 13.

“It is Rybakina’s first U.S. Open title, and her third Grand Slam title overall. It means she leaves the tournament as both the champion and the new world No. 1: Rybakina will replace Sabalenka at the top of women’s tennis on Monday,” reads the article.

Astana Arena in the capital of Kazakhstan selected to host 2028 UEFA Super Cup

The prestigious match, UEFA Super Cup, will take place at the Johan Cruyff Arena in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2027, before passing the baton to Astana Arena in Astana, Kazakhstan, in 2028. Kazakhstan has obtained the chance to host such a major match, marking a historic first for the country, Euronews reported on Sept. 15.

The decision was made and officially announced by the UEFA Executive Committee. Since 2013, the Super Cup venue has changed every year, moving to a new location each time. Kazakhstan has obtained the chance to host such a major match, marking a historic first for the country. For the uninitiated, the UEFA Super Cup is a single-match curtain-raiser where the Champions League and Europa League winners meet.

Kazakhstan is upgrading its oil export strategy: Here’s how

Astana is looking for more ways to move its oil. Russia, its principal export outlet, is rife with disruptions. Damage to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s (CPC) Black Sea terminal in November 2025 suppressed exports into early 2026, while the recent July attacks on tankers threatened roughly 1.5 million barrels per day, writes Joseph Shumunov for EU Reporter on Sept. 15.

The vulnerability would not be so enormous if 80% of Kazakh oil exports did not move through the CPC terminal near Novorossiysk. But is Kazakhstan merely searching for emergency alternatives amid instability? Or is this a transformation it has been preparing for? The answer is consequential: Kazakhstan is attempting a wholesale upgrade of its oil-export strategy, one befitting a rising regional power. It is moving from rational efficiency toward strategic resilience, from accepting routes toward shaping them, and from concentrated dependence toward managed interdependence.

World.title: Italy, Central Asia Launch B5+Italy Platform to Expand Regional Business Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – Government and business representatives from Central Asia and Italy convened on Sept. 16 in Astana for the launch of the B5+Italy platform aimed at turning growing political engagement into investment, industrial cooperation and stronger trade links across the region.

The forum in Astana brought together government officials and businesses from Italy, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, with discussions focused on connectivity, sustainable growth and new opportunities for companies operating across Central Asia.

The meeting follows the first Central Asia-Italy summit at the leaders’ level, held in Astana in May 2025, when Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the presidents of the five Central Asian states agreed to deepen cooperation across trade, investment, transport, energy and other sectors.

The platform, proposed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, is designed to complement the political dialogue in C5+1 format by giving businesses a more direct role in shaping economic cooperation.

Italian Undersecretary of State for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Maria Tripodi said the new business format was intended to give that political dialogue an economic dimension.

“We consider that today’s meeting is important because it is the beginning of a new era. (…) We want to transform the political dialogue into investments, partnerships and new opportunities for our countries,” Tripodi told the forum participants.

“It is the companies, in fact, that are subject to transform the political relationship into a more solid one, investing time and effort,” she said.

A dynamic market

Addressing the gathering, Kazakh Minister of Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev said the forum gives an opportunity to Italian companies to approach Central Asia increasingly as a regional market rather than five isolated economies.

“Today, Central Asia is a market with a rapidly growing economy,” said the minister. “For Italian businesses, today’s forum represents an opportunity to work with the entire region and to expand production and market presence across several countries simultaneously.”

He said Central Asia should increasingly be viewed as an interconnected economic space where companies can establish production in one country while reaching consumers and supply chains across several neighboring markets.

For Kazakhstan, the regional format also offers an opportunity to use existing business infrastructure with Italy more broadly. Shakkaliyev highlighted the Kazakh-Italian Trade House that opened in Almaty earlier this year, saying it could serve not only bilateral commerce but wider links between Italian companies and Central Asia.

Growing interest from businesses

The push toward a regional format is also coming from companies and business associations that have traditionally worked through bilateral Kazakhstan-Italy ties. Marco Beretta, president of the Italian-Kazakh Trade Association, said the leaders’ summit in May 2025 convinced businesses that cooperation could be expanded beyond the two countries.

“In the last three years, we have been working very hard in order to promote collaboration between Italy and Kazakhstan,” Beretta told The Astana Times. “But after the visit of our prime minister last year in May, we understood that a much wider scope of work can be executed.”

He described Central Asia as an increasingly important economic link for Europe and said the expansion toward a five-country regional format represented a significant shift. Beretta said the association now wants to expand its Kazakh-Italian business forum into a broader Central Asian platform while keeping Kazakhstan as its base.

Diversifying trade structure

The forum comes at a time as Italy expands its economic engagement with Central Asia, with Kazakhstan accounting for a large share of that relationship. Italy was Kazakhstan’s third-largest trading partner last year, with bilateral trade reaching almost $17 billion in 2025, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration. Trade reached $9.79 billion in January-July this year, including $9 billion in Kazakh exports to Italy and $789.6 million in imports.

But Shakkaliyev said maintaining high trade volumes alone was not enough. He pointed to the big role of commodities in the current structure of bilateral commerce.

Kazakhstan is seeking to expand exports of higher-value goods and estimates that it has an additional $307.5 million in export potential on the Italian market, particularly in metallurgy, petrochemicals, food products, chemicals and machinery.

Shakkaliyev said Kazakhstan was interested in changing the structure of trade by increasing exports of processed and higher-value products. He pointed to opportunities in agriculture, chemicals, manufacturing and industrial cooperation, while Tripodi emphasized Italian expertise in engineering, machinery and advanced industrial technologies.

This ambition reflects a broader challenge for Central Asian economies of moving from exports of raw materials toward local processing, manufacturing and bigger participation in international value chains.

Connectivity as central theme

Transport and logistics featured prominently in the forum as Central Asian states seek to strengthen links between Asian and European markets. Kazakhstan, which has invested around $35 billion in this area in the past 15 years, has promoted its position along transcontinental trade routes, particularly the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea. The Middle Corridor, formally known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, links China and Central Asia with Europe through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

Shakkaliyev said the region’s transport infrastructure could provide Italian producers and investors with access not only to Central Asian markets but also to wider international supply chains.

Tripodi said Italy was ready to share technology and experience to support Kazakhstan’s economic diversification, pointing to logistics as one area for cooperation.

“Our connectivity depends on growth and on being connected in a safe, self-sufficient way in large international markets,” she said. “We want Italy to be at the same time the driver of this new road to Europe and also the protagonist of its realization. Our companies are ready to contribute.”

Diversifying economic ties

Beretta pointed to logistics, agriculture, technology and petrochemicals as areas where Italian companies could work across the region. He also tied diversification to the development of higher-value production in Kazakhstan rather than continued reliance on raw-material exports.

“We need to create added value,” Beretta said.

Beretta also said one project under discussion is the development of a logistics hub in Kazakhstan accompanied by local production, including sustainable aviation fuel. He said such projects could also be part of a wider push into decarbonization, renewable power generation, sustainable development and water treatment.

“Decarbonization, power generation in a green way, sustainable development and water treatment are very important for Central Asia,” he said, stressing that Italian companies could bring technologies and industrial experience in those areas.

According to Tripodi, Italian companies have built extensive presence in oil and gas, but they are also looking to expand into renewable energy, critical minerals and areas linked to energy transition.

Shakkaliyev also noted Italy’s experience with small and medium-sized industrial companies could be particularly relevant for Central Asia, where governments are seeking investment that creates production capacity and jobs.

In her remarks, Tripodi noted the region offered a large and relatively young market of around 80 million people, combined with energy resources, critical materials and a strategic position between Europe and Asia. The country sees potential for its companies in sectors where Central Asian governments are trying to move further up value chains, she said.

Tripodi said Italian companies could contribute through design, engineering and industrial technologies as Central Asian economies seek greater diversification.

World.title: Apple TV Officially Launches in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA — Apple TV has officially launched in Kazakhstan, giving users direct access to Apple Original films and series for the first time.

The streaming service is included in all iCloud+ plans alongside Apple Arcade, with no separate Apple TV subscription required.

The basic iCloud+ plan costs 499 tenge (US$1) per month and includes 50 gigabytes (GB) of cloud storage.

The service is available on Apple devices, compatible smart TVs, gaming consoles and other platforms.

World.title: Expert: Astana’s Financial Center Rating Rises 18 Points on Structural Progress
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana’s eight-place rise in the Global Financial Centers Index 40 (GFCI 40) should ultimately be measured by whether growing international confidence translates into more investment, deeper capital markets and greater cross-border financial activity, Bakhtiyar Tleubekov, chairman of the Management Board of Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC Authority), told The Astana Times on Sept. 18.

In the 40th edition of the Global Financial Centers Index, Kazakhstan’s capital ranked 57th among 117 financial centers worldwide, climbing eight places from 65th. Astana’s rating increased by 18 points, from 684 to 702.

Astana retains regional leadership

The city retained its leading position in Eastern Europe and Central Asia, which it has held for more than three years. Astana was followed by Cyprus, which ranked 72nd globally, and Warsaw, which placed 78th.

Astana’s rise came against a 1.09% decline in the average rating of financial centers in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. It was also named among the ten financial centers survey participants expected to play a more significant role in the global financial system over the next two to three years, ranking ninth with 45 mentions.

In the separate FinTech ranking, Astana rose four places from 55th to 51st.

“Astana’s eight-place rise and continued regional leadership send an important signal of growing confidence in the AIFC and Kazakhstan among the international financial community. For us, a position in the ranking is not an end in itself, but an independent assessment of the work we are consistently pursuing: improving the legal and regulatory environment, developing capital markets and financial technologies, and expanding international ties,” said AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov.

From ranking to capital flows

“The real measure of success is whether growing international confidence translates into more investment, deeper capital markets, more international financial institutions operating in Kazakhstan, and greater cross-border financial activity,” Tleubekov said.

According to him, over the next two to three years, the priority is to reinforce the conditions that international investors value most: political and macroeconomic stability, a predictable and transparent regulatory environment, consistent application of the law, and effective protection of investor rights.

Astana and Kazakhstan also need to continue strengthening their role as a regional gateway connecting international capital with opportunities across Central Asia and the wider Eurasian region.

“Kazakhstan’s geographic position and growing role in trans-Caspian transport and logistics create an opportunity to complement physical connectivity with financial connectivity,” he said.

Structural progress and international confidence

Tleubekov noted that the GFCI combines assessments from financial-sector professionals with quantitative indicators from more than 80 external sources covering the business environment, human capital, infrastructure, financial-sector development and reputation.

“Therefore, an 18-point increase cannot be attributed solely to improved perception, nor can it be explained by any single indicator,” he said.

He attributed Astana’s performance to both external conditions and structural progress, including Kazakhstan’s relative political and economic stability, regulatory continuity and openness to international investment.

The AIFC has been consistently developing a legal and regulatory framework based on international standards, independent dispute-resolution institutions, capital-market infrastructure, fintech and digital-asset regulation, and mechanisms for international and regional investors.

“Ultimately, progress should be measured not only by rankings, but by new investment, international companies choosing the AIFC, and new opportunities for Kazakhstan’s businesses,” Bekturov said.

The GFCI is published twice a year by the Z/Yen Group in partnership with the China Development Institute and assesses financial centers across five areas: business environment, financial sector development, infrastructure, human capital and reputation.

Continuing the conversation

The Astana Times has been following the AIFC’s development and Kazakhstan’s evolving role in the international financial system through its coverage and interviews with AIFC leadership.

At the recent Astana Finance Days, Bekturov joined discussions on the future of finance and Kazakhstan’s role in the next digital frontier.

The AIFC also recently shared the results of its first 10 years with The Astana Times team, offering a closer look at the centre’s development, growing international presence and priorities for the next decade. Also watch our YouTube interview with AIFC leadership.
