World.title: Kyrgyz President arrives in Utah on high-level U.S. working visit
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov arrived in the U.S. state of Utah on a working visit on September 18.

This was announced in a statement published by the press service of the Kyrgyz President.

According to the information, Japarov was met at Salt Lake City International Airport by Utah Senate President Stuart Adams.

During his stay in Utah, the president will hold meetings with state officials and familiarize himself with the U.S. experience in tourism and sustainable mining development.

Japarov will then travel to New York, where he will participate in events of the high-level week of the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

The Kyrgyz president is also scheduled to hold a number of bilateral meetings with heads of state and senior executives of major US companies.

The visit comes as Kyrgyzstan and the United States mark 35 years of diplomatic relations established in 1992. Bilateral goods trade reached an estimated $187.2 million in 2025, with U.S. exports to Kyrgyzstan at $155.6 million and a U.S. goods trade surplus of $124 million. Tourism and mining remain priority sectors for Kyrgyzstan, which recorded foreign trade turnover of $10 billion in the first seven months of 2026 and continues to seek foreign investment and technology transfer in sustainable resource development. Earlier this month, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor met with Japarov in Bishkek on the sidelines of the World Nomad Games.

World.title: UNEP highlights successful methane mitigation in Turkmenistan (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. UNEP says eight methane sources in Turkmenistan have been successfully mitigated and remain under monitoring.

The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) told Trend this in an exclusive response to questions about the latest progress in addressing methane emissions from Turkmenistan’s oil and gas infrastructure.

"These mitigated methane sources originated from pipelines, wells and flares. Emissions at pipelines were caused by leaks in corroded portions of gas flowlines. Several emissions were associated with unlit flaring at gas wells that resulted in direct venting of the gas. Finally, other emissions resulted from leaks that were caused by well integrity or equipment issues," the organization said.

UNEP estimates that the eight sources had emitted more than 27,000 tonnes of methane before they were addressed.

"UNEP estimates that the eight sources in Turkmenistan had emitted over 27,000 tonnes of methane before they were addressed. The near-term climate impact of these emissions was equivalent to the climate impact of over 500,000 passenger vehicles driven for one year," the organization said.

At the same time, UNEP noted the effectiveness of mitigation measures is assessed through several sources of evidence, including satellite observations conducted after repairs.

"Verification of methane mitigation via the Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) requires multiple lines of evidence. A case can be considered for verification when stakeholders have received an alert of emissions through MARS, taken action on the ground, and provided detailed feedback to UNEP on the nature of emissions and mitigation steps taken," UNEP said.

The organization said its technical experts then compare information provided by stakeholders with satellite observations.

"UNEP technical experts then review the reported circumstances and timeline against available satellite data to assess whether the reported mitigation is consistent with operational information and observations from space," it said.

UNEP added that the monitoring continues after mitigation measures are implemented, with the organization confirming the result only when follow-up observations show that emissions are no longer detected at the relevant location.

"Furthermore, UNEP continues to monitor the source using high-resolution satellite observations. Mitigation is confirmed only when follow-up observations show that emissions are no longer detected at the location in question," the organization said.

A mitigated source also remains under observation to identify any possible recurrence and enable further action.

"A mitigated emission source remains under monitoring so that, if emissions recur, UNEP can identify the re-emission and quickly follow up with stakeholders for further action," UNEP said.

The organization outlined that its International Methane Emissions Observatory (IMEO) has been working directly with stakeholders in Turkmenistan since 2023.

"This engagement has built strong lines of communication to share MARS alerts directly with individuals in the government and companies who are positioned to take mitigation action," UNEP said.

According to the organization, cooperation with international partners has also contributed to capacity building in methane emissions management.

"Beyond this, IMEO has worked with and alongside partners – including GIZ, World Bank, and the Asian Development Bank – to build capacity on methane emissions management that supports action on MARS alerts," it said.

UNEP also outlined a potential next stage of cooperation with Turkmenistan, noting that it has proposed a joint program focused on comprehensive methane emissions reduction.

"UNEP, in collaboration with UNOPS and UNECE, has proposed a UN Joint Programme for Methane Emissions Reduction in Turkmenistan, which would provide the framework for a comprehensive emissions reduction program between the Government and international partners," the organization said.

According to UNEP, the proposed program is being reviewed by the government of Turkmenistan.

"The Programme is currently awaiting approval from the Government. If formally approved, it would mark the first UN Joint Programme on methane emissions reduction and an important commitment by a government to advance the global methane agenda," UNEP said.

Beyond the MARS alerts and mitigation of individual sources, UNEP also pointed to longer-term efforts focused on methane measurement, reporting and verification.

"In addition to MARS, UNEP’s IMEO manages the Oil and Gas Methane Partnership 2.0 (OGMP 2.0). OGMP 2.0 is the leading global standard for measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV), with more than 160 member companies representing nearly 45% of global oil and gas production," the organization said.

According to UNEP, OGMP 2.0 provides companies with a framework for comprehensive methane measurement and reporting.

"OGMP 2.0 outlines a framework for companies to comprehensively measure and report on their methane emissions in a credible, verifiable manner. IMEO actively engages with all companies where possible, including in Turkmenistan, to join OGMP 2.0 and support efforts towards achieving "Gold Standard" reporting," UNEP said.

Meanwhile, the methane mitigation efforts come amid a broader environmental agenda in Turkmenistan, where environmental protection, rational use of natural resources and climate-related cooperation have remained among the areas of focus in recent state and international activities.

In June 2026, Ashgabat hosted an international scientific and practical conference dedicated to World Environment Day, bringing together representatives of government bodies, the UN and other international and regional organizations. The event highlighted Turkmenistan’s National Strategy on Climate Change, its contribution to the implementation of the Paris Agreement and its accession to the Global Methane Pledge.

Environmental cooperation has also remained a focus of Turkmenistan’s international engagement. In August, the country hosted a scientific and practical conference on protecting the Caspian Sea ecosystem and sustainable development, with participants discussing environmental monitoring, rational use of natural resources, including gas reserves in the Caspian, climate change and the development of international cooperation. The event also highlighted Turkmenistan’s initiatives on climate change technologies and its accession to the Global Methane Pledge.

More recently, in early September, Turkmenistan and the UN Development Programme held a national seminar in Ashgabat on updating the country’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plans for 2026-2035. The discussions covered biodiversity conservation and sustainable development, as well as the country’s reporting under the Convention on Biological Diversity. In addition, it included the rational use of natural resources.

For reference, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) is the United Nations’ leading global environmental authority, working with governments and other partners on environmental protection, climate action and sustainable development. In the area of methane emissions, UNEP’s work includes the International Methane Emissions Observatory (IMEO), which provides data and analysis to support governments and companies in identifying and reducing methane emissions.

A key part of this work is the Methane Alert and Response System (MARS), a satellite-based system launched by UNEP at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP27) in 2022. MARS uses satellite data to identify and analyze major methane emission sources and notifies governments and companies so they can take mitigation measures. The system also tracks the progress of those measures and supports verification of mitigation through further observations.

MARS is therefore designed not only to detect methane emissions, but also to connect satellite-based information with practical action on the ground. Its process includes detecting and attributing major emission sources, notifying relevant stakeholders, supporting mitigation action and tracking the results.

World.title: EDB highlights 18.4% growth in Tajikistan’s investment
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. Investment in fixed capital in Tajikistan increased by 18.4% year-on-year from January through June 2026, with private-sector capital expenditure rising 1.5 times.

This was announced in a report published by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB)

According to the EDB’s latest macroeconomic review, investment activity remains an important driver of Tajikistan’s economic growth. The overall increase in fixed capital investment was recorded across all sources of financing during the first half of 2026.

The bank noted that private-sector capital expenditure became the main driver of the investment process, increasing 1.5 times year-on-year. Most of these investments were directed toward housing construction.

State investment also increased during the reporting period, rising by 7.9% year-on-year from January through June 2026, according to the EDB.

At the same time, foreign investment declined by 31.4% year-on-year during the first six months of the year.

The EDB said Tajikistan’s economy continues to maintain high growth rates, supported by resilient domestic and external demand and the development of the production sector.

The bank previously reported that Tajikistan’s GDP increased by 8.2% year-on-year in the first half of 2026. The EDB expects the country’s economic growth to reach 8.3% for the full year.

Trend’s analysis indicates that continued investment activity, particularly from the private sector, could support Tajikistan’s economic expansion over the medium term, while the gradual development of the domestic investment base could help sustain capital formation.

Based on the EDB’s 8.3% GDP growth estimate for 2026, Trend’s indicative calculation assumes economic growth of around 7.8% in 2027, 7.4% in 2028, 7% in 2029 and 6.7% in 2030.

Using 2025 as an index of 100, the calculation puts the indicative real GDP level at approximately 108.3 in 2026, 116.7 in 2027, 125.4 in 2028, 134.2 in 2029 and 143.2 in 2030. This would mean an increase of approximately 43% in the real size of Tajikistan’s economy between 2025 and 2030.

If investment activity remains supportive, capital formation could continue contributing to economic growth alongside domestic consumption, production and exports. Private-sector investment is likely to remain particularly important as the economy expands and demand for housing and related infrastructure increases.

At the same time, the decline in foreign investment highlights the importance of maintaining favorable conditions for external capital inflows, which could complement domestic investment and support larger-scale projects.

These figures are Trend’s indicative calculations based on the economic dynamics reported by the EDB and its 2026 GDP growth estimate and do not represent an official forecast by the EDB or the Government of Tajikistan.

World.title: Moody’s upgrades Kazatomprom's Baseline Credit Assessment
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 19. Moody’s Ratings has affirmed Kazatomprom JSC’s (KAP) long-term issuer rating at Baa1 and upgraded its Baseline Credit Assessment (BCA) to baa2 from baa3.

This was announced in a report published by the Moody’s Ratings.

According to the agency report, the outlook remains stable.

Moody’s said the upgrade reflects Kazatomprom’s sustained strong operating and financial performance, high profitability, robust liquidity and conservative financial policies.

"The upgrade of KAP's BCA reflects the continuing track record of the company's strong operating and financial performance, high profitability, robust liquidity and adherence to conservative financial policies," Moody’s said.

The agency also highlighted KAP’s strong credit metrics, liquidity and net cash position, which have been maintained throughout the uranium price cycle.

According to Moody’s, the assessment is supported by Kazatomprom’s low-cost position based on in-situ leaching recovery (ISR) technology, its leading share of around 20% of global uranium production and one of the largest uranium reserve bases globally.

Moody’s also cited the company’s long-term contracts with customers and geographical diversification of sales.

At the same time, the agency pointed to KAP’s limited business diversification, with more than 90% of revenue derived from uranium and uranium products, geographical concentration of assets in Kazakhstan, exposure to uranium price volatility and risks inherent to the uranium extraction process.

The assessment also takes into account high capital spending and sizeable dividend payouts under the company’s dividend policy.

"KAP's stable outlook is in line with outlooks of the Government of Kazakhstan and Samruk-Kazyna," Moody’s said.

According to Trend analysis, the assessment is in line with a broader trend of international rating agencies maintaining or improving their assessments of major Kazakh companies in recent months. S&P Global Ratings has upgraded the ratings of KazMunayGas (KMG), Tengizchevroil (TCO), QazaqGaz and several financial institutions following its revision of Kazakhstan’s sovereign rating.

Fitch Ratings recently affirmed Kazatomprom’s Long-Term Issuer Default Rating at BBB with a Stable Outlook.

The trend also extends to Kazakhstan’s sovereign credit profile. The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) said successful implementation of planned reforms could improve the country’s sovereign credit profile and increase its chances of reaching the A rating category.

"Successful implementation of the planned reforms increases Kazakhstan’s chances of obtaining a sovereign rating in the ‘A’ category. S&P’s upgrade to ‘BBB’ was another step in this direction. Kazakhstan’s current sovereign ratings are ‘Baa1’ from Moody’s and ‘BBB’ from Fitch and S&P," the bank said.

World.title: Minister issues 'extraordinary' catch-and-kill order for shark after fatal attack
World.content:
Western Australia's fisheries minister has taken the unusual step of issuing a catch-and-kill order for a great white that fatally attacked a swimmer at a beach in Perth's northern suburbs on Friday.

Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis, however, has ruled out a widespread shark cull.

The search continued this morning for the great white, which killed the 63-year-old man close to the Sorrento Beach shoreline yesterday morning in front of shocked onlookers.

Beaches across Perth's northern suburbs remain closed today as emergency services continue their search for the man's body.

The victim's grief-stricken family visited the beach earlier today, as locals paid their respects with a floral tribute at the site.

A floral tribute was laid at Sorrento Beach on Saturday morning. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Ms Jarvis said she took the "extraordinary step" of giving authorisation for the shark to be captured and killed after it was positively identified as the animal involved in the attack.

"In making that decision, I considered the exceptional circumstances of the attack, the hazard posed by the shark, and the potential recovery of coronial evidence," she said.

Loading...

She said capture gear, which is essentially a type of drum line that is normally used to tag sharks, was deployed yesterday in an effort to catch the untagged great white.

The gear could not be set up today, however, due to unfavourable weather conditions and choppy waters.

Shark cull 'not appropriate'

Ms Jarvis believed it was the first time in 10 years that a catch-and-kill order had been issued in WA, but said a widespread cull of white sharks was "not appropriate in these circumstances".

"White sharks are protected internationally," Ms Jarvis said.

"This is not the return to the idea that we would cull all apex predators in the ocean.

"I don't want to give people a false sense of security. I cannot mitigate all risks."

WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis has addressed the media following yesterday's shark attack. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

The man's death was the third fatal shark attack in Western Australia this year and has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe.

More drones, tagging on the table

Western Australia's shark mitigation strategies have been focused on tagging and tracking, an app for notifications, warning sirens, shark enclosures and personal deterrents.

Third person killed by sharks in WA this year The often-heated debate over how to protect beachgoers from sharks is likely to get hotter after the death of a third person this year.

Ms Jarvis said the government would review this strategy to see what more could be done to protect beach goers.

"This is incredibly distressing and I will certainly be talking to my colleagues across emergency services and police to better understand what more we can do for shark mitigation," she said.

Ms Jarvis said she had spoken with the police minister, and deploying more drones to spot sharks along WA's vast coastline was "absolutely under consideration".

The state government already funds the use of drones for Surf Life Saving WA clubs who want to use them for events, including those involving children.

She said the government would also review its tagging program to see if it could be increased.

More than 300 sharks have been tagged in Western Australia, including 227 white sharks.

When asked about the shark enclosure that was removed from Sorrento Beach in 2020, Ms Jarvis said she would be happy to revisit the issue with the City of Joondalup.

"There are funds available for local governments who wish to put up beach enclosures and so I'm happy to talk to any local government that wishes to go down that path," she said.

Beaches remain closed

All beaches in the City of Joondalup, from Marmion to Iluka, will remain shut while authorities assess the situation.

It has been a decade since there have been this many shark attack deaths in the Perth metro area.

Friday's fatality comes days after 56-year-old firefighter Mel Ismail was injured in a shark attack at a Geraldton beach, about 400 kilometres north.

Earlier this year Steven Mattaboni died after a shark attack off Rottnest Island and spearfisher Daniel Turpin was killed near Albany a few weeks later.

The last time three people died in shark attacks in WA in a single year was 2020, when two people were killed off Esperance, and another person was fatally attacked off Cable Beach in Broome.

World.title: Alex de Minaur dines out on home cooking as tricky year winds down
World.content:
Some home cooking has proved just what the doctor ordered for Alex de Minaur as a rough year approaches its end.

De Minaur got Australia off to a perfect start in its Davis Cup tie against Poland, with a 6-3, 6-0 win over Maks Kasnikowski, looking refreshed from a surprisingly lengthy rest period after the US Open.

De Minaur's 231st-ranked opponent was right in the fight in a 35-minute opening set, but the temperature was dialled up as he flew to a second-set bagel in just 20 minutes.

On multiple occasions throughout the dominant performance, de Minaur took time out of his celebrations to fire up the packed Pat Rafter Arena crowd.

"We play outside Australia for 10 months of the year, so we don't really get too many chances to play back here in front of a packed crowd," he said.

"It was a great atmosphere and one that I've missed."

While he remains an admirable ninth in the ATP world rankings, 2026 has by almost every measure been one of de Minaur's toughest in recent memory (albeit with a wedding to British player Katie Boulter mixed in) as evidenced by him sitting 13th in the race for the year-end ATP finals.

He only reached the quarters of one major, losing to eventual champion Carlos Alcaraz at the Australian Open, before falling to players ranked lower than him in Paris, London and New York.

His most recent disappointment against 70th-ranked Botic van de Zandschulp at the US Open marked just his second loss in the second round of a grand slam since 2023.

De Minaur fell in the second round at the US Open. (Getty Images: USTA/Manuela Davies)

It came in a major tournament without world number one Jannik Sinner and with seven-time slam winner Carlos Alcaraz returning from a wrist injury.

Not for the first time, de Minaur cut a dejected figure as he lamented an early exit after consistently being a presence in the last eight in the past few years.

The 27-year-old also endured three first-up losses at the Masters and the only time he reached the quarters, his loss to Valentin Vacherot actually saw him lose ranking points due to a semifinal charge in 2025.

But the good thing for de Minaur is all that is in the past, and the jam-packed tennis schedule means there is always a chance to turn things around.

Alex de Minaur was tasked with starting the tie on the right foot. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

After the Davis Cup comes the Laver Cup in London, where de Minaur will lead Team World against Europe, with the Australian hoping this period can "springboard me back to where I wanna be".

"I know the tennis is there, it hasn't gone anywhere. I've just gotta step up and keep doing what I'm doing," he said.

"It's a different environment and I think I thrive in these types on environments, team competitions. It's a little bit different to your day to day on tour.

"The pressure is different. I'd say it's probably more in team events because you're not just playing for yourself, you're playing for the boys around you and I think that brings out the best in me."

World.title: Gemini hacked three companies in first known breakout by Google's AI
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Google's Gemini AI model has accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, in the first known example of the company's artificial intelligence systems autonomously committing such an act.

The hacks occurred in May during a test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations.

During the cybersecurity assessment, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google's vice-president of security engineering, said in a statement.

Ms Adkins said that in all three instances, the model ceased the hacking when it learned it had accessed a real company.

"We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes," Ms Adkins said.

" These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly. "

Irregular notified Google about the hacks in July, the two companies told the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), which first reported on the hacking incident on Friday local time.

Google told the WSJ it didn't consider it necessary to disclose the incidents earlier because its model stopped the hacking upon learning the companies were real and did not cause harm to them.

AI escaped testing environment

The hacks happened while Gemini was participating in a "capture the flag" exercise conducted on infrastructure belonging to Irregular to test the model's cybersecurity capabilities.

AI 'kill switch' As the heads of the biggest AI companies in the world call for a "kill switch" to be mandated, an expert says it's only a "distraction".

It was tasked with retrieving information from software operated by a fictional company inside the testing environment, Google told the WSJ.

The fictional company in the test exercise shared the same name as a real company.

Although the model was not intended to be able to get online, internet access was unintentionally made available, Irregular said.

In one of the cases, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system.

In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to then access protected systems, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Testing company linked to multiple incidents

The testing company Irregular has been involved in a number of incidents in which AI models escaped their testing environments and hacked other companies during evaluations.

Similar incidents linked to Irregular have been disclosed by Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI.

The hack by Google's Gemini is one in a sequence of incidents involving testing company Irregular. (Reuters: Issei Kato)

Irregular told the Wall Street Journal that the incident with Google Gemini was due to the same problem as the earlier breaches during tests with other AI models.

All relevant labs were notified in late July, an Irregular spokesperson said.

"All known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago," the spokesperson said.

Irregular said it was working on best practices for securely conducting AI cybersecurity evaluations.

Loss of control incidents on the rise

The hacking incidents have raised questions about the safeguards needed as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to the internet and computer systems.

The July incidents prompted more than 1,000 tech workers to sign a petition calling on the US government to support a coordinated slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI systems.

Incidents of AI escaping user control are on the rise, prompting calls for a slowdown and regulation. (Four Corners: Mark Hiney)

The initiative, called Pacing the Frontier, includes employees from Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google's parent company Alphabet.

During testing, AI agents will often resort to cheating if they get stuck and realise a task is impossible.

A recent example involved OpenAI's model attacking start-up AI company Hugging Face during an internal evaluation.

How AI agents swarmed another company Tens of thousands of messages from hundreds of rogue OpenAI agents reveal how the self-described "collective" coordinated the attack on AI infrastructure company Hugging Face.

While the test was intended to run without internet or any communication between agents, an autonomous AI agent found a loophole and created a secret message board where the agents shared information.

The agent had identified a potentially useful dataset at AI start-up Hugging Face and shared the information with other agents, hundreds of which proceeded to attack the company.

Once OpenAI staff realised that something was amiss, Hugging Face's infrastructure had already been compromised.

Incidents of AI escaping user control are on the rise, and those incidents are worsening, according to research by the Loss of Control Observatory by UK think tank, Centre for Long-Term Resilience.

The Loss of Control Observatory has detected 1,664 real-world loss of control incidents in 2026, including ones that showed agents circumventing controls and forging approval to escalate privileges.

"If AI models continue to become far more powerful, and continue to evade control, there is the potential for much more serious incidents to come, including ones with catastrophic consequences," said Tommy Shaffer Shane, researcher and senior policy manager at the think tank.

ABC/wires

World.title: Woman charged after police intercept drug importation bound for Mildura
World.content:
A woman has been arrested and charged in Mildura after police intercepted an illegal drug importation en route to the regional Victorian city.

Victoria Police allege the 33-year-old attempted to import about 500ml of 1,4-Butanediol, also known as bute, which Australian Federal Police describe as "a harmful substance that is linked to sexual assaults and overdoses".

The woman's arrest was part of a multi-agency investigation, with Australian Border Force intercepting the drugs at Melbourne Airport in June.

Detectives from the Mildura Divisional Response Unit arrested the woman at a Mildura address on Friday morning.

She was charged with the Commonwealth offence of importing a marketable quantity of a border-controlled substance.

She has been remanded to appear before the Mildura Magistrates Court on December 16.

World.title: Teenage girls arrested after brawl at Melbourne shopping centre
World.content:
Four girls and an 18-year-old woman have been arrested following a brawl at Melbourne's Northland Shopping Centre, the latest in a series of incidents at the popular retail precinct.

Victoria Police confirmed officers were patrolling the food court of the shopping centre in Preston when they saw a group of females brawling on Friday night.

Four girls aged 12, 14, 16, 17 and an 18-year-old woman were taken into custody.

The 14-year-old sustained minor injuries and was taken to hospital while the 12-year-old also suffered minor injuries and was treated by ambulance paramedics. She was released pending further enquiries.

Police officers patrol Northland Shopping Centre's food court shortly after a brawl on Friday night. (ABC News)

The 18-year-old Coburg North woman along with the 16-year-old and 17-year-old were interviewed by police and are expected to be charged on summons.

Victoria Police said Operation Pulse officers seized a knife, which was allegedly produced during the brawl.

A police spokesman said Banyule Crime Investigation Unit detectives would be looking into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Friday's brawl is the latest in a series of violent incidents at Melbourne shopping centres in recent years.

In a high profile May 2025 incident, large crowds of people fled Northland as a brawl between 10 people involving machetes broke out in the food court.

At the time, police believed the attack occurred between two rival gangs, which left one man with serious injuries, and was motivated by "retaliation".

In a separate June 2025 incident, a sports utility vehicle was captured on a smart phone camera driving at speed through Northland Shopping Centre.

Figures from the Crime Statistics Agency (CSA) showed there were 5,901 reported crimes at 13 major Melbourne shopping centres in the 2024-25 financial year, an increase of 20 per cent on the previous year.

Bayside Frankston recorded the highest number of incidents during the surveyed period, with Northland in second position and Westfield Fountain Gate in third spot.

World.title: NSW Liberals pledge to scrap gun buyback amid election countdown
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The New South Wales Liberals have pledged to freeze the state's buyback of guns and scrap ownership limits for farmers if elected next year.

NSW was the first state to sign up to the national gun buyback promised in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack on December 14, 2025.

The state Liberals voted with the government in support of gun caps and a buyback last year, but now the party is vowing to scrap the caps and freeze the buyback.

Changes would be subject to the results of a commission of inquiry and stakeholder feedback.

NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley described the move as a backflip by the state Liberal party.

"We know that after Bondi, [the NSW Liberals] stood up and they voted for strong gun laws. Months later, they're walking away from that decision," she said.

"We know that One Nation wants weaker gun laws. Now the Liberals and Nationals are following them down that road.

"New South Wales cannot afford a Coalition that lets One Nation write its policy on guns. The safety of our community is too important for that."

Yasmin Catley is critical of the Liberals' proposed gun reforms. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

'Entirely offensive'

NSW opposition leader Kellie Sloane rejected the criticism.

"In the aftermath of [the terror attack at] Bondi, we offered bipartisanship support, but it was conditional on feedback from stakeholders and if we saw any unintended consequences, we should get back to the drawing board," she said.

Ms Sloane said she found it "entirely offensive" that people would criticise her for coming up with what she described as a better plan.

"While we spent hundreds of millions of dollars taking guns off of law abiding citizens, we are failing to recognise the real threat in our communities and we just can't afford to do that," she said.

"An elected Liberals-Nationals government would have a commission of inquiry to look at gun reform to make sure we are targeting the terrorists, we're targeting organised crime, we are taking guns out of dangerous hands."

Ms Sloane says the Liberals' proposed firearms reforms are pending stakeholder feedback. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Sydney's south and south-west have borne the brunt of a spate of tit-for-tat violence linked to underworld tensions over the past 18 months, with innocent parties falling victim to bungled operations.

The issue has become hot political fodder six months out from the NSW state election, with Ms Sloane repeatedly accusing the Labor government of losing control of Sydney streets.

The state government this week introduced legislation to parliament aimed at targeting criminal networks and bolstering police powers to disrupt underworld groups.

Under the reforms, young people charged with some offences linked to organised crime would be tried or sentenced as adults in the district or supreme courts, where they face tougher maximum penalties.

Liberals face uphill battle

Ms Sloane was today asked to respond to reports an anonymous MP described the NSW Liberal party as "sleepwalking to defeat".

"I'm not going to comment on an anonymous, unattributed quotes," she said.

Kellie Sloane's colleague faces ICAC This week, ICAC's gaze is likely to feel even closer for state opposition leader Kellie Sloane, as the anti-corruption commission hears from one of her most senior parliamentary colleagues.

"We're going to win this election, I am certain of it, because we are the only ones to turn our economy around that has flatlined under Labor.

"What I'm hearing on the streets are people are looking for policies like we've announced today, they're looking for reasons to vote Liberal and I'm going to give them plenty of reasons to vote Liberal or Nationals."

A high-profile anti-corruption probe into the actions of a right-wing Liberal party faction has cast a pall on the Liberals' election campaign.

In another blow, Liberal frontbencher James Griffin this month announced he would not seek re-election for the seat of Manly, which has been held by the Liberals for almost 20 years.

The NSW Liberals must also deal with growing support for One Nation ahead of the state election. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The embattled Liberals must also contend with growing support for One Nation, with Premier Chris Minns conceding the party was perhaps Labor's biggest threat.

"If the government falls in March of next year, it's likely to be a One Nation-led government," he told parliament earlier this week.

"That's the grim numbers as we're looking at it."

World.title: Fired lawyer Melat Kiros represents change sweeping US Democratic Party
World.content:
Melat Kiros knows she doesn't fit the mould of a typical member of the US Congress.

The Ethiopian-born Democratic Socialist is on track to become the first gen Z woman to enter Congress, hoping to ride a wave of anti-establishment sentiment on the American left.

"Americans right now are reckoning with the fact that things have been broken for quite a while," she told the ABC.

"We've found that the mainstream ideas coming out of both parties have failed."

Kiros, 29, is vying for a safe Democratic seat in Denver, Colorado, after winning a primary election to bump the incumbent of nearly three decades from the Democrats' ticket.

Before her run in politics, she was fired from her job as a corporate lawyer.

In 2023, she wrote an open letter criticising the stance numerous US law firms, including her own, took in support of Israel after the Hamas terrorist attacks.

In her post, she condemned antisemitism, calling it "the longest hatred", but argued it should not be conflated "with the geopolitical question of Israel's legitimacy".

She was asked to take it down and refused.

Her criticism of the Israeli government over the Gaza war now forms a key part of her campaign.

Melat Kiros appears on track to become the first gen Z woman elected to the US Congress. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

Like many Democratic Socialists, she is calling for a total arms embargo on the country: a position that has angered "moderate" elements of the party and contributed to their widening split with "progressives".

"Our tax dollars are actively participating in this," Kiros said of Israel's bombardment of Gaza.

"We have the ability to end the violence right now if only we just end our tax dollars that are being sent there."

She also wants to make dramatic cuts to defence spending and instead put money towards universal healthcare, childcare and expanding public housing.

"This notion that what we're calling for is extreme is detached from reality [when] all these developed nations that are our peers already have a lot of these programs."

Factional fight

Kiros is one of several candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which have had success in recent Democrat primary races ahead of the midterm elections.

The organisation, whose policies include higher taxes on the wealthy and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, is proving popular on the left.

A recent CBS-YouGov poll found 71 per cent of participants who identified as liberal voters held favourable views on socialism.

But the rise of the progressive left has sparked a civil war within the Democratic Party as it fights over its future direction.

The inner city area of Denver, Colorado, is safe Democrat territory. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

Centrist Democrat group Third Way has launched a $US15 million ($21 million) campaign to discredit democratic socialism within the party.

"The fight is important to have," said Third Party co-founder Jim Kessler, a former staffer to Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer.

"It's important to push the Democratic Party back to the centre because we cannot win with a far-left candidate in a general election.

"We are a centre-right nation, and there are more conservatives in America than there are liberals … so the math is such that we just have to win a super-majority of moderates.

"Republicans don't have to."

Trump's 'Mini-Mamdani' crackdown Democratic socialism is on the rise in the US, and it is sparking a sharp campaign from Republicans.

While socialism polls favourably among liberal voters, a New York Times/Siena poll this month found about half of Americans view it unfavourably.

Most DSA-backed candidates who won their primaries are in safe Democratic seats, and Kessler said moderate candidates have seen success in swing seats where they are more appealing to independent or disillusioned Republican voters.

"A lot of the solutions on the far left are slogans; they're not really solutions," he said.

"There needs to be flesh on the bones, and they don't want to put the flesh on the bones because it opens them up to criticism."

Trump's midterms attacks

But Kiros argues the US and the world are in precarious times and cannot afford another "do nothing Democratic administration".

"We have no choice but to fight for bold solutions, or else this democracy will not survive," she said.

"Voters are desperately looking for anybody or any group that's actually offering ideas and solutions that can meet this moment right now.

"I think Democratic Socialists are the only ones that have done that in a meaningful way and that's why we're winning."

Republican President Donald Trump has leapt at the opportunity to attack the rising left faction of the Democrats.

The tactics at 'Trump-a-palooza' Donald Trump's approval rating is at dire lows. But he has deliberately tied his party's fortunes to his own popularity, and "Trump-a-palooza" showed his tactics are not changing.

"They call themselves Democratic socialist, but actually they're communists," he told the Republican midterm convention earlier this month.

He and other Republicans hope to paint them as a danger to the economy and country ahead of the November midterms, where Republicans risk losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

"If they win, the greatest legislative body in history will, for the first time ever, be controlled by a communist caucus," Trump said.

But in progressive Denver, and cities across the US, the movement is spreading.

Craig Skinner joined the local branch after watching Zohran Mamdani win the New York City mayoral election.

He felt inspired to "get off the couch" and "be part of something", so he joined Kiros's campaign and started volunteering.

"Our membership has nearly doubled since the beginning of the Melat campaign," he said.

Craig Skinner was motivated to get involved in politics by Zohran Mamdani's win in the New York mayoral race. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

Skinner argues Trump once made similar promises to the American people about lowering the cost of living and rooting out establishment politics, but failed to deliver.

"When you go to so many doors and hear so many people excited about what Denver DSA stands for and what Melat stands for, it's hard to say that's radical," Skinner said.

"It's policy that changes the way that people can interact with the economy, whether that's publicly financed campaigns or giving everybody healthcare.

"We're already paying so many taxes and [yet] some people aren't being taxed enough: the millionaires, the billionaires and the corporations in this country.

"That is a message that people get behind when you tell them."

World.title: Here's how to safely intervene when a loved one is experiencing DV
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Molly Ticehurst's three closest friends never thought someone their age could be a victim of a domestic violence homicide.

Molly was stabbed to death by ex-partner Daniel Billings in April 2024. Earlier this month Billings was sentenced to 28 years in jail with a non-parole period of 20 years.

"It still feels like we're living in a horror movie. I never had thought that would have been the outcome for her," friend Gaby Shepherd told Australian Story.

Aidan Clarke, who knew Molly from the time they were both babies, said he did not think intimate partner violence was a problem for young people.

"The image is a 45 to 55-year-old male comes home from the pub, the wife asks where they were and they slap them around a bit," Mr Clarke said.

Loading...

In fact, rates of intimate partner violence for 16 to 24-year-olds are higher than for those aged 45 and older, according to the Australian Child Mistreatment Study published in 2021.

The study found that 48 per cent of 16 to 24-year-olds surveyed had experienced psychological, physical or sexual abuse at the hands of a partner, compared to 40 per cent of people aged 45 and older.

"These are things you see on TV, on the news. This doesn't happen in our little community. This doesn't happen to my best friend," Ms Shepherd said.

She said she "holds a lot of guilt" for not stepping in when she realised that Molly was in an abusive relationship.

But recognising a friend is at risk of harm, and safely stepping in to help, can be tricky.

Triple j hack has asked two experts for advice on what to do if you think a loved one is in a domestic violence situation. Here's what they told us.

Listen and take them seriously

Pia Birac, the deputy CEO of Domestic Violence NSW, said the first step was simple: listen uncritically to what they're telling you about what's happening in their relationship.

"Start by believing them, listening without judgement, and reassuring them that the abuse is not their fault," she said.

Karen Bevan from Full Stop Australia said you shouldn't dismiss the severity of the problem if your loved one is young.

"One of the things that's really important is that we take it seriously because young people's relationships are serious, they're important to them at that time," she said.

Ms Bevan said it's important to reassure them that they're not being judged because of what's happening to them.

"[Tell them] nobody thinks the less of you because you're in a relationship that isn't working out and it's OK if you need time," she said.

Come from a place of compassion rather than judgement

Ms Bevan said coming to the conversation with a firm idea of what a person should or shouldn't be doing can backfire.

"Bringing your own view about what's OK and what's not OK can often shut someone down if they're going to seek help," she said.

Instead, Ms Bevan recommended coming to the conversation with a sense of compassion or concern by asking, "how are you feeling? How did this land for you?"

She said checking in or noticing patterns can be a helpful way to start a chat.

For example, "I've noticed that you've stopped coming out with us lately," or "I was disappointed you couldn't make our weekend away".

" As a friend please be careful to notice gently and ask how the person is feeling, to create a safe space for them to share. And if they don't, respect their decision. "

Ms Bevan said it was vital that you constantly check in and make sure you're respecting the needs of your friend or loved one. She reflects on the time she lost a friendship because she failed to do that.

"I stepped in and took a bit of control out of my friend's hands and as a result her trust for me was lost," she said.

Ms Birac agreed that giving the person the autonomy to make decisions for themself is crucial.

"It is important to follow their lead, respect their choices and support them to make decisions that feel safe and achievable for their circumstances. They are the experts in their own lives and safety," she said.

Be ready to offer practical support

Ms Bevan said friends should be ready to support a person if they decide to leave, without pushing for it.

"That's the sort of friend where, in the end, that person may well be prepared to take that step towards trust," she said.

Ms Birac said it's important to remember "you cannot force someone to leave an abusive relationship".

"Offer practical support, such as helping them connect with a specialist service or trusted adult, and seek advice yourself if you're unsure what to do," she said.

You can refer your loved one to a reputable online source of information too.

"Young people are more likely to use digital platforms to find information and connect with support which creates an important opportunity to make clear, accessible information about DV available where young people are already looking for help," Ms Birac said.

Ms Bevan said that people who were unsure of how to help can themselves reach out to support services.

"If you are a little bit worried about someone, maybe a friend, maybe a sister, maybe even your mum, it's okay for you to ring and ask for help too because this is hard stuff," she said.

And it's important to remember if your friend or loved one is in immediate danger to call Triple Zero without hesitation.

World.title: ‘Extraordinary step’: Shark that killed 63-year-old Perth swimmer to be destroyed
World.content:
NationalWASharks ‘Extraordinary step’: Shark that killed 63-year-old Perth swimmer to be destroyed Rebecca Peppiatt September 19, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The shark that killed a 63-year-old swimmer at Sorrento Beach on Friday will be caught and destroyed, in what Fisheries minister Jackie Jarvis said was “an extraordinary step”. The man was swimming “very close to shore” when he was witnessed being pulled under water by a large white shark at approximately 10.30am on Friday. Lifesavers raced to rescue the man but were unsuccessful in locating him. Forensics police and specialist detectives taped off a section of the car park on Friday. Hannah Murphy A witness told this masthead there was blood in the water, while the swimmer who had accompanied the victim had to be consoled by rescuers once he got to shore. On Saturday morning Jarvis said it was “an incredibly sad and distressing incident” before saying the shark was later located by water police and “positively identified as the shark involved in the incident”.



Related Article Updated

Tragedy Police continue search for missing Perth swimmer after horror shark attack “WA police requested that the shark be captured to assist with the recovery of potential coronial evidence,” she said. “Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack, and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if it could be captured.” Jarvis said the circumstances of the attack were “exceptional” and that the rare catch and kill order was carefully considered, weighing up the safety of water police and fisheries officers involved in recovery efforts and the response to the incident. “Capture gear was deployed by fisheries officers yesterday,” she said.



Related Article Sharks Government must step in over escalating shark attacks in WA, experts warn “However, at this stage, the shark has not been captured. A WA Police water police vessel remains on the water today. Police conducted a search of the shoreline this morning, and beaches in the area remain closed.” Jarvis said the shark was not one of around 300 tagged sharks in WA waters before claiming the state has a comprehensive shark mitigation program. “We will never be able to mitigate all of the threats,” she said. “And people make an informed decision when they go into the water because it was so close to the shore, because of the circumstances, and because we were able to identify the shark, is why I have taken somewhat extraordinary step to issue a catch and kill authorisation for this shark.”



She said the government’s shark mitigation plan had been added to in recent years with the inclusion of beach emergency number signs, increased tagging efforts and the SharkSmart app. “Of course, we will regularly review this, and we’ll see what more we can do,” she said. “I cannot remove the risk of of all apex predators in the ocean, but we want to make sure the public have as much information as possible, and we will of course review what we’re doing and seeing if we can do more.”

World.title: Caulfield track review ordered after safety dramas on group 1 race day
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing Caulfield track review ordered after safety dramas on group 1 race day Danny Russell September 19, 2026 — 3:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Track safety dramas have forced Melbourne Racing Club into a review of its Caulfield Racecourse just four weeks out from one of the major races of the spring carnival. Last-minute maintenance was ordered at Caulfield on Saturday after a group of jockeys identified a stretch of dangerous ground along the home straight before the group 1 program had even started. Ground staff move running rails at Caulfield on Saturday to avoid a dangerous stretch of the track. Getty Images Stewards ordered the inside running rail be moved out an extra 4m in the home straight to take the unsafe surface out of play. Caulfield will host the $3 million group 1 guineas on October 10 and the $6 million Caulfield Cup the following Saturday. Almost 30,000 people attended last year’s Caulfield Cup.



Related Article Victorian racing Legal feuds, boardroom battles and a 24-year-old taking on racing’s elite “During a routine track inspection on Saturday morning, an issue was identified with a number of the standard track-repair ‘plugs’ near the inside rail, some of which appeared uneven or loose,” the MRC said in a statement. Pre-race images showed jockeys being able to pick up and move large clumps of turf. Plugs are used to fill divots and small holes in a track’s surface. The MRC came under fire several times from punters during the winter months for the standard of its tracks at Caulfield and Sandown. The surface had raced better in recent weeks. Two barrier attendants were lucky to escape injury in June when starting barriers were accidentally reversed into a lake in the middle of Sandown Racecourse. They were later fished out with a crane.



Racegoers were shocked to hear of the rail being moved on a race day so close to the Caulfield Cup carnival. “It would probably be a good idea for MRC to change their name back to VATC … Very Amateur Turf Club as the legend of racing writers used to refer to it,” prominent owner Nick Williams posted on X. The Caulfield rail is moved before the first race on Saturday because of track safety concerns. Getty Images Jockey Patrick Moloney told Racing.com the track surface was fine after the pre-race alterations, but the changes had made it “really awkward” to navigate for riders. “You go from a normal position to an obscure position in the straight,” he said.



Victorian Jockeys Association CEO Matthew Hyland said a number of jockeys had identified safety concerns before the first race and told stewards of their concerns. He said they were happy with the outcome. View post on X Stewards put out a statement, saying they had identified several areas of concern. “Out of an abundance of caution, stewards directed that the moveable rail be placed out an additional four metres in the straight (350m to the winning post) to ensure the areas identified will not be in use for today’s meeting,” a Racing Victoria statement said. The MRC said the use of plugs was a standard maintenance practice undertaken regularly at racecourses.



“With the safety of horses and riders paramount, the decision was made to move the rail out as a precautionary measure,” the club said. “The Melbourne Racing Club will undertake a review immediately following today’s meeting.”

World.title: Trump’s love of AI is more complicated than it looks
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

President Donald Trump made clear in the past week that he views fears that artificial intelligence could lead to mass extinction as a “HOAX”, and that he sees opponents of data centres as people who “want to end up being backwards and poor”. People who have discussed the subject with Trump say his outbursts are rooted in worries that if the artificial intelligence boom fuelling the American economy slows down, the market could crash and recession could quickly follow. Tesla chief Elon Musk, US President Donald Trump, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. Monique Westermann His anti-regulatory, anti-slowdown outbursts have been encouraged by a slice of Silicon Valley’s most influential voices. Chief among them has been David Sacks, a venture capitalist who interceded to weaken an executive order in May that would have required safety reviews of new AI models. Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia have also spoken to the president. All have advised Trump that the bigger risk is being overtaken by Chinese competitors. But inside the administration, the debate is far more complex, and there are other voices in Trump’s ear, urging caution.



The more cautious tone inside the White House reflects a growing concern that despite the strategic challenge posed by China, a summer of AI surprises has raised the prospect of risks that were often dismissed a year ago as the wild talk of “doomers”. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘I am the Hoax Buster’: Trump takes on America with seven-post rant promoting AI, data centres Now, even the biggest AI boosters in the administration concede that AI-fueled hacks into infrastructure, biological threats, attacks on nuclear command-and-control systems, job losses and global financial instability seem more possible than they did before AI agents went rogue. The issue of AI safety is expected to come to a head this weekend as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent meets in New York with his Chinese counterpart to set the agenda for Trump’s visit in Washington with President Xi Jinping of China, which starts Wednesday. Bessent is trying to negotiate some kind of agreement between Trump and Xi that would suggest the two countries are working together on mutual AI safety concerns. But already, officials say, some of the most expansive ideas being discussed among AI safety experts, including an agreement on safety standards and reviews of forthcoming Chinese and American AI models before their public release, are unlikely to be part of any initial accord. One diplomat involved in the effort said he believed “the best we can hope for” is the creation of some kind of US-China working group that might build on a Biden-era agreement with China to bar the use of artificial intelligence in decisions about the employment of nuclear weapons. But that does not begin to get at the complexity of the problem of unpredictable AI-driven agents, which took the industry and the government by surprise this northern summer.



Related Article Analysis

China relations ‘Whoever wins AI, wins’: How the world’s two most powerful leaders can find common ground Nor does it get to the fundamental issues surrounding imposing safeguards on frontier models. The United States could go its own way and impose mandatory reviews of the safety of new, American-generated models, but Trump and his aides believe that would effectively drive the global market to Chinese largely open-source alternatives. And because those open-source models can be modified by users — who could remove the “guardrails” meant to limit their powers — a safety review may mean little. Trump wants to meet with the AI executives next week, according to company representatives. (A White House official said Thursday that nothing was on the schedule as of now.) If that session happens, it would presumably include some of the AI executives who, in recent days, have been calling for the kind of slowdown in the release of new models that Trump says he opposes. Few expect Dario Amodei, a founder of Anthropic, to be among the invitees: His company’s products have been banned by the Pentagon, and he appeared to anger Trump by proposing last weekend a detailed plan for the industry to pace itself and bring in independent safety inspectors. Trump dismissed him, and denounced an unnamed class of “Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors and Leakers” who were politicising the debate over AI and undercutting American leadership. But another Anthropic founder, Tom Brown, who raises less ire in the White House, talks to officials regularly. In recent days, Trump has also talked with Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of SpaceX, both of whom endorsed Amodei’s plan to slow down, test new models for vulnerabilities and let in outside inspectors, at least in general terms.



Bessent and the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, have been increasingly concerned over the past several months that AI could cause massive disruptions across industries, including hacks into major financial institutions that could destabilise the world economy. Wiles this year began organising an informal group to think about how to deal with the risk created by new, more powerful models. Bessent is chief among the members of that informal group, an administration official said, but other experts are called in depending on the topic. President Trump is saying that Democrats using AI concern as a way to score points is a hoax, just like their claims that climate change would kill everyone in six years. Elizabeth Huston, a White House spokesperson. The White House pointed to Wiles’ social media post on May 6 as the foundational statement of how Trump balances the risks and opportunities of the new technology. “This administration has one goal: ensure the best and safest tech is deployed rapidly to defeat any and all threats,” she wrote at the time. She said that “the White House will continue to lead an America First effort that empowers America’s great innovators, not bureaucracy, to drive safe deployment of powerful technologies while keeping America safe”. Asked about Trump’s accusation that AI risk is overblown, Elizabeth Huston, a White House spokesperson, said, “President Trump is saying that Democrats using AI concern as a way to score points is a hoax, just like their claims that climate change would kill everyone in six years.” She added that Trump had reversed the “failed approach” of the Biden administration, which she said had “stifled innovation, hurt consumers and nearly cost America its competitive edge over China.”



But at a moment when AI has emerged as arguably the most important long-term issue for the country’s economic health and national security, in the Trump White House there is no single person in charge of coordinating AI policy. Marco Rubio, in his role as national security adviser, is rarely discussed as a player on these issues. The White House eliminated the post of deputy national security adviser for cyber and emerging technologies created during the Biden administration. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI And the national cyber director, a position created by Congress, has only indirect authority over artificial intelligence issues. The current director is Sean Cairncross, a former senior official at the Republican National Committee, who was light on cyber and AI experience before taking the post. And there has been a purging of some technical expertise, including at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, part of the Department of Homeland Security. (The acting director of CISA said last week that the agency was hiring about 250 new employees after shedding about 1000 jobs — roughly one-third of its workforce — since Trump returned to the White House.) As a result, AI has become the administration’s latest hot potato, with various officials dipping in and out of influence depending on the topic, or the day of the week. Still, there are other officials, particularly in the much-shrunken National Security Council and the Energy Department, who share Amodei’s fears about charging ahead with new, more powerful models amid growing evidence that they are increasingly unpredictable.

World.title: ‘Skewed perception of market conditions’: First home buyer bids $190k for outer east unit which sold for $492k
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘Skewed perception of market conditions’: First home buyer bids $190k for outer east unit which sold for $492k Caroline Zielinski September 19, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After a bold first bid of $190,000, a first home buyer missed out on a two-bedroom unit in Clayton, in the outer east, which ultimately sold for $492,000. Listed with a range of $480,000 to $520,000, the home at 2/6 Wright Street, featuring separate living and dining areas and generous bedrooms, had a reserve price of $490,000. McGrath Clayton lead agent Elroy Malowney said the ambitious bidder “tried an opening bid of $190,000, likely based on a perception that the market has dropped significantly. They did not bid again after that”. The offer was countered by a second bidder, who offered $460,000, which was again countered by a vendor bid of $490,000, Malowney said. The second bidder, also a first home buyer, purchased the property for a final bid of $492,000.



Related Article Melbourne house prices The one choice that can cost Melbourne home buyers an extra $110,000 Malowney said that buyers seemed to have a “skewed perception of market conditions”. “After recent news reports mentioned a drop in the Melbourne market... many ‘buyers assume they can discount property prices by another 15 to 20 per cent below the quoted range, failing to realise that those price adjustments have already been factored in,” he said. The property was one of 929 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. A young professional woman paid $941,000 for an inner-city Melbourne apartment at auction after first submitting a private offer of $860,000.



The spacious, three-bedroom apartment at 143/283 Spring Street, comes with floor-to-ceiling windows and is only a three-minute walk from Parliament Station. Ray White Southbank listing agent Tommy-Lee Davies said the auction drew four bidders, including investors and upsizers, all after a centrally located unit. The property had a price guide of between $850,000 to $900,000 and a reserve of $880,000. In the end, the contest was between the professional woman, a lawyer, and an overseas investor family, he said.



Related Article Property prices The suburbs where house sellers want up to $1.75m more than buyer budgets “The investor kept placing larger bids of up to $9000 raises, while the owner-occupier kept countering with $1000 increments until the investor gave up,” Davies said. Davies has noticed buyers more confident with lower offers. “Buyers come in assuming they have all the power and expect bargain prices,” he said. Davies said Melbourne’s one-bedroom apartment market was doing well, especially among investors, due to offering strong rental yields. “Otherwise, many campaigns are struggling for buyer numbers. Buyers are cautious, taking their time, and acting as if they are the only buyer in the entire market.”

World.title: An activist depicted a female councillor as Miss Piggy. A judge says it’s political speech
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLocal council An activist depicted a female councillor as Miss Piggy. A judge says it’s political speech Lachlan Abbott September 19, 2026 — 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A self-styled council watchdog has won an appeal against an intervention order granted to an inner-eastern Melbourne mayor after a judge ruled his social media posts, including one depicting her as Miss Piggy, were protected political speech. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston hailed the County Court judgment released late on Friday as a win for democratic scrutiny of elected officials, as it overturned the court order Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr was granted last year. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston (left) and Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr. Simon Schluter, Luis Enrique Ascui Magistrate Michelle Hodgson previously found “the gendered and personal undertones” of Hurlston’s posts and text messages to Sehr in recent years “crossed the line from fair commentary into targeted ridicule” that was intended to cause mental harm. But County Court judge Julie Clayton disagreed and on Friday threw out the personal safety intervention order against Hurlston.



Clayton found the magistrate’s interpretation of political commentary protected under Victorian law was too narrow and Hurlston’s posts were primarily motivated by concern about the City of Stonnington’s governance. Related Article CBD Council activist apologises – twice – after accusing councillor of sexual harassment “The personal integrity of politicians, quite apart from their policy positions, is a legitimate subject for news and current affairs,” Clayton wrote. On Saturday, Hurlston criticised Stonnington chief executive Dale Dickson for claiming the magistrate’s initial ruling was a “landmark court decision” before it was overturned. “The council’s triumphal public statement now stands as a monument to poor judgment,” Hurlston said.



“This case should concern every journalist, activist, ratepayer and community watchdog. If robust criticism of public officials can be repackaged as a personal safety matter, democratic scrutiny itself is placed at risk.” Sehr compiled an almost 500-page dossier of posts from Hurlston’s Stonnington Council Watch Facebook page and other messages that she said had escalated to personal harassment. The judge accepted Sehr (pictured) felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but found her fear wasn’t the same as a fear for her safety. Ruby Alexander Clayton said Hurlston was “an enormous nuisance” to Sehr and some posts were hurtful, including one that accused the mayor of using her mother’s death to avoid questions. She accepted Sehr felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but added: “That sort of fear, however, is not the same as a fear for one’s safety.”



The judge ultimately found Hurlston’s posts were published without legal malice and thus an intervention order could not be made. The previous order restricted Hurlston’s online commentary towards Sehr and barred him from coming within two metres of her. “Mr Hurlston may not abide by a journalistic code of conduct in relation to fair and balanced commentary,” Clayton said. “This does not mean he is not entitled to the protection afforded by [the Personal Safety Intervention Orders Act].” She added: “It is permissible for Mr Hurlston to publish, filled with ill-will, animosity, spite and hostility if the actuating motive for the publication is not improper.” Clayton said the images Hurlston posted of Miss Piggy and a cartoon of a stereotypical housewife could be seen as demeaning or derogatory towards Sehr.



Hurlston said the Miss Piggy image referred to Sehr as a “muppet” – a common derogatory term in politics that was not intended to attack her appearance. Related Article City life Toorak councillor banned over ‘obscene’ remarks after heated menorah debate The judge acknowledged Sehr felt humiliated, but was not persuaded Hurlston was primarily motivated by something other than his political opinion that the mayor was “not up to the job”. The judge also said the housewife cartoon was not substantially different from thousands of other political caricatures. “Women in public life generally, and politics in particular are often unfairly targeted in relation to their appearance,” Clayton wrote.



“While one might bemoan this sorry state of affairs it is not a state of affairs that the act was intended to address.” Sehr told The Age she was awaiting further legal advice after Friday’s decision. In a statement on Saturday, Stonnington chief executive Dale Dickson also said: “I will continue to actively support and protect the safety of council employees and councillors, particularly women, including of course Mayor Sehr.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Vendor rejects higher offer to sell Northern Beaches home for $4 million
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Vendor rejects higher offer to sell Northern Beaches home for $4 million Robyn Willis September 19, 2026 — 1:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A vendor accepted a bid of $4 million when her Balgowlah property passed in on Saturday, $20,000 less than she was offered by another party. Two parties expressed interest in four-bedroom 28 New Street West earlier in the week, sales agent for Cunninghams Real Estate, Georgi Bate said. But one group, a family from interstate, advised her on Friday that while they would attend, they would not be registering. The other party, a couple with adult children, were the sole registered bidders and said they would rather negotiate privately after the property passed in. On that advice, auctioneer Emma Brown-Garrett passed it in without a bid and Bates asked everyone to leave. Negotiations then began, with the registered bidders increasing their pre-auction offer of $3.8 million to $4 million.



Related Article Property market It’s a buyers’ market, but property buyers just vanished The vendors advised they were open to that offer. However, the unregistered party, who was still present at the property, then made a counteroffer of $4,020,000. The vendor decided to take the original offer from the registered bidders. The property had a guide of $3.8 million and a reserve of $4,050,000. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



“The vendors were happy with their decision,” said Bates. “I said, ‘You could have gone with the higher offer.’ “[The vendor] said, ‘I could see they were ready and here to register, and I was happy with that price.’” The property has multiple living areas, including an alfresco living space and pool. Domain The vendors plan to move closer to their adult children on the lower north shore. The property was one of 600 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week.



In Glebe, a single bid of $4.2 million secured the keys to a four-bedroom terrace in the prestigious Toxteth Estate. Two parties registered on the day to bid for 20 Toxteth Road but when the auction opened, no one raised their paddles. The auctioneer then placed a vendor’s bid of $4.1 million. A bidder, an investor with an interest in blue chip property, offered a further $100,000 and the property sold. The property had a reserve of $4.2 million, the same as the guide. Sales agent for BresicWhitney Inner West Chris Nunn said some buyers saw current market conditions as an opportunity to bid for a property with less competition.



The house retains many of its original features, such as patterned ceilings, but has also been renovated for contemporary living. Domain “At the moment, nerves are getting the better of people, and it’s leaving a good opening for discerning buyers who can hold their nerve to purchase at a fair price,” he said.
