World.title: International students flock to Australian universities. Here is what they study
World.content:
NationalUniversity International students flock to Australian universities. Here is what they study Siena Fagan September 19, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Luis Guzman grew up with Australia in his sights. After watching the film Kangaroo Jack as a six-year-old in Guatemala, he told his mother the country would one day be his home. At 18 he came down under to travel. At 28 he enrolled in a master’s degree in event management at the UTS Business School. Luis Guzman moved to Sydney from Guatemala to study. “The quality of life, the opportunities that I can have here … I think it’s really nice.” Wolter Peeters Now in his final semester, Guzman has high hopes for the future. He dreams of working in Formula 1 racing, and meanwhile is developing his entrepreneurship skills. He hopes to stay in Australia after graduating. The opportunities, he says, are unparalleled.



“I know that in Australia, if I work hard and I put effort in, I can achieve more.” Related Article Updated

Immigration Labor’s tough new migration rules target backpackers, foreign students and overstayers Guzman is one of hundreds of thousands of international students who come to Australian universities to pursue their dreams. Since 2021, international student enrolments at Australian universities increased by 46.2 per cent – from 314,619 to 460,090. Those numbers have been a primary target of the federal government’s plans, revealed on Thursday, to curb net migration from about 300,000 to 225,000 next year. It aims to curb the number of international students by targeting visa hopping and by reducing the influx of family members.



The most popular broad field of study for international students enrolled in Australian universities was management and commerce, accounting for 120,136 enrolments in 2026. Information technology ranked second, followed by society and culture. The most studied management and commerce disciplines were business and management (61,222 enrolments), followed by accounting (14,566 enrolments). Speaking before the migration changes were unveiled, International Education Association of Australia chief executive Phil Honeywood said those degrees had broad appeal to international neighbours, offering in-demand skills taught in a native English setting. “The overwhelming number of overseas students doing such courses come from family businesses where the parents would like their child to learn business practices in a native English-speaking country, and … go home to run the family business or to start in a larger corporation.”



Honeywood said on Thursday the reforms were “really a mixed bag” for international students but the changes were unlikely to impact the types of degrees that were most popular. Related Article Exclusive

University From Concord to the country: The student search for greener pastures in an AI world Guzman, who hopes to remain in Australia after his degree, says the variety of skills taught in business degrees made them desirable for domestic and international students. “People just want to gain … skills for management and skills for HR and skills for marketing,” he says. “You have more options whenever you’re looking for a job.” Guzman understood the need for the government to balance immigration with domestic matters but he was worried such reforms would affect perceptions of international students.



“If I talk with my friends who are international students, I think they are going to feel anxious about their futures,” he said. While management and commerce has maintained its position as the most-studied field by international students over the past five years, its contribution to enrolments dropped by 21.5 per cent. Honeywood says this coincides with the removal of finance and accounting from the Australian government’s skills-in-demand list. He warns that maintaining international access to these degrees is key to Australia’s soft power diplomacy in the region, as many neighbouring countries have relied on Australia for its educational experts for decades. There has also been an uptick in international enrolments in other fields.



In the past five years, enrolments in broad education degrees shot up 297.7 per cent – from 12,026 students in 2021 to 47,824 in 2026. Teacher education increased from the ninth-most-popular ‘narrow field of study’ in 2021 to the second in 2026. This discipline encompasses early childhood, secondary education and teaching English as a second language. Phil Honeywood, chief executive of International Education Association Australia, at Melbourne University in 2020. The most-studied teaching degree in 2026 is early childhood, making up 36.9 per cent of international enrolments. The biggest increase for a specific teaching degree in the past five years was in vocational education and training, which increased from 159 students in 2021 to 4047 in 2026. Honeywood says a portion of this increase is driven by education degrees being classified as a skill in demand by the Australian government, making postgraduate education diplomas a migration pathway.



Related Article Immigration With their families barred, international students say they face an agonising choice “We all live in hope that teaching vacancies and childcare and other skills supply shortages will be met,” he said. “There’s a dichotomy between, on the one hand, skills in demand that Australia needs, and the motivation of some overseas students as to why they’re actually enrolling in that course. “We’re heavily reliant as a nation on overseas students who’ll be our future childcare workers and, indeed, our future aged care workers.” As international student enrolments fluctuate, Honeywood says there is “no secret recipe for the right proportion” of international to domestic students.



“It’s a very powerful opportunity … to have this diversity of people and cultures.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Five years, millions of dollars: The battle to fix a defective Sydney building
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Andrew and Lisa Cook moved into their new apartment in Baulkham Hills on December 12, 2020, they thought they were getting the dream: a modern unit, a sprawling balcony with views of the city skyline and access to shops at the base of their building. Just 23 days later, the dream became a nightmare: the company that developed the building collapsed. Ten months after that, the state’s building regulator identified serious defects in the development, including one that was labelled a “hazard to human life”. The Cooks were shocked. They didn’t know who would be responsible for fixing the defects, and what it meant for their new home. “[We were] a bit scared because they didn’t know what was going to happen at the time,” Lisa said. Andrew and Lisa Cook on their balcony, which is still being repaired. Jessica Hromas Known then as the Modena, the four-tower project was developed by Hills Shoppingtown Pty Ltd, a subsidiary of Dyldam Group – once one of NSW’s biggest apartment builders before it collapsed with debts of half a billion dollars. There were 230 apartments and plans for a retail precinct in a project designed to combine luxury and comfort. When the receivers for the development and the building regulator visited the site, they found it was far from that vision. In addition to non-compliant waterproofing, an awning in danger of collapse, balconies without water overflows, the glass elevator – designed as a key feature for the project – had already rusted and was leaning slightly.



For five years, the Cooks and a handful of other residents have lived in a construction zone as millions of dollars were funnelled into rectifying defects. The scale of the work is so significant that the Cooks have lived in another unit since January while work on their own apartment continues. “There’s been a lot of noise for quite a few years, so that’s sort of a bad thing, but I keep thinking they’re doing it, they’re fixing it, it’s not costing us any money,” Andrew said. The Baulkham Hills building, formerly known as the Modena. Jessica Hromas. The stairs to the lower lever remain fenced-off while work continues. Jessica Hromas “We’re one of the fortunate buildings in Sydney.” Buying a home with defects is not an uncommon experience in NSW. Building Commission NSW ordered major developer Bathla Group, which entered voluntary administration last month, to fix serious defects in two of its developments. It’s left those who purchased off the plan uncertain if they would ever move in. So when developers collapse owing millions of dollars, how do you fix a defective building?



The $70 million fix When McGrathNicol was appointed the receiver of the Modena development in 2021, partner Jason Ireland said they were told the project was 95 per cent complete. But what was anticipated to be a quick fix soon became a mammoth project that would take years and $70 million to rectify defects – bringing the total cost of completing the development to $185 million. Ireland describes the project as being a bit like an onion, “in that when you peeled back [layers], you found more problems that made you cry,” he said. More than 60 defects were found throughout the four buildings. McGrathNicol’s Jason Ireland said it has cost $70 million to fix the defects left behind by the original builder. Jessica Hromas Fixing the overflow holes in balconies was considered a simple job. Then the tiles began to be removed, and a new problem appeared: No one could identify what waterproofing material had been used. Ireland said it was clear it was a non-compliant product. “We eventually got to the conclusion that the only way to actually get the sign-off in the end was to rip up the balconies, replace all of the waterproofing, and replace all of the tiling, which is a lot because there’s over 200 apartments,” he said. Through it all, the four buildings have been partially occupied. In a Tetris-like process, residents had to be moved from their apartments to another in the development to allow for each to be rectified in turn.



When the Herald visited last month, work was continuing. The elevator had been replaced, the stairs to the lower level remained fenced off and some balconies – including the Cooks’ – were still under repair. The new elevator, which the replaced the original, rusted one. Jessica Hromas Ireland said there is light at the end of the tunnel, with 90 per cent of the defects fixed. Building Commission NSW lifted its building work rectification and prohibition order for the development, which has been rebranded as “Alfresco Quarter”. An interim occupation certificate remains in place. In May, the commission accepted a voluntary undertaking from McGrathNicol, which will provide additional independent oversight of the development. About 50 per cent of the apartments have now been sold, and the empty retail precinct has been acquired by property services provider Mintus. The lower level will have a gym, and cafés and restaurants are planned for the upper level. Work will be completed next year. An artist’s impression of what the cafe at the Baulkham Hills development would look like. Alfresco Quarter Ireland said: “The silver lining to the cloud is that if you buy a property in this building, you know it’s been through the highest of verification standards by the building commissioner’s team. They have been through it with a fine tooth comb.



“Some of the people [living] here have been to hell and back, but importantly, back.” The lucky ones Related Article Exclusive

Bathla collapse Developer Bathla told to fix defects as it staves off liquidation It’s been a difficult, drawn-out process for the Cooks, but they’ve remained positive and hope to move back into their own apartment before the end of the year. “This is our forever home,” Andrew said. “And the tiles they put down are much nicer than the old ones.” Despite the stress it’s caused, the Cooks consider themselves lucky; unlike many other owners living in buildings with defects built by collapsed developers, the family didn’t have to fund the repairs. At the Vicinity complex in Canterbury, owners are still picking up the tab after major structural defects were discovered in parts of the 276-apartment complex, which was built by collapsed developer Toplace.

World.title: ‘Extraordinary step’: Shark that killed 63-year-old Perth swimmer to be destroyed
World.content:
NationalWASharks ‘Extraordinary step’: Shark that killed 63-year-old Perth swimmer to be destroyed Rebecca Peppiatt September 19, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The shark that killed a 63-year-old swimmer at Sorrento Beach on Friday will be caught and destroyed, in what Fisheries minister Jackie Jarvis said was “an extraordinary step”. The man was swimming “very close to shore” when he was witnessed being pulled under water by a large white shark at approximately 10.30am on Friday. Lifesavers raced to rescue the man but were unsuccessful in locating him. Forensics police and specialist detectives taped off a section of the car park on Friday. Hannah Murphy A witness told this masthead there was blood in the water, while the swimmer who had accompanied the victim had to be consoled by rescuers once he got to shore. On Saturday morning Jarvis said it was “an incredibly sad and distressing incident” before saying the shark was later located by water police and “positively identified as the shark involved in the incident”.



Related Article Updated

Tragedy Police continue search for missing Perth swimmer after horror shark attack “WA police requested that the shark be captured to assist with the recovery of potential coronial evidence,” she said. “Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack, and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if it could be captured.” Jarvis said the circumstances of the attack were “exceptional” and that the rare catch and kill order was carefully considered, weighing up the safety of water police and fisheries officers involved in recovery efforts and the response to the incident. “Capture gear was deployed by fisheries officers yesterday,” she said.



Related Article Sharks Government must step in over escalating shark attacks in WA, experts warn “However, at this stage, the shark has not been captured. A WA Police water police vessel remains on the water today. Police conducted a search of the shoreline this morning, and beaches in the area remain closed.” Jarvis said the shark was not one of around 300 tagged sharks in WA waters before claiming the state has a comprehensive shark mitigation program. “We will never be able to mitigate all of the threats,” she said. “And people make an informed decision when they go into the water because it was so close to the shore, because of the circumstances, and because we were able to identify the shark, is why I have taken somewhat extraordinary step to issue a catch and kill authorisation for this shark.”



She said the government’s shark mitigation plan had been added to in recent years with the inclusion of beach emergency number signs, increased tagging efforts and the SharkSmart app. “Of course, we will regularly review this, and we’ll see what more we can do,” she said. “I cannot remove the risk of of all apex predators in the ocean, but we want to make sure the public have as much information as possible, and we will of course review what we’re doing and seeing if we can do more.”

World.title: Caulfield track review ordered after safety dramas on group 1 race day
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing Caulfield track review ordered after safety dramas on group 1 race day Danny Russell September 19, 2026 — 3:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Track safety dramas have forced Melbourne Racing Club into a review of its Caulfield Racecourse just four weeks out from one of the major races of the spring carnival. Last-minute maintenance was ordered at Caulfield on Saturday after a group of jockeys identified a stretch of dangerous ground along the home straight before the group 1 program had even started. Ground staff move running rails at Caulfield on Saturday to avoid a dangerous stretch of the track. Getty Images Stewards ordered the inside running rail be moved out an extra 4m in the home straight to take the unsafe surface out of play. Caulfield will host the $3 million group 1 guineas on October 10 and the $6 million Caulfield Cup the following Saturday. Almost 30,000 people attended last year’s Caulfield Cup.



Related Article Victorian racing Legal feuds, boardroom battles and a 24-year-old taking on racing’s elite “During a routine track inspection on Saturday morning, an issue was identified with a number of the standard track-repair ‘plugs’ near the inside rail, some of which appeared uneven or loose,” the MRC said in a statement. Pre-race images showed jockeys being able to pick up and move large clumps of turf. Plugs are used to fill divots and small holes in a track’s surface. The MRC came under fire several times from punters during the winter months for the standard of its tracks at Caulfield and Sandown. The surface had raced better in recent weeks. Two barrier attendants were lucky to escape injury in June when starting barriers were accidentally reversed into a lake in the middle of Sandown Racecourse. They were later fished out with a crane.



Racegoers were shocked to hear of the rail being moved on a race day so close to the Caulfield Cup carnival. “It would probably be a good idea for MRC to change their name back to VATC … Very Amateur Turf Club as the legend of racing writers used to refer to it,” prominent owner Nick Williams posted on X. The Caulfield rail is moved before the first race on Saturday because of track safety concerns. Getty Images Jockey Patrick Moloney told Racing.com the track surface was fine after the pre-race alterations, but the changes had made it “really awkward” to navigate for riders. “You go from a normal position to an obscure position in the straight,” he said.



Victorian Jockeys Association CEO Matthew Hyland said a number of jockeys had identified safety concerns before the first race and told stewards of their concerns. He said they were happy with the outcome. View post on X Stewards put out a statement, saying they had identified several areas of concern. “Out of an abundance of caution, stewards directed that the moveable rail be placed out an additional four metres in the straight (350m to the winning post) to ensure the areas identified will not be in use for today’s meeting,” a Racing Victoria statement said. The MRC said the use of plugs was a standard maintenance practice undertaken regularly at racecourses.



“With the safety of horses and riders paramount, the decision was made to move the rail out as a precautionary measure,” the club said. “The Melbourne Racing Club will undertake a review immediately following today’s meeting.”

World.title: Trump’s love of AI is more complicated than it looks
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

President Donald Trump made clear in the past week that he views fears that artificial intelligence could lead to mass extinction as a “HOAX”, and that he sees opponents of data centres as people who “want to end up being backwards and poor”. People who have discussed the subject with Trump say his outbursts are rooted in worries that if the artificial intelligence boom fuelling the American economy slows down, the market could crash and recession could quickly follow. Tesla chief Elon Musk, US President Donald Trump, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. Monique Westermann His anti-regulatory, anti-slowdown outbursts have been encouraged by a slice of Silicon Valley’s most influential voices. Chief among them has been David Sacks, a venture capitalist who interceded to weaken an executive order in May that would have required safety reviews of new AI models. Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia have also spoken to the president. All have advised Trump that the bigger risk is being overtaken by Chinese competitors. But inside the administration, the debate is far more complex, and there are other voices in Trump’s ear, urging caution.



The more cautious tone inside the White House reflects a growing concern that despite the strategic challenge posed by China, a summer of AI surprises has raised the prospect of risks that were often dismissed a year ago as the wild talk of “doomers”. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘I am the Hoax Buster’: Trump takes on America with seven-post rant promoting AI, data centres Now, even the biggest AI boosters in the administration concede that AI-fueled hacks into infrastructure, biological threats, attacks on nuclear command-and-control systems, job losses and global financial instability seem more possible than they did before AI agents went rogue. The issue of AI safety is expected to come to a head this weekend as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent meets in New York with his Chinese counterpart to set the agenda for Trump’s visit in Washington with President Xi Jinping of China, which starts Wednesday. Bessent is trying to negotiate some kind of agreement between Trump and Xi that would suggest the two countries are working together on mutual AI safety concerns. But already, officials say, some of the most expansive ideas being discussed among AI safety experts, including an agreement on safety standards and reviews of forthcoming Chinese and American AI models before their public release, are unlikely to be part of any initial accord. One diplomat involved in the effort said he believed “the best we can hope for” is the creation of some kind of US-China working group that might build on a Biden-era agreement with China to bar the use of artificial intelligence in decisions about the employment of nuclear weapons. But that does not begin to get at the complexity of the problem of unpredictable AI-driven agents, which took the industry and the government by surprise this northern summer.



Related Article Analysis

China relations ‘Whoever wins AI, wins’: How the world’s two most powerful leaders can find common ground Nor does it get to the fundamental issues surrounding imposing safeguards on frontier models. The United States could go its own way and impose mandatory reviews of the safety of new, American-generated models, but Trump and his aides believe that would effectively drive the global market to Chinese largely open-source alternatives. And because those open-source models can be modified by users — who could remove the “guardrails” meant to limit their powers — a safety review may mean little. Trump wants to meet with the AI executives next week, according to company representatives. (A White House official said Thursday that nothing was on the schedule as of now.) If that session happens, it would presumably include some of the AI executives who, in recent days, have been calling for the kind of slowdown in the release of new models that Trump says he opposes. Few expect Dario Amodei, a founder of Anthropic, to be among the invitees: His company’s products have been banned by the Pentagon, and he appeared to anger Trump by proposing last weekend a detailed plan for the industry to pace itself and bring in independent safety inspectors. Trump dismissed him, and denounced an unnamed class of “Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors and Leakers” who were politicising the debate over AI and undercutting American leadership. But another Anthropic founder, Tom Brown, who raises less ire in the White House, talks to officials regularly. In recent days, Trump has also talked with Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of SpaceX, both of whom endorsed Amodei’s plan to slow down, test new models for vulnerabilities and let in outside inspectors, at least in general terms.



Bessent and the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, have been increasingly concerned over the past several months that AI could cause massive disruptions across industries, including hacks into major financial institutions that could destabilise the world economy. Wiles this year began organising an informal group to think about how to deal with the risk created by new, more powerful models. Bessent is chief among the members of that informal group, an administration official said, but other experts are called in depending on the topic. President Trump is saying that Democrats using AI concern as a way to score points is a hoax, just like their claims that climate change would kill everyone in six years. Elizabeth Huston, a White House spokesperson. The White House pointed to Wiles’ social media post on May 6 as the foundational statement of how Trump balances the risks and opportunities of the new technology. “This administration has one goal: ensure the best and safest tech is deployed rapidly to defeat any and all threats,” she wrote at the time. She said that “the White House will continue to lead an America First effort that empowers America’s great innovators, not bureaucracy, to drive safe deployment of powerful technologies while keeping America safe”. Asked about Trump’s accusation that AI risk is overblown, Elizabeth Huston, a White House spokesperson, said, “President Trump is saying that Democrats using AI concern as a way to score points is a hoax, just like their claims that climate change would kill everyone in six years.” She added that Trump had reversed the “failed approach” of the Biden administration, which she said had “stifled innovation, hurt consumers and nearly cost America its competitive edge over China.”



But at a moment when AI has emerged as arguably the most important long-term issue for the country’s economic health and national security, in the Trump White House there is no single person in charge of coordinating AI policy. Marco Rubio, in his role as national security adviser, is rarely discussed as a player on these issues. The White House eliminated the post of deputy national security adviser for cyber and emerging technologies created during the Biden administration. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI And the national cyber director, a position created by Congress, has only indirect authority over artificial intelligence issues. The current director is Sean Cairncross, a former senior official at the Republican National Committee, who was light on cyber and AI experience before taking the post. And there has been a purging of some technical expertise, including at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, part of the Department of Homeland Security. (The acting director of CISA said last week that the agency was hiring about 250 new employees after shedding about 1000 jobs — roughly one-third of its workforce — since Trump returned to the White House.) As a result, AI has become the administration’s latest hot potato, with various officials dipping in and out of influence depending on the topic, or the day of the week. Still, there are other officials, particularly in the much-shrunken National Security Council and the Energy Department, who share Amodei’s fears about charging ahead with new, more powerful models amid growing evidence that they are increasingly unpredictable.

World.title: ‘Skewed perception of market conditions’: First home buyer bids $190k for outer east unit which sold for $492k
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘Skewed perception of market conditions’: First home buyer bids $190k for outer east unit which sold for $492k Caroline Zielinski September 19, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After a bold first bid of $190,000, a first home buyer missed out on a two-bedroom unit in Clayton, in the outer east, which ultimately sold for $492,000. Listed with a range of $480,000 to $520,000, the home at 2/6 Wright Street, featuring separate living and dining areas and generous bedrooms, had a reserve price of $490,000. McGrath Clayton lead agent Elroy Malowney said the ambitious bidder “tried an opening bid of $190,000, likely based on a perception that the market has dropped significantly. They did not bid again after that”. The offer was countered by a second bidder, who offered $460,000, which was again countered by a vendor bid of $490,000, Malowney said. The second bidder, also a first home buyer, purchased the property for a final bid of $492,000.



Related Article Melbourne house prices The one choice that can cost Melbourne home buyers an extra $110,000 Malowney said that buyers seemed to have a “skewed perception of market conditions”. “After recent news reports mentioned a drop in the Melbourne market... many ‘buyers assume they can discount property prices by another 15 to 20 per cent below the quoted range, failing to realise that those price adjustments have already been factored in,” he said. The property was one of 929 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. A young professional woman paid $941,000 for an inner-city Melbourne apartment at auction after first submitting a private offer of $860,000.



The spacious, three-bedroom apartment at 143/283 Spring Street, comes with floor-to-ceiling windows and is only a three-minute walk from Parliament Station. Ray White Southbank listing agent Tommy-Lee Davies said the auction drew four bidders, including investors and upsizers, all after a centrally located unit. The property had a price guide of between $850,000 to $900,000 and a reserve of $880,000. In the end, the contest was between the professional woman, a lawyer, and an overseas investor family, he said.



Related Article Property prices The suburbs where house sellers want up to $1.75m more than buyer budgets “The investor kept placing larger bids of up to $9000 raises, while the owner-occupier kept countering with $1000 increments until the investor gave up,” Davies said. Davies has noticed buyers more confident with lower offers. “Buyers come in assuming they have all the power and expect bargain prices,” he said. Davies said Melbourne’s one-bedroom apartment market was doing well, especially among investors, due to offering strong rental yields. “Otherwise, many campaigns are struggling for buyer numbers. Buyers are cautious, taking their time, and acting as if they are the only buyer in the entire market.”

World.title: An activist depicted a female councillor as Miss Piggy. A judge says it’s political speech
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLocal council An activist depicted a female councillor as Miss Piggy. A judge says it’s political speech Lachlan Abbott September 19, 2026 — 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A self-styled council watchdog has won an appeal against an intervention order granted to an inner-eastern Melbourne mayor after a judge ruled his social media posts, including one depicting her as Miss Piggy, were protected political speech. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston hailed the County Court judgment released late on Friday as a win for democratic scrutiny of elected officials, as it overturned the court order Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr was granted last year. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston (left) and Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr. Simon Schluter, Luis Enrique Ascui Magistrate Michelle Hodgson previously found “the gendered and personal undertones” of Hurlston’s posts and text messages to Sehr in recent years “crossed the line from fair commentary into targeted ridicule” that was intended to cause mental harm. But County Court judge Julie Clayton disagreed and on Friday threw out the personal safety intervention order against Hurlston.



Clayton found the magistrate’s interpretation of political commentary protected under Victorian law was too narrow and Hurlston’s posts were primarily motivated by concern about the City of Stonnington’s governance. Related Article CBD Council activist apologises – twice – after accusing councillor of sexual harassment “The personal integrity of politicians, quite apart from their policy positions, is a legitimate subject for news and current affairs,” Clayton wrote. On Saturday, Hurlston criticised Stonnington chief executive Dale Dickson for claiming the magistrate’s initial ruling was a “landmark court decision” before it was overturned. “The council’s triumphal public statement now stands as a monument to poor judgment,” Hurlston said.



“This case should concern every journalist, activist, ratepayer and community watchdog. If robust criticism of public officials can be repackaged as a personal safety matter, democratic scrutiny itself is placed at risk.” Sehr compiled an almost 500-page dossier of posts from Hurlston’s Stonnington Council Watch Facebook page and other messages that she said had escalated to personal harassment. The judge accepted Sehr (pictured) felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but found her fear wasn’t the same as a fear for her safety. Ruby Alexander Clayton said Hurlston was “an enormous nuisance” to Sehr and some posts were hurtful, including one that accused the mayor of using her mother’s death to avoid questions. She accepted Sehr felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but added: “That sort of fear, however, is not the same as a fear for one’s safety.”



The judge ultimately found Hurlston’s posts were published without legal malice and thus an intervention order could not be made. The previous order restricted Hurlston’s online commentary towards Sehr and barred him from coming within two metres of her. “Mr Hurlston may not abide by a journalistic code of conduct in relation to fair and balanced commentary,” Clayton said. “This does not mean he is not entitled to the protection afforded by [the Personal Safety Intervention Orders Act].” She added: “It is permissible for Mr Hurlston to publish, filled with ill-will, animosity, spite and hostility if the actuating motive for the publication is not improper.” Clayton said the images Hurlston posted of Miss Piggy and a cartoon of a stereotypical housewife could be seen as demeaning or derogatory towards Sehr.



Hurlston said the Miss Piggy image referred to Sehr as a “muppet” – a common derogatory term in politics that was not intended to attack her appearance. Related Article City life Toorak councillor banned over ‘obscene’ remarks after heated menorah debate The judge acknowledged Sehr felt humiliated, but was not persuaded Hurlston was primarily motivated by something other than his political opinion that the mayor was “not up to the job”. The judge also said the housewife cartoon was not substantially different from thousands of other political caricatures. “Women in public life generally, and politics in particular are often unfairly targeted in relation to their appearance,” Clayton wrote.



“While one might bemoan this sorry state of affairs it is not a state of affairs that the act was intended to address.” Sehr told The Age she was awaiting further legal advice after Friday’s decision. In a statement on Saturday, Stonnington chief executive Dale Dickson also said: “I will continue to actively support and protect the safety of council employees and councillors, particularly women, including of course Mayor Sehr.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Vendor rejects higher offer to sell Northern Beaches home for $4 million
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Vendor rejects higher offer to sell Northern Beaches home for $4 million Robyn Willis September 19, 2026 — 1:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A vendor accepted a bid of $4 million when her Balgowlah property passed in on Saturday, $20,000 less than she was offered by another party. Two parties expressed interest in four-bedroom 28 New Street West earlier in the week, sales agent for Cunninghams Real Estate, Georgi Bate said. But one group, a family from interstate, advised her on Friday that while they would attend, they would not be registering. The other party, a couple with adult children, were the sole registered bidders and said they would rather negotiate privately after the property passed in. On that advice, auctioneer Emma Brown-Garrett passed it in without a bid and Bates asked everyone to leave. Negotiations then began, with the registered bidders increasing their pre-auction offer of $3.8 million to $4 million.



Related Article Property market It’s a buyers’ market, but property buyers just vanished The vendors advised they were open to that offer. However, the unregistered party, who was still present at the property, then made a counteroffer of $4,020,000. The vendor decided to take the original offer from the registered bidders. The property had a guide of $3.8 million and a reserve of $4,050,000. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



“The vendors were happy with their decision,” said Bates. “I said, ‘You could have gone with the higher offer.’ “[The vendor] said, ‘I could see they were ready and here to register, and I was happy with that price.’” The property has multiple living areas, including an alfresco living space and pool. Domain The vendors plan to move closer to their adult children on the lower north shore. The property was one of 600 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week.



In Glebe, a single bid of $4.2 million secured the keys to a four-bedroom terrace in the prestigious Toxteth Estate. Two parties registered on the day to bid for 20 Toxteth Road but when the auction opened, no one raised their paddles. The auctioneer then placed a vendor’s bid of $4.1 million. A bidder, an investor with an interest in blue chip property, offered a further $100,000 and the property sold. The property had a reserve of $4.2 million, the same as the guide. Sales agent for BresicWhitney Inner West Chris Nunn said some buyers saw current market conditions as an opportunity to bid for a property with less competition.



The house retains many of its original features, such as patterned ceilings, but has also been renovated for contemporary living. Domain “At the moment, nerves are getting the better of people, and it’s leaving a good opening for discerning buyers who can hold their nerve to purchase at a fair price,” he said.
